articles.title: Miley Cyrus Tearfully Pays Tribute to Dolly Parton With “Jolene” Performance at Hollywood Bowl: “Me and Dolly, We Are Eternal”
articles.author: McKinley Franklin

paras.en: Miley Cyrus broke down in tears at her Hollywood Bowl performance Friday night during a moving tribute to her godmother, the late Dolly Parton.

The singer projected a photo of the country music icon as the beginning notes of her iconic song “Jolene” played. The Grammy winner told the crowd that one of the things that inspired her to play the venue was the memory of the only time she was able to sit and enjoy a Parton show at the Hollywood Bowl.

She recalling telling her “Aunt Dolly” that for once, she just wanted to sit in the crowd and enjoy her like everyone else. Cyrus began, “If she had it her way, and she was playing a show, I’d be standing right beside her in a matching costume. And so when I was coming to the show at the Bowl to see her, I said, you know, ‘I would love a night where I can just experience you. I can just enjoy you like the rest of the world has gotten to.'”
The “Flowers” singer said her godmother responded by saying, “Okay, Miley,” but Cyrus joked “that never means okay.”

Instead of having Cyrus onstage to perform alongside her, Parton instead opened the show with “The Best of Both Worlds,” Cryus’ hit track from Hannah Montana: “All of a sudden, Dolly enters, but I hear ‘The Best of Both Worlds.’ Yeah, Dolly opened performing Hannah Montana.”

“But that’s just not the end of that story,” she continued. “And she goes, like a proud aunt, ‘I don’t know if y’all know this, but my goddaughter is Hannah Montana, and she’s actually here tonight, but she’s sitting out in her seat. She didn’t want anyone to bug her. She said she just wanted to watch the show,’ which defeated the entire purpose of the conversation that we had just had, because absolutely no one was aware that I was at the concert until she drew an obnoxious amount of attention to it.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: “But like so many things Dolly did, I didn’t understand at the time,” Cyrus said, adding that she could feel Parton’s presence with her during her Hollywood Bowl performance.

“And I can’t fucking wait because I miss her,” Cyrus said in between tears. “Some of the greatest music that we have today was written, produced, performed by my Aunt Dolly, and this is one of those songs,” she concluded before launching into a rendition of “Jolene.”

Parton died Aug. 25, after a “brief battle with cancer,” a rep announced. She was 80. Many celebrities paid tribute to the queen of country music after her death, including Cyrus who penned a tribute, writing on Instagram, “The feeling of losing my Aunt Dolly is beyond what feels right to share.”

“I have an angel by my side. I always have. One of our last conversations was about music and metamorphosis. I will always love her and want to make her proud,” she wrote. “My heart breaks for the world, her family and friends who will miss her deeply. We’re in this loss together and we will see her in all of the most beautiful things.”
During Cyrus’ Friday night show, she also clutched a frame in the shape of a heart with an image of Parton during “Wrecking Ball,” as that was one of her favorite songs.
The Grammy winner played her first of two shows at the Hollywood Bowl on Friday. Her next performance will be on Sunday. Cyrus recently dropped her 10th studio album Bass Persuades on Sept. 18.

articles.title: Katie Zacharia out as Trump's White House press secretary

paras.en: New White House press secretary Katie Zacharia is leaving her job after just five days in the face of criticism over her performance, a White House official confirmed to CNBC on Friday.
Earlier Friday afternoon, President Donald Trump told reporters that he had just suggested to Zacharia that she quit.
"I just spoke to her about it. I said, 'Katie, is this for you?'" Trump said outside the White House.
"'If I were you, I'd reconsider,'" the president said he told Zacharia.
The White House official, who asked not to be named in order to discuss the staffing shake-up, confirmed Fox News' report that Zacharia is "transitioning" out of the press secretary role.

Zacharia's five-day tenure in the Trump administration is shorter than that of Anthony Scaramucci, who in 2017 served as White House communications director for less than 11 days. That length of time became jokingly referred to as a "Scaramucci" and was used to measure the durations of other officials who served briefly.
By that metric, Zacharia lasted one-half of one Scaramucci.
"Records are made to be broken. But I take no pleasure in other people's pain," Scaramucci said in an X post later Friday.

Zacharia, a conservative commentator who worked at Trump Media & Technology Group, had faced widespread criticism in the days since she led a short and shaky first press briefing. She also came under mounting scrutiny about her legal background.
Trump spoke to reporters before heading to Georgia for a political rally as he hopes to boost Republicans' electoral chances with just 18 days until the midterms.

But Trump's efforts to sell his agenda have been muddled in part by Zacharia, who ended her first, and only, press briefing on Tuesday after delivering halting remarks and taking questions from just three reporters.

In the less than six minutes she spent answering questions, Zacharia revealed that U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle had been asked to step down. That departure, and Zacharia's, follow those of a number of other high-ranking female officials in the Trump administration who have quit or been fired in recent months.
"You know, she's been treated very rough. And she's a nice person," Trump said of Zacharia outside the White House.

He accused the media of treating her "very badly" and said that even Fox News TV host Sean Hannity, a supporter of the administration, was "a little bit tough" on Zacharia during her appearance on his show Thursday night.

Hannity, after calling Zacharia's debut briefing "widely panned," had asked about her past claims about her legal work in light of reports that she never passed a bar exam. Zacharia has defended identifying herself as a lawyer, drawing a distinction between that label and calling herself an "attorney."
Hannity pointed out that Zacharia had called herself an attorney in multiple social media posts. "I think they were retweets, and I corrected the record," she replied.

Trump called Zacharia "an attorney" in his Oct. 9 Truth Social post announcing her selection to replace Karoline Leavitt, who left the Trump administration in late August. Zacharia's first day was Columbus Day.

White House officials had defended Zacharia earlier this week. "Up and down the White House, everyone has been thoroughly impressed with Katie in just a few short days on the job," White House communications director Steven Cheung said in an X post Wednesday.
"At the end of this second term, she'll be remembered as one of the all-time greats," Cheung wrote.

CNN chief White House correspondent Kaitlan Collins, however, reported Friday that Trump was "embarrassed by the coverage of Zacharia's briefing and when he polled other aides about her, Zacharia had few allies willing to stand up for her or defend her performance."

"She's been treated, I would say, pretty nastily," Trump said of Zacharia in Friday's remarks outside the White House. "And I said to Katie just two minutes ago, I said, 'Katie, you know, you don't have to do this if you don't want.'"
Asked if he would keep her in the role, Trump said, "I'm going to let her make that decision."

articles.title: Apple’s $1,999 iPhone Duo puts the company's status-symbol power to the test

paras.en: Apple's iPhone Duo, its most expensive iPhone ever, went up for preorder Friday, with launch-day pickup inventory selling out and some online delivery estimates already slipping into late January.
The company said in a statement that the preorder demand was "nothing short of extraordinary."
"We are working hard to get this revolutionary new product into customers' hands as quickly as possible, and we will continue accepting orders online," Apple said.

Apple's first foldable phone starts at $1,999 and passes $3,000 at the 2TB storage tier. It is the biggest change to the physical design of the iPhone in years and establishes an entirely new price point above the Pro and Pro Max.
The early rush offers a first glimpse at the demand behind Apple's bet: Whether a dramatic new design can persuade customers to spend more and push the iPhone even further as a status symbol.

But analysts who spoke with CNBC said Apple's bet is not that foldables suddenly become a mass-market product. It is that a relatively small group of its highest-spending customers can become significantly more valuable.

Foldables are expected to make up just over 2% of global smartphone units this year but nearly 7% of industry revenue, according to IDC. By 2030, IDC expects the category to account for 10% of smartphone revenue while still representing only about 3% of units.
That gap between volume and value is central to Apple's opportunity.
"Duo is fast becoming an aspirational foldable," IDC's Nabila Popal told CNBC, comparing its appeal with Apple's broader position as an aspirational smartphone brand.

Popal, global senior research director for the Consumer Device Team at IDC, said the technology itself is not necessarily the breakthrough. Foldable Android phones have existed for years. What's new is Apple bringing that form factor to the enormous base of consumers already invested in the iPhone ecosystem.

Apple itself has been exploring the form factor for more than a decade. In 2011, Ternus and five other Apple engineers filed a patent application for foldable electronic devices, according to a recent Time profile.
"It's not that it's a breakthrough or new technology, but it's from Apple," Popal said.
The Duo could also prove more accessible than some industry watchers had anticipated.
Anshel Sag, an analyst at Moor Insights who attended Apple's launch event, said many expected the foldable iPhone to start between $2,400 and $2,500.
Apple coming in at $1,999, Sag said, suggests the company "wants a lot of share."
Sag expects the Duo to become "very much a status symbol" during the holiday season and potentially into next year.
That status appeal could be reinforced by scarcity.
Counterpoint Research Director Tarun Pathak told CNBC the firm expects initial demand to exceed supply.

Apple has an installed base of roughly 1.4 billion iPhones, he noted, meaning even a small percentage of early adopters could overwhelm the roughly 6 million or fewer units Counterpoint expects to be available in the near term.
IDC also expects supply to be constrained initially because of the complexity of the device and Apple's manufacturing and quality standards.
"Exclusivity is part of the current appeal," Popal said.
And Apple has made explicit luxury plays before.

When the first Apple Watch launched, the company offered the 18-karat gold Edition starting at $10,000. Apple also formed a long-running partnership with Hermès around premium watch bands and designs.

That push came during the tenure of Angela Ahrendts, the former Burberry CEO who joined Apple in 2014 to lead retail and online stores, as the company experimented with bringing more of the language and presentation of luxury fashion into its stores and products.
The Duo takes that idea into Apple's largest product business.
IDC expects Apple to ship roughly 7 million units this year, or roughly 3% of Apple's total shipments in 2026.

Popal, the IDC analyst, forecasts Duo shipments could grow another 70% next year. That would give Apple roughly 40% of the global foldable market and would make it the category's largest player, surpassing Samsung and Huawei.
According to her forecast, Apple could ship as many Duos in the next six months as the previous category leaders did in all of 2025.
But the more important number for Apple may not be units.

A large share of Duo customers are expected to be existing iPhone owners, analysts said, including consumers who otherwise might have purchased a Pro Max and are now trading up to a device costing hundreds of dollars more.
Others could add the Duo as a second smartphone, with Apple's ecosystem allowing users to move relatively seamlessly between it and their primary iPhone.

Popal said that migration from roughly $1,200 premium iPhones to a device starting at nearly $2,000 should provide a "healthy boost" to Apple's revenue even if overall volumes remain relatively small.

The bank expects the Duo to have a disproportionate impact on iPhone revenue because of its much higher average selling price, even as overall iPhone shipments are expected to remain roughly flat next year.
JPMorgan said the iPhone 18 cycle is increasingly likely to be driven by price and product mix rather than unit growth.
D.A. Davidson analyst Gil Luria said Apple needs the Duo to succeed as it comes up against a difficult set of earnings comps with its strongest upgrade cycle in years.
"Without an uplift from Duo, they may experience some pretty pedestrian revenue growth," Luria told CNBC.
The device gives Apple several ways to generate that uplift, he added.

It raises the company's average selling price by capturing die-hard Apple customers who might otherwise have bought a Pro Max. It could bring in some consumers who previously bought folding Android phones because Apple did not offer one. And it could create a halo around the rest of the iPhone lineup.
Luria said some consumers will visit Apple stores specifically to see the Duo, "but probably walk out with an iPhone or iPhone Pro at half the price."
That means the Duo can potentially help Apple even when someone decides not to buy it.
Lead times for the iPhone 18 Pro have softened in several markets compared with the prior cycle, while the more expensive Pro Max has held up better, according to JPMorgan's tracking.

Morgan Stanley has separately said its supply-chain checks are consistent with unusually early component order reductions for the Pro and Pro Max, though the firm has not yet seen evidence that those adjustments have translated into cuts to finished iPhone production.
That puts more pressure on the Duo to pull buyers toward the very top of Apple's lineup.
Apple's move toward a more expensive iPhone comes as the economics of the broader smartphone market become increasingly difficult.
Consumers are already holding on to phones for longer, and global smartphone growth is slowing.
Wayne Lam, an analyst at TechInsights, said moving the iPhone further upmarket gives Apple another way to protect the revenue generated by its most important product.
"Given that the iPhone is almost 20 years old, there really isn't anywhere else to head to, given Apple's market position," Lam told CNBC.
With smartphone sales expected to slow, he said, "moving upmarket allows Apple to maintain the all-important iPhone revenues they report every quarter."
Lam described the Duo as an aspirational or luxury product rather than something designed for the average consumer.

But unlike Apple's Vision products, he believes the foldable phone has a path toward becoming a larger category over time, particularly as artificial intelligence changes how consumers interact with their devices.
The trade-off is that pushing prices higher could also make consumers wait longer to upgrade.

Higher iPhone prices could stretch already-long upgrade cycles even further, Lam said, creating what he described as a potential negative feedback loop: devices become more expensive, consumers hold on to them longer and overall demand falls.
Still, Lam expects demand for the Duo to be high relative to its initially limited supply and said the device could "set the bar for premium iPhones moving forward."

articles.title: Analysis: Why a $2 trillion deficit and 5% Treasury yields are becoming America's biggest economic challenge

paras.en: Long-term bond yields above 5% and a $2 trillion deficit are giving Americans a taste of what a U.S. debt crisis would be like. A true emergency would hurt much more, and isn't baked in. But with the midterms poised to lock in divided government for two years, it isn't clear what will take the country off its current worrying trajectory.

Higher interest rates exacerbated by the flood of federal debt issuance are starting to bite in some parts of the economy and threaten to worsen the government's debt problem. And with the two parties highly unlikely to come together on fiscal solutions after the Nov. 3 midterms, any fixes are years off in the future.

The housing market is showing signs of slowing as the average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage hovers around 7.5%. Pending home sales fell 4% in September, Redfin said Monday, the biggest monthly drop in three years.

Mortgage rates track the 10-year Treasury yield. The 10-year has climbed 114 basis points, or hundredths of a percentage point, since the end of February through midday Friday, when the 10-year traded at 5.1%.

Several factors are pushing up the 10-year, including the war with Iran, which kicked off on Feb. 28 and precipitated the rise in long-term yields. Oil and diesel prices are up sharply, and that has bond traders asking for more yield to account for the possibility that central banks such as the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates.

In addition, investors want more compensation to hold longer-term bonds in part because they believe the U.S. government will continue to flood the market with them. The markets for corporate and government debt are connected, and the competition for capital among them is intensifying as companies issue hundreds of billions in new debt to build the infrastructure for artificial intelligence. Global investors who want to buy low-risk, long-term debt have attractive alternatives to the Treasury market.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: If the U.S. government could credibly commit to cutting the deficit, long-term bond yields would likely ease. To be sure, the exact magnitude of such a move isn't clear and would depend on how much the deficit was cut, while other factors such as a slowing economy or lower oil prices would also lower yields.

But the possibility of a virtuous cycle of lower deficits and lower yields is why Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has argued that the U.S. ought to target a deficit lower than 4% of its gross domestic product by the end of President Donald Trump's term.

There is almost no way the U.S. will hit that target. The deficit was $1.992 trillion for the 2026 fiscal year, up 12% from last year, data released Friday by the U.S. Treasury showed. That deficit amounts to approximately 6.2% of gross domestic product, based on an estimate of third-quarter GDP.

Higher rates make debt reduction tougher. If interest rates stay a half-point above the CBO's expectations, the cumulative deficit over 10 years will come in $1.9 trillion higher, the agency estimates. If rates overshoot by 1.5 points, that adds $6 trillion in deficits.
The CBO expects the 10-year Treasury to average 4.3% over that period, compared with 5.1% today. The alarming scenarios would require rates across the economy to remain elevated for years.

"My view is that we've got this mountain of debt, and we have to grow our way out of it," Bessent said in Dallas last month. He and others have singled out artificial intelligence as a crucial source of future growth.

AI could help but can't fix the problem entirely. It would take a decade of 7.2% growth to balance the budget with growth alone, according to the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, a research group that advocates for balanced budgets.

GDP growth was recently revised up for the second quarter from 1.5% to 2.2% at an annualized rate. The acceleration that quickly would get us to 7.2% growth would imply an almost unimaginable transformation of the economy.

Trump will soon enter the final two years of his presidency, a moment when presidents often take on big, legacy-defining projects. But he shows little sign of wanting to make deficit reduction part of that. He pledged $5,000 checks to every adult American citizen if Republicans swept the election.

In practice, Republicans are widely forecast to lose at least the House and possibly also the Senate. Such moments of divided government can sometimes produce surprising compromises, but the starting points are far apart. Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, Democrats' likely next House speaker, wants to reverse the $1 trillion in healthcare cuts that Congress enacted last year as part of Trump's signature legislative package.
And that's leaving aside the deep animosity between the parties.

The overall U.S. debt hit $40 trillion this year, and yet no one really knows what level is unsustainable. A full-on debt crisis likely remains much further out in the future. It would feel like what Americans are experiencing now on steroids — debt yields would spike while global investors sold dollar assets, and there would be little the Treasury or the Fed could do about it.

For now, though higher yields are also attracting investors to U.S. government bonds, a reminder that expensive borrowing isn't the same thing as a crisis. But the bottom line is that economics alone can't solve the problem. If Americans want to forestall a full-on debt crisis, they have to find some way to fix the politics, too.

articles.title: Honeybees deemphasize potential ‘misinformation’ in their waggle dances

paras.en: When a bee wants to tell its hive mates how to find a scrumptious field of flowers, it wiggles its rear end. A complicated combination of figure eight–like movements known as a waggle dance tells nearby bees what direction to fly in and how far to go. But what happens if a waggling bee is unsure of its directions?

A study published in Behavioral Ecology and Sociobiology earlier this year shows that bees amplify their communication based on how certain they are that their information is true. It seems the more confident a bee is in what it’s conveying, the more emphatically it communicates with the hive, says study lead author Karmi Oxman, a behavioral ecologist at Hebrew University of Jerusalem.

“Confidence is sort of a human-y word, but it’s useful in this context,” Oxman says. Confidence reflects the communicator’s belief in a message’s relevance or reliability, “and the dance is a self-report of the situation in the field.” This extra information also prevents the bee from accidentally misleading the hive.

If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.

The experiment started with one bee flying to a specialized feeder. This first bee, also known as the focal bee, was always met with a sugar solution. The researchers then manipulated the scenario by changing what happened after the focal bee returned to the hive and gave directions to the feeder. In the “honest” scenario, the feeder remained full, and all the bees following the directions got a sugary treat. In the “liar” scenario, the feeder was found empty. And in the “unverified” scenario, all the bees were caught before they could return to the hive and report what happened.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: When given the chance to communicate the feeder’s location to the hive again in a later experimental stage, the focal bee in the honest scenario tried harder to convince its fellows to visit the sugar source by performing more waggle dance circuits—suggesting the bee could assess the reliability of its own signal. Unverified and “liar” bees did not show that same increase; in fact, unverified bees decreased their recruitment efforts.

“For me, the big takeaway is that bees are not little robots,” says James C. Nieh, a behavioral ecologist at the University of California, San Diego, who was not involved in the study. “They’re getting information from their environment, and that [information] also includes how successful they are in communicating to their nest mates.”

Both Oxman and Nieh say they wonder what other types of communication beyond what we can see—such as chemical signals or vibrations—could be playing a role in waggle dances. Further research into how bees communicate can help with efforts to “maintain the world in a way that they can still thrive,” Nieh says.

articles.title: Everything you need to know about flu season 2026

paras.en: The beginning of fall and back-to-school time means cold virus season has arrived. Usually, colds hit as lesser-evil infections before influenza season takes over. But already, the flu is popping up early in pockets of the U.S. Here’s why that might be and everything else you need to know as we head into the dreaded annual flu season.

According to the Centers of Disease Control and Prevention’s latest FluView report, released on October 9, flu activity has been climbing since early September. Flu season in the U.S. generally begins gaining momentum in the fall, with activity peaking between December and February. But surveillance indicators show that certain strains of influenza are rising fast. The CDC’s latest data show a nationwide percent positivity rate for influenza—the percentage of all positive influenza tests—of 3.6 percent. That’s a sixfold increase compared with this time in 2025, when the rate was 0.6 percent.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Parts of the U.S. are showing much higher positive rates. The CDC splits the country up into regions, and Region 9, which includes Arizona, California, Hawaii and Nevada, had 9.5 percent positivity, according to the latest data. Experts say that is exceptionally high for this time of year.

If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.

“It’s not unheard of to see things rising at this stage,” says Andrew Pekosz, an immunologist at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. “But it’s also something that we probably shouldn’t be seeing until maybe November or December at the earliest.”

Flu can be caused by different types of influenza, including influenza A (and its subtypes) and influenza B. Usually, flu season brings a mix of types. Right now, in the areas of the country with the highest positivity rates, H1N1, a subtype of influenza A, is dominant. According to the CDC, the most recent weekly testing data showed that 98.4 percent of the positive tests indicated H1N1 and that 1.6 percent revealed H3N2, another influenza A subtype.
Still, experts say it’s too early to predict whether these spikes could signal a particularly severe winter flu season.
Will this year’s flu vaccines work well?

One of the best ways to protect yourself from the flu is to get a flu vaccine. Every year experts reformulate these vaccines depending on what strains of the virus are circulating or predicted to circulate during the coming winter season.

Whichever subtype dominates matters because it can help predict which groups will experience the greatest disease burden. It can also determine how well existing immunity will protect people, as well as how the year’s flu vaccines will perform.

H1N1 and H3N2 are both influenza A subtypes, but they are evolutionarily distinct and can affect people differently. H3N2-dominant seasons have historically been associated with particularly severe illness among older adults. H1N1, on the other hand, has had a greater effect on younger populations—but both can cause serious disease at any age.

“The version [of H1N1] that’s circulating seems to be a little bit different from the vaccine strain that we have and from H1N1 strains that have circulated before. It’s what we call an antigenic drift,” Pekosz says. That could be why the virus is emerging so early, he adds. If it can evade prior immunity, the pathogen will be easier to transmit.
But it’s still too early to know how that might influence the effectiveness of the current flu vaccines.
When is the best time to get vaccinated?
Trish Perl, a professor of internal medicine and a specialist in infectious disease at UT Southwestern Medical Center, says that right now is the best time to get a flu shot.

“Immunity from the flu vaccine is strongest for about four to six months, and we usually expect flu to peak in December or January,” Pekosz says. “So a September or October vaccination will get you through the worst part of the flu season.”

Perl agrees—she says that she often tells her people to, at the very least, get a flu vaccine before Thanksgiving. Because after that, she says, people have unlimited excuses for why they can’t find the time.
And with certain areas already seeing spikes, getting the shot earlier than usual may be best, Pekosz adds.
“The best time to get vaccinated is before you see influenza in your area,” he says.
What about the newly approved mRNA vaccine for flu?

On August 5, 2026, the Food and Drug Administration approved Moderna’s mFLUSIVA, the first mRNA seasonal influenza vaccine, for adults aged 50 and older. In a phase 3 clinical trial, the vaccine was found to be 26.6 percent more effective at preventing the flu than a standard flu shot.

FDA approval and inclusion in federal vaccination recommendations—informed by guidance by the CDC’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP)—are separate regulatory steps, however. The disruption to ACIP under the Trump administration has made incorporating newly approved vaccines into guidance more complicated.
Moderna had said the vaccine would be available at select retailers during the 2026–2027 flu season. But so far, access appears to be limited.

Experts, including Pekosz and Perl, say that if people who qualify for the new mRNA vaccine have access to it, they should consider it. “The data would suggest that if you can get the mRNA vaccine, you probably will get a stronger response to most of the components in the vaccine than if you get the standard one. But again, the standard one is pretty good as well,” Pekosz says.

He and Perl are optimistic about the potential of mRNA technology to improve flu vaccines in the future. Because mRNA vaccines can be developed and manufactured more quickly than traditional shots, scientists could wait until later in the year before selecting which influenza strains to target. That added time could help us better predict which strains will circulate during flu season—ultimately meaning more effective vaccines.

The best thing anyone can do right now is to get their flu shot as soon as possible. And if you do end up getting sick, Perl says not to forget about antivirals, such as Tamiflu, which can be very effective and, in many cases, could reduce the amount of time you are infectious.

articles.title: Here’s what scientists think about Theranos a decade after it imploded

paras.en: Around a decade ago Theranos, one of the buzziest science start-ups ever, imploded. Swamped by allegations of fraud, the actions of the company and its enigmatic CEO, Elizabeth Holmes, shone a harsh light on problems with scientific start-ups. Now scientists say these issues have only gotten worse.
In a new documentary titled You Can See Everything, filmmaker Nathan Fielder follows Holmes in the lead-up to starting a prison sentence in May 2023, after she was found guilty of fraud.

The film retraces the saga of Theranos, which claimed to have a machine that could perform hundreds of clinical tests using a single drop of blood. After years of fundraising, high-publicity support and partnerships with pharmacies to make the tests accessible, scientists and journalists revealed in 2015 that Theranos’s claims were false: there was no scientific evidence that its product worked.

If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Theranos is, in many ways, a cautionary tale and a relic of 2010s Silicon Valley. But for scientists, Theranos’s problems are anything but history.

John Ioannidis is a professor at Stanford University’s medical school and was among the first to question Theranos’s bona fides in a 2015 article. Eleven years later Ioannidis says he worries the problems of transparency and a lack of strong evidence in science and technology start-ups are, if anything, worse today.
“I feel kind of uneasy about this being presented as a sensationalist, movie-quality story [about] a single bad apple because I see very similar phenotypes to Theranos,” Ioannidis says.

Ioannidis argues that, in some ways, claims of scientific progress are a public relations game. As private companies have become increasingly powerful agents in driving research forward, the trend has shifted fields away from more traditional, publicly funded research and academia.
“Holmes is in jail, but the recipe of her success has been even more widely adopted,” he says.

Ian Papautsky, a microfluidics researcher at the University of Illinois Chicago, says that Theranos’s public downfall and time in the spotlight create a strong case for validating scientific findings. But he, too, worries that, as start-ups and private companies increasingly drive discovery, opportunities for secrecy or fraud may grow.

“Many of the start-ups are not transparent in their technology development,” he says. “On the one hand, you would argue that they have to be, because they’re trying to compete with everyone else. But that also makes it a lot easier to hide the mismanagement and all these other various issues.”

Holmes’s husband, Billy Evans, who also appears in the documentary, is himself quietly building a new blood testing company. The start-up, called Haemanthus, plans to use artificial intelligence tools to run diagnostic tests. Holmes is listed as a scientific adviser to the company, and Evans has raised millions of dollars in funding, according to NPR.
“The idea is to put the band back together and do it all again,” Evans tells Fielder in the movie.

Theranos has made it harder for academics who study blood testing or microfluidics to get funding, says Umut Gurkan, a biotechnology researcher at Case Western Reserve University. He creates blood testing products for conditions such as sickle cell anemia. Gurkan remembers going to Silicon Valley in 2015 to seek funding and being told, “We don’t invest in diagnostics anymore.”
Even as diagnostic technology has advanced, it remains difficult to bring it into markets, he says.

“Trust in science is fragile, and ‘a drop of blood’ now sounds like a scam,” Gurkan says. “Honest companies trying to save lives pay that tax. And at the end of the day, patients and real people pay the price with lack of working diagnostics and technologies that deserve to be in the market.”

As for Theranos’s claims: even after more than 10 years of advancement in clinical testing and microfluidics, its premise remains impossible, the researchers consulted for this article say—at least at the scale that Holmes promised. A drop of blood doesn’t hold nearly enough biological information to conduct the hundreds of tests that Theranos claimed.
Theranos’s mission was noble, Papautsky says, but the science did not and does not hold up.

“Doing multiplex testing on a small volume of blood is a good concept—it would be an important advancement in technology,” he says. “But having experts with the right knowledge and good management is very important, and it’s becoming more and more important these days. Expertise is not necessarily being valued as it used to be.”

articles.title: Scarred blood vessels may be one clue to APOE4’s Alzheimer’s risk
articles.author: RJ Mackenzie

paras.en: The gene APOE4 is the strongest common genetic risk factor for Alzheimer’s disease. But it’s still something of a mystery to researchers.

Now, new work suggests one way the gene variant does its dirty work. It influences the production of scar tissue throughout vital vascular connections carrying blood to and from the brain, researchers report September 24 in Cell. This process may also contribute to the buildup of the protein amyloid-beta, which is thought to be one of the first signs of Alzheimer’s disease in the brain.

APOE4 is an allele, one of three slightly different, common forms of the APOE gene, which makes a protein that helps carry fats in the bloodstream. The variant is common among people who have Alzheimer’s disease. “If you had a room of 10 people with Alzheimer’s disease, and you asked how many of those people have the APOE4 allele, six of them would,” says neuroscientist Joel Blanchard of the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai in New York City. Yet many people who carry APOE4 never develop the dementia-causing disease, leaving researchers trying to understand what the gene variant actually does to make the brain more vulnerable.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: One clue came from people who seemed unusually resilient to that risk. In 2024, researchers examined more than 3,500 people, including some who carried two copies of APOE4 but had not developed Alzheimer’s. Genetic analysis showed that they had a mutation in their DNA that meant their blood vessels had far lower levels of a protein called fibronectin, a kind of cellular superglue that assists wound healing. The reserachers suggested that too much fibronectin could make it harder for the brain to clear amyloid-beta from the brain. A buildup of those plaques is a hallmark of the disease.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: That result pushed Blanchard and his colleagues to look more closely at blood vessels. “The prevailing thought in the field is basically that the Alzheimer’s disease is so bad that the blood vessels break down,” Blanchard says. ”But we wanted to ask the question: Is it the other way around?”

Blanchard and his colleagues built an atlas that mapped gene expression — how DNA is read and converted into proteins — across the human brain vasculature at a cellular level. Stitching together data from three existing brainwide maps, their atlas represented 66,000 cells from 220 people. They team examined how this map differed in people with two copies of APOE4 compared with those with less harmful gene variants.

APOE4 carriers had fewer pericytes, starfish-shaped cells that wrap around and stabilize blood vessels. They also had higher numbers of myofibroblasts, cells normally formed during tissue injury that pump out fibronectin, the team found.

The map offered a snapshot, but it couldn’t show whether the missing pericytes were actually transforming into myofibroblasts. The researchers turned to 3-D models of human brain tissue grown from stem cells. In models carrying two copies of APOE4, pericytes began taking on the characteristics of scar-producing myofibroblasts. The transformation also offered a possible explanation for the earlier clue from resilient APOE4 carriers: Myofibroblasts produce large amounts of fibronectin. And when the researchers prevented cells in their models from producing fibronectin, amyloid accumulation dropped.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The researchers also found a possible trigger for the cellular switch. In the APOE4 models, signaling through the immune molecule TGF-beta helped drive pericytes toward the scar-producing state. Blocking that signaling in cell models and aged mice restored the proportion of blood vessels wrapped up by pericytes.

The TGF-beta data are “particularly interesting,” because inhibiting the protein reversed some of APOE4’s effects on pericytes, says Abdel Ali Belaidi, a neuroscientist at the Florey Institute of Neuroscience and Mental Health in Parkville, Australia. But TGF-beta performs many jobs throughout the body, he says, making it a difficult molecule to target safely with a drug.

And damage to the brain’s blood vessels is only one of the many ways APOE4 has been linked to Alzheimer’s. Other studies have shown that the gene variant alters inflammation and interacts with another Alzheimer’s-linked protein, tau. How all these changes lock together to link APOE4 so strongly to Alzheimer’s disease is a greater mystery than one study can solve. ”As a field, we’re all progressing toward an answer,” Blanchard says.

articles.title: Voyager 1 is nearly one light-day from Earth. What’s out there?
articles.author: Lisa Grossman

paras.en: NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft has been breaking distance records for decades. Launched almost 50 years ago, it became the farthest human-built object from Earth when it overtook the pathfinding Pioneer 10 probe in 1998. It was the first spacecraft to leave the solar system’s protective bubble, and it will be humankind’s first emissary to the stars.

The cameras on Voyager 1, along with those on its twin spacecraft, Voyager 2, captured powerful megastorms in the outer solar system, the first images of dozens of moons and never-before-seen details of the gossamer rings around Jupiter, Saturn, Neptune and Uranus. The images and data sent home have shaped theories of how the solar system formed and evolved, inspired subsequent missions and posed enough new questions to keep space scientists busy for decades.

And this month, Voyager 1 will set another big record. On November 18 at 5:16:07 a.m. Eastern Standard Time, it will become the first spacecraft to reach one light-day from Earth: the distance light travels in 24 hours. That’s a journey of 25.9 billion kilometers, or more than four times the distance from the sun to Pluto. At that point, signals from Earth will take a full day to reach Voyager 1; it will take another day to hear back.

“I just never imagined [the mission] would last that long,” says Linda Spilker, a planetary scientist at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, Calif., who began working on Voyager shortly before the probes launched in 1977. Spilker was in Cape Canaveral, Fla., for the first launch. She even planned the births of her children, now in their 40s, around mission milestones. After stepping away to lead another mission, she is now back as Voyager head scientist.

Two other scientists have been with Voyager since the beginning. Others weren’t yet born when the spacecraft launched. “Voyager, to this day, is a multi-generational mission,” Spilker says. But it isn’t a mission of nostalgia. There’s still a world of discovery out beyond the solar system’s edge.

“Every piece of data, every day that goes by that we get data from the Voyagers, tells us something new,” says physicist Jamie Rankin of Princeton University, who started her Ph.D. in August 2012, the same month that Voyager 1 left the solar system for the cold, calm seas of interstellar space. “Every day, it’s in places nobody’s ever explored before.”

The original mission of the Voyager probes was to explore the outer parts of our solar system, which until then had remained largely mysterious. A rare planetary alignment meant that a spacecraft launched in the late 1970s could swoop past Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune, getting a gravitational boost from each planet that it passed. With these gravitational assists, the spacecraft could complete the tour in less than 15 years. Such an alignment won’t happen again until the 2150s.

The project was a bold step for its time. When work began in the early 1970s, no spacecraft had gone farther than Mars. NASA set a conservative goal for the mission: flybys of Jupiter and Saturn. In 1972 and 1973, NASA launched two Pioneer probes, which made sure the trek was possible and gathered data along the way. As with Voyager, there were two spacecraft in case one failed.

After nail-biting launches and a wait of nearly two years, the Voyagers began uncovering many of Jupiter’s and Saturn’s long-held secrets, including the volcanoes on Jupiter’s moon Io, details of Jupiter’s Great Red Spot and hints of geologic activity on Saturn’s moon Enceladus.

Mission accomplished, Voyager 2 went on to pass Uranus and Neptune. It took the first images of the planets’ rings and discovered more than a dozen moons along the way. The spacecraft also spotted a perpetually churning storm on Neptune and erupting geysers on Neptune’s moon Triton.

“The highlights of Voyager were clearly the planetary encounters,” said Ed Stone, the mission’s original head scientist, in a NASA interview before his death in 2024. “We had a lifetime of discovery packed into each one.”

The uncontested stars of these encounters were the images shared in news reports and TV broadcasts as the planets and their moons came into view. Jupiter’s moon Io turned out to be a shocking splotchy orange color that looked like a pizza.

A humble navigation image of that moon led to one of the most surprising discoveries of the entire mission. Four days past Voyager 1’s closest approach to Jupiter, after the excitement had died down, project astronomer Linda Morabito of the Jet Propulsion Laboratory started processing additional images of Io. These images had been taken after the flyby, when Voyager was looking back over its shoulder.

As Morabito enhanced one image’s brightness, she spotted an odd bulbous formation protruding from Io’s edge. “What’s that?” she asked herself. Her supervisor had the same reaction: “Jesus, what’s that?” she later recalled him saying.

The bulb turned out to be a volcanic plume — an erupting fire fountain extending 250 kilometers above Io’s surface. It was the first discovery of active volcanism anywhere other than Earth, and it transformed our view of the outer solar system. Instead of a cold, inert icebox, this was a bubbling and dynamic region.

The findings inspired many future missions. While visiting Jupiter from 1995 to 2003, the Galileo probe found that Europa may have a subsurface ocean that could be hospitable to life. When the Cassini probe orbited Saturn from 2004 to 2017, it discovered that the moon Enceladus also has a potentially habitable ocean that spews icy geysers into space.

In 1990, with Voyager 1 about 6 billion kilometers from the sun, astronomer Carl Sagan convinced mission leaders to turn the spacecraft backward for one last look at the planets. Voyager 1 took a family portrait in which Earth appeared faintly as a “pale blue dot,” Sagan said. “Everyone you love, everyone you know, everyone you ever heard of, every human being who ever was, lived out their lives … on a mote of dust suspended in a sunbeam,” he wrote in the 1994 book Pale Blue Dot.
To save power, Voyager 2’s cameras were shut off in 1989. After the family portrait, Voyager 1’s cameras were also turned off. Where the spacecraft were headed, there wouldn’t be much to see.

The probes were now on their way out of the solar system along their own separate paths, both headed toward a mysterious boundary that no human emissary had ever crossed. In this next phase of their voyage, no one knew what to expect. How long would the spacecraft keep communicating? How far would the powerful forces that drive the sun reach? And what would it be like to taste interstellar space?

For its first 35 years in space, Voyager 1 was swaddled in the solar wind. This stream of hot, charged particles flows constantly from the sun, forming a vast bubble called the heliosphere. The bubble surrounds the solar system, protecting it from cosmic radiation; it extends billions of kilometers past the planets up to a boundary called the heliopause. Heliophysicists consider this boundary, where the solar wind bumps into interstellar space, the edge of the solar system, although the sun’s gravitational influence extends much farther.

paras.en: Scientists expected the Voyagers to cross the heliopause, but they didn’t know when — or what the spacecraft would find when they did. Rankin had just started her Ph.D. at Caltech when in August 2012 Voyager 1 detected an abrupt jump in the number of high-energy cosmic rays alongside a drop in solar particles, hinting that the spacecraft had crossed the boundary. But magnetic field measurements suggested otherwise. Instead, those measurements indicated that the sun still exerted some influence. The interstellar magnetic field diverted around the heliosphere like a river around a rock.

paras.en: A Voyager instrument that could have settled the question of whether the probe had passed the heliopause was no longer working. But scientists got a lucky break in April 2013 when an eruption on the sun sent a pressure wave rippling outward. It set the electrons around Voyager 1 vibrating, which allowed scientists to estimate the density of charged particles nearby.

The results showed that Voyager 1 had in fact crossed the heliopause on August 25, 2012, when it was about 18 billion kilometers away, or 120 times Earth’s distance from the sun. Data from Voyager 2 later backed up that finding. “This is the beginning of a new era of exploration for us,” Stone told Science News in 2013.

But the line between our solar system and interstellar space isn’t solid. The sun’s reach extends farther than anyone expected, and “this boundary is not very sharp or very thin,” says physicist Jeewoo Park of NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Md.

With Voyager on the other side of the heliopause, particle speeds and gas temperatures have dropped. The magnetic field is weaker. Even dust particles are about half as abundant compared with inside the heliosphere. “For the most part, it’s been very quiet and very consistent,” Rankin says.

But it’s not entirely silent. In four instances, scientists saw spikes in the magnetic field strength and particle density measurements around the probe. After the fourth, in mid-2020, those numbers have remained high. No one knows why. Perhaps Voyager 1 continues to ride the aftershocks of solar eruptions, says Park, who reported on the events in June in the Astrophysical Journal.

Where pure interstellar space begins is still an open question. So is the heliosphere’s shape. Most scientists think it is elongated, like a comet, but others think it is a sphere or even a croissant.
Space telescopes launched in 2008 and 2025, the Interstellar Boundary Explorer and Interstellar Mapping and Acceleration Probe, could help answer that question.

Meanwhile, the Voyager probes are silently sailing onward. Scientists estimate that the onboard power sources that keep the crafts’ instruments running will dry up in 10 to 15 years, preventing them from sending data back to Earth. Our conversation will come to an end. But the journey goes on.

Voyager 2 will approach a red dwarf star known as Ross 248 in about 42,000 years, coming within 700 light-days. It will be 44,000 years before Voyager 1 next encounters another star, Gliese 445, at a similar distance. “The Voyagers become our silent ambassadors, a little bit of us that continues into space,” Spilker says.

They carry a message, should anyone find it, contained on the Golden Record. A copy of the phonograph record, which is plated in gold, rides on each of the probes. The long-distance dispatches feature sights and sounds of Earth, including a map of the solar system; images of Earth’s monuments; greetings in dozens of languages; and the sounds of whale song, laughter, classical composers and Navajo chants.
That time capsule captures the optimism and promise of the mission, Spilker says. “It may well outlast humanity.”

articles.title: Tiny implants can use the body itself to talk to each other
articles.author: Brendan Pierson

paras.en: Medical implants are getting smaller and smarter. But getting them to talk to each other remains tricky.

Now, researchers have developed a way for tiny implantable devices to send electrical signals through the body’s own tissues. The approach could offer a low-power way for implants to work together, with one detecting a symptom and another delivering treatment, the team reports September 24 in Science.

Currently, getting devices to communicate through tissue comes with trade-offs. Some medical devices, such as insulin pumps linked to glucose monitors, use Bluetooth, which relies on radio signals. Receiving those signals requires power even when a device is only listening, increasing the need for battery power and making devices harder shrink. Radio signals also weaken as they travel through body tissue, limiting how far apart communicating devices can be.

The new network called SWANS, the Smart Wireless Autonomous Networking System, works differently. A wearable external hub or implant generates an electric pulse that produces a small current in the surrounding tissue. Tiny implants can detect those electrical signals while using almost no power when they are only listening. And without large batteries, those implants can be small enough to inject through a syringe.

To demonstrate how the network works, the team attached motion sensors to the front legs of rats. When the animals moved their front legs, the system’s external hub sent signals through their bodies to neurostimulator implants in the sciatic nerves, causing muscles in the back legs to contract.

The synchronized limbs weren’t really the point. The experiment was designed to show that signals could travel through the body, linking different kinds of devices, says Alex Abramson, a biomedical engineer at Georgia Tech in Atlanta. It was “a proof of concept showing that you can really connect this system to anything.”

Abramson says a network of smart implants could automatically deliver a drug or stimulate a neuron exactly when needed to treat complex conditions like Parkinson’s disease. Simple signals can be sent from one implant to another, while an external hub can coordinate more complex networks of sensors and devices, possibly using artificial intelligence.

Before the new network can be used in humans, researchers will need to show that the electrical signals do not cause unintended problems like heart rhythm disruptions. Such issues have not turned up in the experiments in rats yet, but the technology will need to be tested over longer periods of time and in larger animals, Abramson says.

Materials engineer Amir Alavi says the network’s potential could grow as other technologies improve, including wearables, AI systems and miniature, battery-free implantable sensors like those his lab is developing. “There are now several really interesting directions converging,” says Alavi, of at the University of Pittsburgh’s Swanson School of Engineering. “If those pieces eventually come together, you could have implants that are much smaller, simpler, longer-lived, and more connected than what we have today.”
