articles.title: Mysterious 'Golden Tree' Coral Is So Weird, Scientists Had to Create a New Family on The Tree of Life
articles.author: Michelle Starr

paras.en: In the twilight deeps of the Eastern Pacific Ocean, a magical sight can be found on a seamount off the coast of Costa Rica.

As the underwater vehicle SuBastian glides over a rocky outcrop oddly coated with a fuzzy pink patina and punctuated with basket-shaped gleaming white sponges, a majestic yellow form emerges from the darkness.
It looks like a golden tree, so vividly yellow you can imagine it glowing.
Then, as the camera zooms closer, you can see the pink fuzz moving – a thick carpet of stars from which the golden tree blooms.
The stars, of course, are not real stars, but a teeming multitude of pink brittle stars; nor is the golden tree a real tree.
Instead, it's a species of octocoral unlike any scientists have ever seen – one so unusual that it required a whole new branch of the tree of life to accommodate its strangeness.

In a paper describing the species, researchers led by Odalisca Breedy of the University of Costa Rica have named the coral Laurinque elenya – a name derived from Tolkien's Elvish language Quenya, meaning "golden tree of the stars".
You can see the golden coral forest for yourself in the footage from SuBastian's dive, starting at around the 20-minute mark in the video below.
Corals – for all the resemblance many of them bear to plants – are animals, and they take many different forms adapted to life beneath the waves.
Octocorals are one specific group containing more than 3,000 species, named for the eightfold symmetry of the tiny polyps that line their branches.

They are a diverse bunch, and their number includes some very strange colonies indeed – so when Laurinque was found at depths of 360 to 529 meters (1,181 to 1,735 feet) during dives in 2019 and 2023, it would not have surprised scientists to find it had a few idiosyncrasies.
But Laurinque wasn't just another eccentric aunt in a family full of them.
Its colonies can grow more than a meter tall and 1.2 meters wide, with densely branching structures covered in unusually elongated polyps – the tiny animals that collectively make up a coral colony.
These polyps can partially retract into the branches, and the microscopic skeletal structures that support the coral, called sclerites, have a distinctive assortment of shapes.
Together, these features – found in different octocoral groups, but not together in a single species in this way – made it difficult to match Laurinque with any known family of octocorals.
And its DNA only exacerbated the conundrum.

The researchers analyzed three genetic markers from the coral's DNA, comparing them with sequences from other octocorals to see where their mysterious specimen belonged on the evolutionary family tree.
They got a match on a mitochondrial gene.
Then they got another one on the other mitochondrial gene.
Normally, this would be good news – a slam dunk that could confidently place a vexing species into a clean category.
Unfortunately, both markers matched with different octocoral families. One placed it strongly in Incrustatidae. The other was equally strong for placement in Eunicellidae.
And they couldn't even use the third marker – ribosomal DNA – as a tiebreaker. It was magnificently inconclusive.

So, after several years of not knowing, they had to bring out the big guns – the collection of new specimens, followed by an analysis of hundreds of genetic regions from Laurinque. And that, finally, yielded an answer.
The coral, Breedy and her colleagues found, is closely related to Eunicellidae – but still distinct from it, the first known member of the Laurinqueidae coral family.

"I saw the octocoral garden for the first time in 2019, and I was impressed by the beauty of the landscape, which inspired, later the elvish name of the taxa. I thought the species could belong to a known family and genera, but after the preliminary morphological analysis I realized that it was something very different that I could not match with the known taxa," Breedy said.

"In 2023 we collected more samples and thanks to the exhaustive molecular analyses made by my colleagues, Cathy McFadden, Catalina Murillo and Andrea Quattrini, we were able to determine the taxonomic placement of the stunning species, in one of the most enigmatic sites."
But there's more than a whole new coral family to the discovery.
The golden coral gardens grow in waters with extremely low oxygen levels, at temperatures between 8 and 11 degrees Celsius (46 and 52 degrees Fahrenheit).
These conditions would be inhospitable to many animals, yet Laurinque forms elaborate, ethereal underwater forests, its branches rising above a seafloor almost completely obscured by brittle stars.

Such coral gardens are important habitats in the deep ocean. Their intricate, three-dimensional structures provide places for other animals to shelter, feed, and thrive, helping support biodiversity in a deeply challenging environment.
And Laurinque may not be confined to Costa Rica. The researchers report possible sightings off Panama and the Galápagos Islands, although these have yet to be confirmed.

For now, the golden tree of the stars remains a poignant and magical reminder of how much of Earth's biodiversity is still waiting to be discovered – even in places where life seems almost impossible.
The research has been published in ZooKeys.

articles.title: After 40 Years, Chornobyl's Radioactive Particles Are Surprisingly Stable
articles.author: David Nield

paras.en: We're now 40 years on from the worst nuclear disaster in history, and scientists have been analyzing radioactive particles blown out by Chornobyl to see what's left of the fuel that got scattered – and what state those particles are in.

Knowing how these chemical pellets have held up to decades of weathering and decay is valuable for understanding the safety of nuclear plants in the future – and for working out when it might be safe to return to the Chornobyl site without a protective suit.
What stood out most from the analysis was the "remarkably persistent" structure of the radioactive dust particles, which showed much more stability than expected.
That means most of the radioactive material remains locked inside.
The researchers behind the work, from Leibniz University Hannover and the Helmholtz-Zentrum Dresden-Rossendorf (HZDR) in Germany, have published their findings in the Journal of Hazardous Materials.

Six fuel particles were analyzed in total, split into three categories depending on what happened to them during the original reactor explosion. Some, for example, had melted and bonded with their coating of zirconium.
"There are three classes of these particles," says physicist Tobias Weissenborn, from Leibniz University Hannover.
"First, there are particles that are chemically and physically still very similar to the nuclear fuel uranium dioxide.
"Then, there are particles that are partially or fully encased in, or completely fused with, their zirconium layer. The third type of particle was created when the graphite moderator caught fire."

Each of these particle classes has ended up with a different chemical composition, which can affect how they degrade. The sampled particles measured a mere 8–50 micrometers in size (so at least 20 would fit inside a single millimeter), and were all collected from inside the Chornobyl Exclusion Zone.
A technique known as diffraction analysis was used to look inside these microscopic specks, with the atomic crystal structure being determined through the way X-rays reflected away from it.
"Ultimately, we fully rotated the particles in an X-ray beam focused down to 100 micrometers – about the thickness of a human hair," says crystallographer Christoph Hennig from HZDR.
"We measured each particle from 2,000 different angles to seamlessly capture all the reflections."

Across all three particle types, the researchers found the structure holding the nuclear fuel had largely remained intact. That suggests a greater chemical stability in these fuel specks than previously assumed.

The study also gives scientists a better idea of how these particle groups are put together – exactly how the disaster and its subsequent chemical chain reaction shifted the composition of the fuel crystals.
"Our findings demonstrate that Chornobyl fuel particles act as remarkably persistent reservoirs," write the researchers in their published paper.
The researchers frame this as potentially good news: It means the particles may be releasing radioactive material into the environment more slowly than previously assumed.
While it's not safe to go back, the findings could help scientists better assess the long-term environmental risks.

The radioactive material hasn't gone anywhere, which means these particles will remain dangerous for decades. Breathing these particles in is still going to be extremely hazardous to health, and they could get kicked up from the ground by wind, erosion, or passing animals.

The researchers also acknowledge that six particles – all sourced from two locations – are a small sample. Weighing up the current risks in Chornobyl will require more comprehensive sets of data collected over longer periods.
"Even if we obtained some averages at some point, we still wouldn't be able to make universal statements about health risks in the region," says Weissenborn.
"Even if the particles decay in a largely uniform pattern, there will always be outliers, more persistent particles, that will release radionuclides at a later point in time."
The research has been published in Journal of Hazardous Materials.

articles.title: There's Another Cat Parasite That Can Infect Humans. A Huge Study Reveals How Common It Is.
articles.author: Peter Dockrill

paras.en: In the annals of 'cat parasite' research, Toxoplasma gondii grabs most of the headlines.

The mysterious pathogen, which may infect up to one-third of the global population, is famous for altering the behavior of its hosts, and it's also of serious concern for its varying effects on human health.
But T. gondii isn't the only parasite that cats and humans have the misfortune of sharing.

In a new study published in PLOS One, scientists shine a spotlight on a protozoan pest called Giardia duodenalis, and the research team says it's the largest investigation to date on the parasite's prevalence in domestic cats in North America.

While most infections with G. duodenalis don't produce symptoms, it can result in the disease giardiasis in both humans and animals, which can cause diarrhea, abdominal pain, weakness, and other signs of poor health, including failure to grow in animals.

In the study, led by veterinarian and first author Margaret Wingerd from VCA SouthPaws Veterinary Specialists & Emergency Center in Fairfax, Virginia, researchers analyzed more than 157,000 stool samples collected from domestic cats across the US and Canada.
Using PCR testing, the team identified G. duodenalis in 9,962 of the samples analyzed, corresponding to an overall detection rate of 6.3 percent – approximately one in every 16 cats tested.
Of those positive samples, 1,840 (18.5 percent) were detections of the A or B assemblages of the parasite with zoonotic potential, which means the infection could potentially spread to humans.
Among cats that carried the parasite, a number of patterns were identified.
Generally, male cats were slightly more likely to be infected than female cats, and younger cats were more likely to be infected than older cats.

Kittens showed a much higher rate of positive cases (10.7 percent) compared to senior cats of 10 years or older (1.3 percent), and kittens also showed the highest proportion of assemblage A/B positivity (19.9 percent).
Adult cats that had not been spayed or neutered were generally more likely to carry the parasite than their sterilized counterparts, although the opposite pattern was observed in kittens.

The researchers speculate that the higher odds in males and intact cats may be due to exposure differences because of housing differences (indoor versus outdoor), increased roaming behavior, or differences in immune competency.

With regard to kittens showing greater chances of infection than older cats, the researchers say it could reflect greater acquired immunity in older animals, or may also indicate differences in exposure due to housing and activity.

In terms of geography, cats in the US Midwest had the highest overall detection rate (7.8 percent), while cats in the Northeast had the highest proportion of potentially zoonotic variants among positive samples (21.6 percent).
Seasonal differences also seem to matter, with significantly lower detection rates in summer (4.6 percent) compared to winter (8.1 percent).
"G. duodenalis cysts can survive for a prolonged time in cool and moist environments," the researchers write.
"This could explain the lower infection rate in summer in general, as summer tends to be warm and dry, and cysts are less likely to survive."
All told, the findings show that only about 1.2 percent of the more than 157,000 samples tested carried parasites that could potentially infect people.
While this represents a relatively small proportion of the cats tested, the researchers say the prevalence of the parasite warrants caution and careful monitoring.
"Given the ability of G. duodenalis to infect a wide variety of hosts including people and animals, this protozoan can present a public health concern," the study authors write.

"Based on our results, about 18 percent of cats in the US and Canada infected with G. duodenalis have potential zoonotic assemblages. This highlights the need for routine fecal screening in domestic cats, especially in cats at a higher risk for G. duodenalis or those living in households with young children, the elderly, and immunocompromised people."

articles.title: NASA captures strange waves high above Hurricane Simon

paras.en: NASA captures strange waves high above Hurricane Simon

- As Hurricane Simon unleashed destructive winds and flooding along Mexicoâs coast, NASA satellites captured an extraordinary sight: massive atmospheric waves rippling high above the storm. The rare images reveal how powerful hurricanes can disturb the upper atmosphere, creating patterns that are usually invisible from space.

Despite remaining offshore, Hurricane Simon battered Mexico's Pacific coast with powerful winds and flooding. At the same time, NASA satellites captured an extraordinary sight high above the storm: enormous waves rippling through Earth's upper atmosphere.

Hurricane Simon was the latest in a series of powerful tropical cyclones to sweep across the Eastern Pacific during the 2026 hurricane season. On October 11, 2026, the Category 4 hurricane moved dangerously close to Mexico's coastline as it traveled north-northwest, with sustained winds reaching 250 kilometers (155 miles) per hour.
Hurricane Simon Batters Mexico's Pacific Coast

At approximately 2:30 p.m. local time (20:30 Universal Time) on October 11, the VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) instrument aboard NASA's Suomi NPP satellite captured an image of the massive storm. At that moment, Simon's eye was located roughly 50 kilometers (30 miles) offshore, between the coastal cities of Manzanillo and Puerto Vallarta.

According to the National Hurricane Center (NHC), sustained winds had weakened to approximately 210 kilometers (130 miles) per hour by the time the image was taken. However, the hurricane's powerful inner core was still moving close enough to threaten communities along the coast.

The Sierra Madre mountains appeared to help limit Simon's strength, with the rugged terrain reducing the storm's intensity and shrinking the area affected by its winds. Even so, the hurricane brought torrential rainfall and flooding to coastal communities, including the port city of Manzanillo. The heavy rain also increased the threat of dangerous mudslides in mountainous regions, according to news reports.
NASA Captures Strange Waves Above the Hurricane
While Simon churned across the Pacific, satellites detected something remarkable happening far above the clouds.

During the early morning of October 11, the storm generated rippling disturbances that traveled into Earth's upper atmosphere. A nighttime satellite image, captured by the VIIRS instrument aboard NOAA-21, revealed atmospheric gravity waves spreading outward from the hurricane.

These waves are created by intense activity within the storm. Near the hurricane's eyewall, the release of latent heat fuels powerful convection, causing warm, moist air to surge upward and form towering cumulonimbus clouds.

The strong updrafts inside these clouds can disturb the surrounding atmosphere, generating waves that travel upward into the stratosphere and mesosphere. Unlike ocean waves, which move through water, atmospheric gravity waves are disturbances that propagate through the air, with gravity acting as a restoring force.
Why the Rare Atmospheric Ripples Were Visible

Although powerful hurricanes can generate atmospheric gravity waves, satellites cannot always detect them. Strong winds at high altitudes can weaken or disperse the disturbances before they reach the mesosphere, where they may become visible through a phenomenon known as airglow.

Airglow is a faint, natural light produced by gases high in Earth's atmosphere. When atmospheric gravity waves pass through this glowing region, they create subtle variations in brightness that can reveal their distinctive ripple patterns.

The VIIRS instrument's day-night band is sensitive enough to detect this faint light. However, it also captures moonlight reflected from Earth's surface and atmosphere, which can make the much weaker airglow difficult to distinguish.

Fortunately, conditions were unusually favorable when the satellite observed Simon. With very little illumination from the Moon, the delicate atmospheric ripples stood out more clearly, allowing the satellite to capture the striking patterns.
Hurricane Simon's Unpredictable Path Raises Concerns
By the morning of October 13, meteorologists were still struggling to predict where Simon would go next and how strong it might become.
The National Hurricane Center described confidence in its intensity and track forecasts as "very low confidence," reflecting how the storm had repeatedly behaved differently than expected.
At the time, one possibility was that Simon could turn northward, enter the Gulf of California, and eventually make landfall.

Regardless of its exact path, large ocean swells generated by the hurricane were expected to create hazardous conditions along portions of Mexico's southwestern and west-central coastlines in the following days.
NASA Earth Observatory images by Michala Garrison, using VIIRS data from NASA EOSDIS LANCE, GIBS/Worldview, the Suomi National Polar-orbiting Partnership, and the Joint Polar Satellite System (JPSS).
Materials provided by NASA Earth Observatory. Original written by Lindsey Doermann. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

articles.title: Scientists discover a plastic-eating “Pac-Man” enzyme with a surprising secret

paras.en: Scientists discover a plastic-eating âPac-Manâ enzyme with a surprising secret

- Scientists have discovered a remarkable âPac-Man enzymeâ that helps bacteria devour certain types of plastic and may offer new hope in the fight against plastic pollution. Researchers found that several biodegradable plastics completely broke down in soil within about a year, while conventional plastic remained largely unchanged.

Plastic pollution is one of the world's most persistent environmental problems. Vast amounts of discarded plastic accumulate in the oceans, sometimes forming enormous garbage patches that threaten marine life. Most conventional plastics break down extremely slowly because microorganisms struggle to digest the synthetic polymers from which they are made. Instead of disappearing, these materials gradually fragment into increasingly smaller particles, including microplastics and nanoplastics.

Yet plastic waste is not completely beyond the reach of nature. Bacteria and other microorganisms can colonize its surfaces, forming communities known as biofilms. These communities create a distinctive microbial ecosystem that scientists call the "plastisphere."

Researchers at the University of Konstanz have now discovered an unusual enzyme that could reveal how some bacteria are becoming better equipped to break down certain types of plastic. The enzyme can digest particular polyesters and biodegradable plastics, but it has another unexpected ability: it can also break down penicillin, suggesting a possible connection to antibiotic resistance.

Scientists have nicknamed it the "Pac-Man enzyme" because its molecular structure features a remarkably wide opening where chemical reactions take place, known as the active site. The discovery suggests that bacteria may be adapting to digest certain plastic materials more quickly than researchers previously believed.

However, the findings also highlight an important limitation. For microorganisms to make a meaningful difference in reducing plastic pollution, more plastic products would need to be made from biodegradable materials that contain chemical bonds microbes can break apart.
Testing How Bacteria Break Down Bioplastics

To investigate how microorganisms digest biodegradable plastics, University of Konstanz biologists Harry Lerner and David Schleheck studied the entire process of microbial decomposition. They wanted to determine not only whether the materials could be completely broken down, but also which microorganisms were responsible and what biological mechanisms allowed them to do it.

The researchers examined the composition of the microbial communities involved and analyzed their collective genetic information (the metagenome). This approach allowed them to search for genes that might produce enzymes capable of breaking apart plastic polymers.

Their experiments focused on long-chain aliphatic polyesters (LCAP), a class of biodegradable plastic materials developed by a research team led by chemist Stefan Mecking. These materials contain chemical bonds that certain microorganisms can potentially break down, unlike the more resistant structures found in many conventional plastics.
The collaborative findings were published in The ISME Journal.
To observe how the bioplastics behaved in a natural environment, the team placed samples beneath the surface of forest soil at the university's botanical garden.
"We buried small pieces of LCAP bioplastic film in the upper humus layer in the forest at the university's botanical garden, about ten centimeters deep," explains Harry Lerner.
"This layer is where the breakdown of cellulose and other natural polymers, such as cutin - a plant-based polyester - takes place."

Humus is the upper layer of soil rich in decomposing organic matter, where microorganisms play a major role in recycling nutrients. Cellulose is the main structural component of plant cell walls, while cutin is a naturally occurring polyester that helps form the protective outer covering of plants.
The researchers selected this environment because its microorganisms already possess the biological machinery needed to break down complex natural materials.
Bioplastics Disappeared Within About a Year

Alongside the outdoor experiment, the scientists carried out laboratory tests using soil collected from the same forest. They mixed powdered bioplastics into the soil and monitored microbial activity over the course of an entire year.

One important measurement was the amount of carbon dioxide, or CO2, released from the samples. As microorganisms consume and metabolize organic materials, they produce carbon dioxide through respiration. Tracking this gas helped the researchers determine how actively the microbes were breaking down the plastics.
The buried plastic films remained in the forest soil for a full year, allowing the team to compare decomposition under natural conditions with the carefully monitored laboratory experiments.
To assess the results, the scientists also tested cellulose, other biodegradable plastics, conventional polyethylene plastic, and soil samples without added materials.

"Cellulose, other types of bioplastics such as PHBV and PCL, as well as high-density plastic (HDPE) and untreated soil were used as controls in the laboratory. We found that all bioplastic materials were completely degraded within roughly 250 to 330 days. Cellulose broke down after about 80 days, whereas virtually no degradation occurred for HDPE," says Lerner.

The difference was striking. While the biodegradable plastics were completely broken down within approximately nine to eleven months, conventional high-density polyethylene showed almost no decomposition.

These results demonstrate why the chemical makeup of plastic matters so much. Some polymers contain bonds that microbial enzymes can attack, allowing bacteria to dismantle them into smaller molecules. Others, including widely used polyethylene, are far more resistant to biological degradation.
Mysterious Holes Reveal How Bacteria Eat Plastic
When the researchers recovered the plastic films from the forest soil, they discovered something unexpected.

Using electron microscopy, which can reveal structures far too small to see with an ordinary light microscope, the team examined the surfaces of the buried materials. They found numerous tiny holes, each approximately matching the dimensions and shape of an individual bacterial cell.
The unusual pattern suggested that bacteria were doing more than simply attaching themselves to the plastic. They appeared to be breaking into the material itself.

"We hypothesized that bacteria are coated with plastic-depolymerases anchored to their cell surfaces. This would enable them to digest their way into the material and become embedded within the film, leaving behind microscopic holes of exactly this type," explains Lerner.

Depolymerases are enzymes that break large molecules called polymers into smaller chemical units. If these enzymes are attached directly to the outside of a bacterium, they could allow the microorganism to digest the surrounding material while remaining in close contact with it.

This would help explain the microscopic cavities observed in the plastic films. Rather than relying entirely on enzymes released into the environment, the bacteria might be able to break down the material directly at their surfaces.
Scientists Identify the Plastic-Eating "Pac-Man Enzyme"
To find the biological machinery behind this unusual behavior, Lerner extracted DNA from the entire community of microorganisms living in the soil samples.
He then sequenced the genetic material and carefully analyzed the extensive data to determine which microbes and genes became especially abundant as the bioplastics decomposed.
One gene stood out. It was strongly enriched specifically in forest soil containing LCAP, suggesting that it could play an important role in breaking down the biodegradable polyester.

Further analysis revealed that the gene produces an esterase, a type of enzyme capable of splitting certain chemical bonds found in esters. These bonds are present in many naturally occurring substances as well as in various biodegradable polyesters.
What made this particular enzyme especially interesting was how it was positioned on bacterial cells.
Its genetic instructions included a secretion signal that directs the enzyme outside the cell, along with a lipid anchor that holds it firmly to the cell membrane.

This arrangement means the enzyme can remain attached to the bacterium's surface while attacking nearby plastic molecules. Its unusually exposed active site also provides space for the enzyme to interact with polymer chains.
The researchers had identified the molecular mechanism they were looking for, along with the enzyme they named "Pac-Man."
A Surprising Connection to Antibiotic Resistance
The discovery became even more intriguing when scientists examined the enzyme's molecular structure.
Although it resembled esterases, which are known for breaking down ester bonds, it also shared structural similarities with another important family of bacterial enzymes: beta-lactamases.

These enzymes are well known for their role in antibiotic resistance. Some bacteria produce beta-lactamases that disable antibiotics such as penicillin by breaking open a critical part of their chemical structure, known as the beta-lactam ring.

"Its structure resembles that of esterases, but also that of beta-lactamases, which are bacterial enzymes that are capable of cleaving the beta-lactam ring of certain antibiotics, such as penicillin, thereby making bacteria resistant to antibiotics," says Lerner.
Laboratory experiments confirmed that the newly discovered enzyme was capable of performing both types of chemical reactions.
It could break polyester chains into their individual building blocks, known as monomers, while also cleaving penicillin.
This dual activity was particularly surprising because plastic degradation and antibiotic breakdown are usually considered separate biological functions.

The finding raises the possibility that some enzymes involved in plastic decomposition could also contribute to antibiotic resistance. However, demonstrating that an enzyme can chemically break down penicillin in the laboratory does not establish that it provides antibiotic resistance to living bacteria.
Could Plastic-Eating Bacteria Help Solve Plastic Pollution?
The discovery also raises a broader question about how rapidly microorganisms can adapt to synthetic materials introduced into their environment.
For most of Earth's history, plastic pollution did not exist. Microorganisms evolved enzymes to digest naturally occurring substances, including plant fibers and other complex organic molecules.
Modern plastics have introduced an enormous new collection of potential carbon sources into the environment, but many of these materials remain chemically inaccessible to microbes.
"The plastisphere is a new habitat in our environment," explains Schleheck.

"Humans have only been introducing plastic into the environment in significant quantities for around 50 to 75 years. Since then, it has theoretically been available to microbial communities - such as bacteria, yeasts and fungi - as an additional source of carbon and energy for their growth. By 'theoretically', I mean that they would certainly like to use the plastic as a growth substrate - but they cannot, because the materials are actually indigestible to microbial metabolism and are therefore hardly degraded."

paras.en: The Pac-Man enzyme suggests that this barrier may not be absolute for every type of plastic.
Some bacteria appear capable of using specialized enzymes to attack biodegradable polyesters, potentially allowing them to exploit these materials as sources of energy and nutrients.

For scientists studying plastic pollution, the finding offers a promising clue about how biological degradation might be improved. It also suggests that microbial communities could be adapting to certain synthetic polymers more rapidly than previously anticipated.

However, the results do not mean that bacteria are suddenly capable of consuming the enormous amounts of conventional plastic already accumulating in the environment. The experiments showed that polyethylene remained largely unaffected, even as the biodegradable plastics decomposed.
Instead, the researchers emphasize the importance of designing materials that microorganisms can actually digest.

"I find this encouraging, because it seems that bacteria can adapt to breaking down polyester plastics more quickly than we expected. To tackle the environmental problem of plastic pollution, we humans need to work with the capabilities of microbes. Ideally, this would involve using only polymers with biochemical breaking points, such as the hydrolysable ester bonds in polyesters like LCAP or other types of bioplastics," concludes Schleheck.

The discovery offers a glimpse of a potentially more sustainable approach to plastic production. Rather than expecting microorganisms to break down materials that are naturally resistant to decomposition, scientists could develop plastics with chemical structures that make biological recycling possible.

The Pac-Man enzyme illustrates how bacteria can exploit these molecular weak points, offering new insight into the relationship between plastic pollution, microbial adaptation, and the future of biodegradable materials.

articles.title: Astronomers discover a strange universal rule behind black hole eruptions

paras.en: Astronomers discover a strange universal rule behind black hole eruptions
Scientists have uncovered a hidden rule that could explain and help predict when black holes unleash enormous jets into space.

- Scientists have discovered that black holes of vastly different sizes appear to launch powerful jets according to the same universal rule. The breakthrough could explain why some black holes suddenly erupt years after devouring a star and help astronomers predict when these spectacular outbursts will happen.

Astronomers have uncovered a surprising rule that appears to determine when black holes unleash powerful jets of material into space. Even though black holes can differ in mass by millions of times, researchers found that they seem to follow the same fundamental pattern when producing these enormous cosmic outflows.

The discovery, published in Nature Astronomy, suggests that black holes can activate their jets at the same critical stage of their feeding cycle, whether they weigh roughly 10 times as much as the Sun or millions of times more.

The research was led by Dr. Adelle Goodwin, an astrophysicist at Curtin University's International Centre of Radio Astronomy Research (ICRAR) and a Forrest Research Foundation Fellow, alongside co-author Dr. Andrew Mummery of the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton.

The breakthrough emerged from years of studying unusual events in which supermassive black holes tear stars apart. By combining observations from telescopes in Australia, the United States, India, South Africa, and space, the scientists pieced together a clearer picture of how black holes behave as they consume matter.

Surprisingly, the crucial insight did not come while examining a telescope. It happened in a bar in Madrid, where Goodwin and Mummery were attending a scientific conference. During a conversation, they recognized that the same rule known to govern jet formation in relatively small black holes also seemed to apply to their supermassive counterparts.
Why Some Black Holes Erupt Years After Devouring Stars
One of the biggest mysteries the researchers wanted to explain was why black holes do not always launch jets at the same time.

When a supermassive black hole tears apart a star, it sometimes produces a powerful jet almost immediately. In other cases, the black hole appears relatively quiet for months or even years before suddenly producing a detectable radio outflow.
"We were looking at these events and asking why the timing was so different," said Dr. Goodwin.
"Then the pattern became clear. The delayed jets were appearing when the black hole's feeding rate dropped to the same critical point already known from much smaller black holes.
"That was the moment we realized this was not just a quirk of one type of black hole, but it looked like a rule that applied across the Universe."
Although black holes are often portrayed as cosmic vacuum cleaners that swallow anything nearby, their feeding behavior is far more complicated.

As material spirals toward a black hole, not all of it necessarily disappears beyond the event horizon, the boundary past which nothing can escape. Some matter can instead be expelled into space through powerful jets and other outflows.
"When a black hole tears apart a star, it does not swallow everything neatly," Dr. Goodwin said.
"Some of the material is consumed, and some is launched back into space in powerful jets and outflows.
"You can think of it as a black hole burp, except these burps can blast material across enormous distances and influence the galaxies around them."
These enormous outflows can carry energy and matter far from the black hole, potentially affecting the surrounding galaxy.
How Scientists Studied Supermassive Black Holes in Action
Astronomers have long suspected that black holes operate according to the same underlying physical laws regardless of their mass. Demonstrating that connection, however, has been difficult.
One major obstacle is time. The feeding behavior of a supermassive black hole can change over thousands of years, making it nearly impossible for astronomers to watch an entire cycle unfold.
Goodwin and her colleagues tackled this problem by examining rare events known as tidal disruption events.

These occur when a star passes too close to a supermassive black hole and experiences such extreme gravitational forces that it is torn apart. Some of the resulting debris falls toward the black hole, temporarily increasing its feeding activity.

Unlike the much longer changes normally associated with supermassive black holes, these dramatic episodes can play out over just a few years. That gives scientists an unusual opportunity to track how a giant black hole responds as its supply of material changes.

The team initially examined 20 tidal disruption events using observations collected in visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, and radio wavelengths. They then selected 10 events for which the available data allowed them to reliably estimate both the rate at which the black hole was consuming matter and the timing of its radio outflows.
By comparing these events, the researchers identified a remarkably consistent pattern.
The observations revealed two distinct stages during which black holes can produce jets.
The first occurs early in the feeding process, when the black hole is consuming matter at an exceptionally high rate.
The second can happen much later, hundreds or even thousands of days after the star is initially destroyed.
During this delayed phase, jets appear when the black hole's feeding rate falls to approximately 2% of its Eddington limit.

The Eddington limit is a theoretical benchmark describing the point at which the outward pressure produced by radiation balances the inward pull of gravity. Astronomers use it to measure how intensely a black hole is feeding relative to a characteristic physical limit.
What makes the finding especially significant is that the same 2% threshold has already been linked to jet formation in much smaller black holes within our own Milky Way galaxy.
In other words, black holes separated by enormous differences in mass appear to activate delayed jets at essentially the same relative feeding rate.
"These black holes are separated by enormous differences in mass, but they appear to switch on their jets at the same point in the feeding process," Dr. Goodwin said.
"That tells us something fundamental about black holes: the physics does not seem to care how big they are."

The finding provides a potential explanation for an otherwise puzzling observation. Some black holes generate radio jets soon after destroying a star, while others appear inactive before producing powerful outflows much later.
Rather than behaving unpredictably, these delayed eruptions may be governed by a common physical threshold.
Predicting When Black Holes Will Launch Jets
Beyond revealing something fundamental about black hole physics, the discovery could help astronomers make much better use of powerful radio telescopes.

Observing time on major scientific facilities is limited and highly competitive. Researchers must carefully decide which objects to study, how frequently to observe them, and when they are most likely to reveal something important.
If astronomers can estimate when a black hole's feeding rate will approach the critical threshold, they may be able to predict when a delayed jet is likely to appear.

"Radio telescopes are incredibly powerful, but knowing when to look is just as important as knowing where to look," said Dr. Goodwin. "If we can anticipate when a black hole is more likely to launch a jet, we can run better targeted campaigns, waste fewer observations and improve our chances of catching these rare events at the moment they matter most."
This could reduce unnecessary follow-up observations while increasing the chances of detecting rare jet-launching episodes at crucial moments.

The implications are particularly important for Western Australia, which will host the low-frequency component of the Square Kilometre Array Observatory (SKA), one of the largest and most ambitious radio astronomy projects ever undertaken.

The Australian Government has invested $387 million in the SKA, while the project's total cost exceeds $2 billion. Making more efficient use of such an expensive facility could provide substantial benefits to astronomers and the wider scientific community, potentially allowing more important discoveries to be made with the available observing time.

As the next generation of astronomical surveys identifies growing numbers of tidal disruption events, researchers will face an increasingly difficult challenge in deciding which ones deserve closer attention.

The newly identified relationship between feeding rates and jet formation could provide a valuable guide, helping scientists focus their observations on the black holes most likely to produce detectable outflows.
A Black Hole Breakthrough Driven by Curiosity

Professor James Arvanitakis, Director of the Forrest Research Foundation, said the discovery highlights the importance of supporting early-career scientists who pursue ambitious questions without knowing in advance where the answers will lead.
This kind of open-ended investigation, often described as 'blue sky' research, can produce unexpected discoveries with benefits extending far beyond the original scientific question.
"The Forrest Research Foundation did not fund a predetermined answer, we backed an exceptional researcher with a difficult question," Professor Arvanitakis said.

"That question has led to a discovery of international significance. This is exactly why fundamental research matters - it expands what we know, sharpens how we use major scientific infrastructure and builds capability that reaches well beyond astronomy.
"The fact this discovery was driven from Western Australia speaks to the strength of our research ecosystem, and the value of giving outstanding people a reason to build their careers here."
By linking the behavior of relatively small black holes to that of supermassive giants, the findings strengthen the idea that the same basic physical processes operate across vastly different scales.
They also offer astronomers a more reliable way to anticipate one of the universe's most dramatic phenomena: the moment a black hole begins launching a powerful jet into space.

articles.title: How to see the Orionid meteor shower 2026 peak this week — and when to look
articles.author: Joe Rao

paras.en: If you love watching meteors, 2026 has given you plenty to enjoy. This summer, the annual Perseid meteor shower peaked on the day of a new moon — and a solar eclipse — so moonlight stayed out of the way. And there's more to look forward to: in December, the Geminids, the year's most prolific shower, will peak after a waxing crescent moon sets early in the evening, opening the door to excellent viewing.
Right between those two headline showers, the dependable Orionids take their turn, reaching peak activity around Oct. 21-22.
So, when and where can you catch the show?

The Orionids take their name from the spot where they seem to fan out: Orion's raised club, just above and to the left of the reddish star Betelgeuse. Orion is usually a winter favorite, so in early autumn the mighty hunter doesn't fully clear the eastern horizon until after 11 p.m. local daylight time. Don't rush outside just yet though. Wait until around 2 a.m., when Orion is well above the horizon. By about 5 a.m., just before dawn, Orion reaches its highest point in the southern sky — and the view should be at its best.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Orionid meteors tend to be faint, so city lights can easily wash them out. If you can, head to a safe, dark rural spot. Get comfortable in a reclining lawn chair or sleeping bag, give your eyes time to adjust, and enjoy the view overhead and toward the southern sky.
And what about the moon? A full moon arrives October 25-26, but there's still a welcome stretch of dark sky for several mornings before Wednesday.

By Oct. 21-22, the waxing gibbous moon will be resting among the dim stars of Capricornus, reaching its highest point around 8:45 p.m. local daylight time. Here's the good news: it will set shortly after 2 a.m., leaving roughly 3½ hours of dark sky before dawn. In that window, one observer may spot as many as 15 to 20 Orionids per hour. Because those hours line up with the shower's peak, the moon shouldn't steal the show this year.
Halley's Comet: the source of the Orionids
So, where do the Orionids come from? Their story begins with Halley's Comet—the same famous visitor behind May's Eta Aquarids.

Meteoroids are tiny leftovers from a comet's nucleus. As a comet nears the sun, frozen material on its surface turns directly into gas, a process known as sublimation. The comet becomes a kind of cosmic litterbug, sprinkling dust and debris along its orbit. Those pieces are tiny and brittle, with the consistency of cigar ash, and every swing past the sun leaves more behind.

Comets are among the solar system's oldest and most fascinating objects. They formed alongside the sun and planets about 4.6 billion years ago, yet they have changed remarkably little. Think of them as time capsules from the solar system's childhood. Far beyond the outer planets, they spend most of their time in a deep freeze, where temperatures hover just above absolute zero, -459.67°F (-273.15°C). In that extreme cold, chemical reactions largely stop, helping comets preserve material from those earliest days.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Over the past 100,000 years, Halley's Comet has probably circled the sun well over a thousand times, leaving a fresh trail of debris on every visit. Each October and May, Earth brushes close to Halley's orbit. Some of that dust meets our atmosphere at a breathtaking 41 miles (66 km) per second, lighting up as the streaks we call "shooting stars."

The Orionids have another lovely feature: about half of these meteors leave glowing trails that linger longer than those of equally bright meteors. Halley's composition may be the reason. The particles begin burning up about 80 miles (130 km) above Earth, perhaps because they're made of lightweight material from the comet's diffuse surface rather than its core.

Perhaps you remember seeing Halley's Comet when it last swept through the inner solar system in late winter and early spring of 1986. With an orbital period of 75.4 years, this celebrated visitor is due back in late July or early August 2061.

For a little perspective, average life expectancy is 79.5 years in the United States, 82.2 years in the United Kingdom, and 83.4 years in Canada. So, if you were born after 1980, there's a fair chance you'll be here to welcome the "mother of all Orionids" home in 2061.
As for me, I saw Halley in 1986 at the "advanced age" of 30. The odds of another reunion are pretty long — you can do the math.
Until then, I'll be more than happy to step outside early on Wednesday morning and greet a few of "Halley's children." I hope you'll join me.

Joe Rao serves as an instructor and guest lecturer at New York's Hayden Planetarium. He writes about astronomy for Natural History magazine, Sky and Telescope, The Old Farmer's Almanac and other publications.

Joe Rao is Space.com's skywatching columnist, as well as a veteran meteorologist and eclipse chaser who also serves as an instructor and guest lecturer at New York's Hayden Planetarium. He writes about astronomy for Natural History magazine, Sky & Telescope and other publications. Joe is an 8-time Emmy-nominated meteorologist who served the Putnam Valley region of New York for over 21 years. You can find him on Twitter and YouTube tracking lunar and solar eclipses, meteor showers and more. To find out Joe's latest project, visit him on Twitter.

articles.title: When not to watch a meteor shower — why I'm not staying up for the Orionids
articles.author: Jamie Carter

paras.en: I used to think being interested in the night sky meant I had to try every meteor shower. If a calendar said "peak," I interpreted that as an instruction. I'd set an alarm, find several layers of clothing and go outside at around 2:00 a.m. when even the neighborhood cats seemed surprised to see me. Then I'd spend an increasingly resentful 45 minutes staring upward, occasionally see one meteor and wonder whether I was somehow doing it all wrong. As I've grown into stargazing, I've become much more selective.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The Orionids peak next week, and normally I'd be tempted. These fast meteors come from debris from Halley's Comet, which is enough of a connection to make almost anyone want to go outside. However, another object is in the sky this year — a big, bright waxing gibbous moon that will brighten the night sky and make "shooting stars" very hard to see.

That doesn't make the Orionids unobservable. In fact, there is a narrow window when the night sky will be free from moonlight. But it does make me far less inclined to sacrifice an entire night for them, and I certainly won't be trying to spend the night camping under a dark sky in a remote rural location far from light pollution. I've discovered that knowing when not to observe is an underrated stargazing skill.

The Orionids are active from Oct. 2 through Nov. 7, with their 2026 maximum expected overnight on Oct. 21-22. They appear to radiate from a point near Orion, although the meteors themselves can streak across almost any part of the sky.

The shower happens because Earth crosses a stream of debris left behind by Halley's Comet, which was last in the inner solar system in 1986 and will return in 2061. Those tiny particles hit our atmosphere at roughly 41 miles (66 kilometers) per second, making Orionids particularly fast meteors.

Under ideal conditions, the International Meteor Organization gives the shower a zenithal hourly rate of 20 or more around maximum. But "zenithal hourly rate" is not the same as promising that I will personally see 20 meteors while standing in my backyard for an hour. It assumes an excellent dark sky, a well-placed radiant and unobstructed viewing. In reality, that's impossible — at the very least you'd have to have eyes in the back of your head. And on each side.

This year adds another complication. The moon reaches first quarter on Oct. 18 and continues waxing toward full on Oct. 26. On the peak night of the Orionids, an 80%-illuminated waxing gibbous moon will be in the night sky as it gets dark on Oct. 21 and sets around 03:00 a.m. local time across Europe and North America on Oct. 22. You can probably see the workaround. Sunrise is roughly 06:30 a.m. local time, which means astronomical darkness — when the sun is more than 18 degrees below the horizon, meaning complete darkness — lasts until around 05:00 a.m. local time (these times work as a ballpark, but you can (check the exact times of moonset and sunrise for your location on Time and Date).
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: So there is a dark window before dawn, and that is when I would try to see the shower if I were determined to see it. The Orionid radiant is also much better placed after midnight than it is in the evening.
Knowing exactly what's going to happen in the sky turns a casual meteor watch into a rather more calculated exercise.
My plan for the Orionids this year is the same as usual — after checking the moon phase and the moonset and sunrise times, there's one more variable. The weather forecast first.
If the forecast is excellent and I'm feeling enthusiastic, I'll target the period after moonset and before morning twilight on Oct. 22. If it's due to be cloudy, I'm staying in bed.

This sounds obvious, but I think beginners are sometimes given the impression that successful stargazing requires heroic commitment. It doesn't. A meteor shower is not a performance that disappears the moment the advertised "peak" passes. The Orionids have a relatively broad period of activity, so meteors can appear on nights either side of maximum, too.
If I do go outside at 3:00 a.m., I'll do so without two hugely valuable resources for meteor showers — a lawn chair and bags of patience.

The moon reaches first quarter on Oct. 18, making stargazing tricky this week. That means I'm changing what I observe rather than declaring the week a write-off. The moon itself becomes an excellent target in early evening around first quarter. Sunlight strikes the lunar landscape along the terminator — the boundary between lunar day and night — throwing mountains and crater rims into strong relief. A cheap pair of binoculars can reveal a surprising amount. With a telescope, you can spend hours getting lost in the Montes Apenninus mountain range and three nearby craters — Eratosthenes and Archimedes on either side, and Plato above. Saturn remains another easy evening target after its Oct. 4 opposition. Look toward the eastern and southeastern sky after dark for its steady yellowish light. Even a modest telescope pointed at Saturn's rings will astound.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Cassiopeia is one of the easiest constellations I know to find because its five main stars form a conspicuous W — or, right now, something that looks suspiciously more like an M. Look toward the northern sky in the evening. From mid-northern latitudes, Cassiopeia is high and prominent during autumn, on the opposite side of Polaris from the Big Dipper. That relationship is more useful to me than memorizing exactly which way the W should point. Cassiopeia circles Polaris as Earth rotates, so its orientation changes through the night. From sufficiently northerly locations, it's circumpolar, meaning it never sets below the horizon.

He is the editor of WhenIsTheNextEclipse.com, author of A Stargazing Program For Beginners, co-author of The Eclipse Effect, and a senior contributor at Forbes.

articles.title: 'It really does change you': SpaceX Crew-12 commander wishes we could all see our fragile Earth from space
articles.author: Mike Wall

paras.en: The astronauts of SpaceX's Crew-12 mission to the International Space Station wish that we could all see Earth as they just did.

An orbital view reveals the immense beauty of our blue planet, the only world we know of that hosts life. But it also highlights how fragile that life is, tethered to our lonely Earth in the vast void of space, according to Crew-12 commander Jessica Meir of NASA.

"You see this very thin, tenuous band of an atmosphere, and you know that that is all that is supporting life, and we really need to do our best to protect it," Meir said on Thursday afternoon (Oct. 15), during a press conference that discussed the recently concluded Crew-12 mission.

"I wish that I could bring all the eyes of all the humans to look back at the Earth in this extraordinary way that we are so privileged to have," she added. "I think it really does change you philosophically and [in] how you see each other, how you see yourself, how you see the human race when you look on it down from the vantage point that we have from above — you know, [it] gives everybody this understanding that we need to protect our planet, that it's not only so beautiful, but it's so precious."
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: From the International Space Station (ISS), Meir said, it's clear that everything on Earth is connected — and that the borders we've laid down between states and nations are artificial constructs.

"You realize that we really are one human when you are in space," she said. "I wish I could share that perspective with all the eyes of all the humans. I think it would be a very healthy thing for everyone to understand.
Crew-12 mission specialist Andrey Fedyaev, of the Russian space agency Roscosmos, voiced similar sentiments, though he would turn an ISS visitor's eyes inward, to focus on the crew.

"I always say that the life of crewmembers on board the space station is the best example of how people need to live on Earth," Fedyaev said during Thursday's briefing (in Russian; in interpreter translated his words into English in real time)."

"We don't have borders. We are all friendly. We're just one crew, and the safety of the crew, the safety of the station, depends on the actions of the entire crew," he added. "So, if humankind does arrive at the same conclusion — that our Earth, our planet, is one and the same space vessel that flies through space — we need to take care of it and not to destroy it. So, that's what I would like to show to everyone on Earth."

Meir and Fedyaev are far from the only ones to have their perpsectives shifted by a space mission. Pretty much every astronaut experiences this phenomenon, which is known as the overview effect, a term coined in 1987 by space philosopher Frank White.

Crew-12 consisted of Meir, Fedyaev, NASA astronaut Jack Hathaway (the mission's pilot) and the European Space Agency's Sophie Adenot (mission specialist). It was the second spaceflight for Meir and Fedyaev and the first for Hathaway and Adenot.
The quartet launched toward the ISS on Feb. 13 atop a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket. Their Crew Dragon capsule, named Freedom, arrived at the orbiting lab a day later.

Crew-12 spent nearly eight months aboard the ISS, finally returning to Earth on Oct. 8. They conducted a wide range of scientific experiments and maintenance work during that time and set a few records as well.

For example, Adenot became the first French woman ever to perform a spacewalk, and she broke the mark for longest continuous spaceflight by a European at 237 days. The previous record, 201 days, was set by Luca Parmitano in 2019-2020.

Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. To find out what his latest project is, you can follow Michael on Twitter.

articles.title: Agile Space Industries Strengthens Board and Corporate Development to Support Continued Growth
articles.author: Agile Space Industries

paras.en: DURANGO, Colo., Oct. 5, 2026 — Agile Space Industries today announced that Jonathan Baliff has joined its Board of Directors, bringing extensive experience in aerospace, finance, and corporate leadership. His appointment, alongside the addition of Theo Squires as Director of Strategy & Corporate Development, strengthens Agile’s ability to execute its long-term growth strategy, support capital formation, and pursue strategic opportunities as the company continues to scale.

Agile is entering its next phase with growing opportunities across the commercial and national security space. In particular, the company’s recent selection for the SpaceWERX Strategic Funding Increase (STRATFI) program reflects support for adding the ability to supply complete propulsion subsystems. As Agile expands its capabilities and production capacity, the company is also strengthening the financial and strategic foundation needed to support its long-term objectives.

“Agile has built significant momentum, and our next phase of growth requires the financial capability and oversight to match our technical expertise,” said Chris Pearson, CEO of Agile Space Industries. “Jonathan’s experience in aerospace, capital formation and corporate transformation, combined with Theo’s focus on strategy and corporate development, will help us evaluate new opportunities, make strategic investments and position Agile for sustainable, long-term growth.”
Jonathan Baliff Joins Board of Directors

Baliff brings extensive experience across aerospace, finance, and corporate leadership. A former U.S. Air Force aviator and engineer, he currently serves as an operating partner at Genesis Park, where he played a central role in the formation and financing of Redwire Corporation and later served as its chief financial officer. He previously served as president and CEO of Bristow Group and held senior leadership positions at NRG Energy and Credit Suisse. His experience raising capital, guiding strategic investments, and leading organizations through periods of growth and transformation will support Agile as the company continues to scale.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: “Agile has proven it has the technology and operational expertise to compete, win, and profitably grow in a rapidly evolving space market,” said Baliff. “Our customers and capital providers will partner with us as we scale Agile’s technology, expand capacity, and efficiently deploy capital to support the company’s growth. I look forward to working with Chris, our proven team and board to help Agile capitalize on the significant opportunities ahead.”
Expanding Corporate Development to Support Long-Term Strategy

Squires serves as Agile’s Director of Strategy & Corporate Development. Before joining Agile, he served as an intelligence officer in the Royal Australian Navy, where his work included a bilateral space program involving the United States and Australia. He also worked at Boston Consulting Group, advising advanced manufacturing companies on strategy and operations. At Agile, his experience supports capital formation, strategic investments and potential acquisitions of complementary technologies and capabilities to support the company’s broader growth strategy.

articles.title: NASA’s Hubble Spies Spiral’s Edge

paras.en: This NASA Hubble Space Telescope image features the edge-on, intermediate spiral galaxy NGC 1827, located roughly 37 million light-years away in the constellation Columba, the Dove. Hubble captured the image as part of a survey looking at 260 satellite galaxies around 22 Milky Way-like host galaxies within a radius of about 32 million light-years from Earth. Hubble has already observed 111 of these satellite galaxies. The remaining galaxies will take an additional 149 Hubble orbits, one orbit for each galaxy, to observe.

paras.en: The image, taken with Hubble’s Advanced Camera for Surveys, reveals bright-blue regions along the galaxy’s disk dotted with dark dust lanes where new stars are likely forming. A bright foreground star appears just to the left of the galaxy’s bright central bulge but is located between us and the galaxy. Its four diffraction spikes are the result of light bending around the internal supports that hold Hubble’s secondary mirror.

Low-mass galaxies like the ones in this Hubble observing program provide a way to test the predictions of cosmological models on small scales, which struggle to match observations. The data Hubble gathers will help us better understand and characterize the properties of low-mass galaxies in Milky Way-like systems, allowing researchers to refine cosmological models.

articles.title: I Am Artemis: Allison Mjoen
articles.author: Jason Costa

paras.en: As the supercooled propellant flowed into the core stage, and NASA’s SLS (Space Launch System) rocket roared to life, Allison Mjoen and her family watched with awe and pride. Mjoen, NASA’s operations manager for the agency’s Exploration Ground Systems Program, helped shape the systems and ground operations that will one day send humans back to the Moon. Over her 20-year career at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida, she supported missions across the Space Shuttle Program, the International Space Station, and now she is applying that experience to Artemis.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: April 1, 2026, was a bright, crystal-clear day along the Florida Space Coast. The sunlight seemed to sharpen every color along the horizon. As Mjoen and her children counted down and the crowd’s voices rose around them, the rumble of the SLS rocket intensified beneath their feet. For her children, it was the chance to see what their mom had helped make possible. For Mjoen, it was a moment she would never forget.

That moment also offered a pause for reflection on the work that led her there. As the spacecraft offline operations manager, Mjoen coordinates the work that happens long before launch day. By supporting the ground systems’ senior vehicle operations manager, Matt Czech, she develops integration plans and oversees ground operations for Artemis vehicle processing, focusing on booster and Orion spacecraft operations.

Mjoen began her career as a flight crew systems engineer with United Space Alliance supporting the Space Shuttle Program. Her team handled mission-specific cabin configurations, including the food, spacesuits, cargo, and payloads astronauts needed aboard the shuttle.

After the Space Shuttle Program retired, she supported the International Space Station Program as a payload integration engineer. In this role, she connected experiment investigators with the organizations developing their hardware. She later worked in the Project Office on the Test and Operations Support Contract before joining NASA’s Operations Project Engineering Office, where she served as the Spacecraft Payloads Integration and Evolution Element lead for Artemis I.

“Early on, I thought every decision had to be perfect, but everything is an opportunity to learn, especially the tasks that seem unrelated at the time. It’s about staying curious, working hard, building relationships, and trusting that each step is preparing you for the next one.
Operations Manager, NASA's Exploration Ground Systems

That preparation took on new meaning when she first supported integrated firing room operations as a certified operations project engineer during Artemis I. Earning the certification was a milestone. Applying it during real time operations brought a new level of responsibility.
“Every decision and communication directly supported the integrated team’s ability to execute safely and properly implement the test procedure,” said Mjoen.
Working at the integration console underscored the importance of preparation, collaboration and trust — lessons she carries into her work coordinating across teams today.

“I get to collaborate everyday with incredibly talented and dedicated people who are all working toward the same goal. It’s especially rewarding to know that our collective efforts directly contribute to the success of the mission.”
Operations Manager, NASA's Exploration Ground Systems

For Mjoen, the shared experience is part of what makes Artemis so important. As the Artemis program continues, she looks forward to another moment families will be able to share as astronauts return to the lunar surface.

“That single moment captured the imagination of people around the world and showed what is possible when we come together for a bold goal,” she said of the first Apollo Moon landing. “Artemis is creating that kind of moment for a whole new generation, and this time to stay.”

articles.title: NASA Names Stephen Cash Marshall Space Flight Center Director
articles.author: Gerelle Q. Dodson

paras.en: NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman has named Stephen Cash director of the agency’s Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, effective Monday, Oct. 19. Cash, a veteran NASA engineer and aerospace executive, returns to lead the center where he began his career more than four decades ago.

“Marshall contributions to NASA’s missions are historic and it’s no question why it’s the Center of Excellence for propulsion,” said Isaacman. “Steve Cash is a Marshall legend, has spent his career around the hardware, the people and has been in the seat before making the decisions when human spaceflight is on the line. As Marshall continues its critical role in Artemis and takes on new challenges in advanced propulsion, nuclear power, and the systems that will carry us deeper into the solar system, Steve brings the experience, technical judgment, and mission focus needed to lead the center into that next chapter. I am also grateful to Rae Ann Meyer for the leadership she has provided to Marshall during this transition and for her continued service to NASA.”

paras.en: “Leading a NASA center requires a commitment to its people and to the technical capabilities entrusted to them,” said Amit Kshatriya, NASA associate administrator and chief engineer. “Steve understands that the jewel of Marshall is its workforce and that engineering excellence is sustained by giving talented people the opportunity to design, build, test, and learn through hands-on work. As Marshall continues strengthening the manufacturing, structural loads and dynamics, and propulsion capabilities that underpin NASA’s exploration enterprise, Steve’s leadership will help ensure the workforce has opportunities to develop and apply the expertise needed to deliver the agency’s most ambitious missions.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: As center director, Cash will lead one of NASA’s largest field centers, overseeing a workforce of more than 5,000 civil service and contractor employees and a broad portfolio of propulsion, space systems, scientific research, and technology development activities. Marshall plays a critical role in NASA’s Artemis program, including the development of NASA’s SLS (Space Launch System) rocket, management of the Human Landing System Program, as well as other capabilities supporting sustained exploration of the Moon and future missions to Mars. Further, Marshall plays a key role in the advancement of nuclear power and propulsion, an area of focus that is expected to grow as NASA works towards sending the first humans to Mars.

paras.en: “It is a profound honor to be back home at the Marshall Space Flight Center,” said Cash. “I am humbled to stand alongside the brilliant minds here as we continue to turn the impossible into everyday history.”

Cash began his NASA career at Marshall in 1982 and spent 34 years with the agency, holding senior engineering and management positions supporting some of the nation’s most significant human spaceflight programs.

During his NASA career, Cash served as manager of Marshall’s Space Shuttle Propulsion Office, overseeing critical propulsion systems supporting shuttle through its final missions. He later served as director of Marshall’s Safety and Mission Assurance Directorate from 2011 until his retirement in 2016, providing leadership in safety, reliability, and quality engineering to support mission success across the center.

Following his retirement from NASA, Cash continued his work in the aerospace industry, including serving as vice president for advanced space systems at Axient, supporting the development and execution of major spaceflight programs. In 2024, he was inducted into the Alabama Engineering Hall of Fame in recognition of his contributions to engineering and the nation’s space program.

Cash succeeds Rae Ann Meyer, who has served as Marshall’s acting center director since September 2025. Meyer, who previously served as Marshall’s deputy center director and associate director, has provided leadership and continuity across the center’s programs and operations during her tenure as acting director. Meyer will return to her role as Deputy Center Director.

Established in 1960, Marshall has played a central role in American space exploration for more than six decades, from developing the Saturn rockets that carried astronauts to the Moon during Apollo to advancing the propulsion systems, infrastructure, and technologies supporting the next era of human spaceflight.
