articles.title: Automotive Parts Headquarters Raises $513K for WACOSA
articles.author: Mary DellaValle

paras.en: Automotive Parts Headquarters Inc. (APH), together with its supplier partners and the Bartlett family, raised $513,000 through its annual fundraiser benefiting WACOSA, a central Minnesota nonprofit serving adults with disabilities. The 2026 event brings the fundraiser’s 14-year total to $3.7 million.
Proceeds support WACOSA programs that provide meaningful employment, day services and opportunities for more than 650 adults with disabilities across central Minnesota.

The event began with a walleye shore lunch and guided tours of WACOSA before attendees gathered at APH’s newest facility (a bulk storage warehouse) in St. Cloud for a pie and ice cream social celebrating its grand opening and APH’s “Building Our Future Together” initiative.

Attendees also participated in a hands-on art experience led by WACOSA artist-in-residence Dan Mondloch. The individual pieces created during the event will be incorporated into a collaborative collage inspired by the northern lights above a Minnesota lake.

“The day captured so much of what makes this event special,” said Jason Vogel, president of APH Stores Inc. “Bringing our supplier partners, employees and friends together to experience WACOSA’s mission firsthand, celebrate a new chapter for APH and create something together was incredibly rewarding.”

The day concluded with a cocktail reception, lobster-themed dinner and awards ceremony hosted by John and Nancy Bartlett at their home. A highlight of the evening was the presentation of a $513,000 check to Nancy Betts, executive director of WACOSA.

“Fourteen years of support from APH, its supplier partners and the Bartlett family has created a remarkable legacy for the people we serve,” Betts said. “This generosity creates opportunities for people to discover their strengths, contribute to their communities and pursue greater independence. We are deeply grateful for the lasting difference this partnership makes.”
Corey Bartlett, CEO and owner of APH, said the event reflects the generosity and commitment of the automotive aftermarket community.

“Every year, this event reminds us of the extraordinary generosity within the automotive aftermarket,” Bartlett said. “What began as a fundraiser has grown into a lasting partnership between APH, our supplier community and WACOSA. Seeing everyone come together to support the people and mission at the heart of WACOSA is what makes this event so meaningful.”
To view highlights from this year’s event, including the celebration, collaborative art project and messages from industry leaders, visit https://vimeo.com/autopartshq/wacosa26.

articles.title: Value Added: Creating a Culture Beyond Cost
articles.author: Thomas Dayton

paras.en: In case you haven’t noticed, the parts business is a pretty crowded marketplace. In my own little hometown of less than 30,000 people, we have EIGHT parts stores! There are also eight OEM dealer franchises, so there is certainly no lack of options for purchasing auto parts and supplies in our area… and that doesn’t even include online options. With 16 places offering parts in the immediate area, if we want to make a sale we have to make our offerings more attractive than everyone else.

In order to stand out in a crowded market, your operation needs to add value to your products beyond whatever your competitors are offering. That “value” may take the form of different things to different consumers, but this sort of “it factor” is integral to making you stand out in a crowd. Since there are so many kinds of added value, identifying those things your customers value can be challenging.

The Value Stick may sound like some off-brand deodorant, but it’s a concept endorsed by Harvard Business School to visualize the four factors that help build a value-based business strategy. At the top of the stick is a customer’s “willingness to purchase” (WTP), and at the bottom lies your own “willingness to sell” (WTS). In between the two are your cost and the selling price of a product. These four markers are all, to some degree, moveable up or down The Value Stick. WTS primarily concerns the vendors who supply your parts and employees who provide labor for your store. It is the lowest price at which you can purchase your stock and pay someone to sell and distribute it to your customers. WTP, on the other hand, depends solely on a customer’s estimation of your product’s value, and represents the maximum amount of money they will hand over for your product at the point of sale.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Price can be a funny thing. For some, a higher price signals an increase in quality over a less-expensive product (brand name vs. generics, for example), or the cache of luxury (they’d pay $50 more for a Tommy Hilfiger shirt than a similar garment from Wal-Mart). For others, a higher price only means your business is making excessive profits… at their expense. (“I can buy the same thing on Amazon for $20 less than your price, why are you so high?”)

I believe that many of our customers (professional and amateur alike) still view the products we sell daily as interchangeable commodities. As parts professionals, we know better, but when we are faced with those customers for whom “any old thing will do,” we have to use other means to attract them to spend their money with us. Of the four variables along the Value Stick, WTP is the one we have the most influence over. Short of renegotiating supplier prices or reducing staffing costs, we don’t have much control over the cost of our inputs. We must maintain a reasonable margin in order to pay our overhead and keep ourselves in business, so deeply discounting prices is not a long-term solution. The only remaining way to move the needle is to increase the value of our product. Not the individual gasket, chassis part, or alternator, but rather through the experience of purchasing it from us.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: All else being equal, people buy from the people and places they know and trust. It is easier to build these kinds of relationships with commercial customers simply because of the volume of their business. We have more opportunities to show them that we are an important partner in their success, and that we value that partnership. Prompt delivery, complete and accurate order fulfillment and ease of doing business are all value-added services that help justify a premium price tag. For the more occasional customer (professional or retail), we have a shorter window of opportunity to make a lasting impression. Superior customer service is still our greatest advantage with this sort of customer. Employing a knowledgeable and friendly staff, or even utilizing online lookup and ordering platforms can streamline the buying process for customers who value convenience.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Many retailers also build value into their product offering by providing additional services like code-reading, battery testing and installation, or loaner tool programs. Geared toward the non-professional segment of their customer base, these services also position the retailer as a trusted partner in maintaining personal vehicles. Adding value beyond the cost and quality of your parts increases retention and creates a scenario in which satisfied customers become advocates for your business. Give them something no one else can, and they have no reason to go anywhere else.

articles.title: Get Smart: Processes for Continuous Improvement
articles.author: Thomas Dayton

paras.en: Continuous improvement is a business strategy aimed at providing superior customer service through the implementation of a series of small changes in your operations and policies. These individual improvements may be centered around efficiency, productivity, employee happiness, or a multitude of other factors, but, ultimately, their purpose is to make your operation better at attracting, serving and retaining customers.

Continuous improvement is most closely associated with the Japanese word Kaizen. The post-World War II rebuilding of the Japanese industry led to several advances in manufacturing efficiency and quality control, many of which were the basis for “modern” manufacturing and business concepts like “lean” or “just-in-time” manufacturing, Six-Sigma quality control and improvement, and “The Toyota Way.” Each of these concepts has its own variation on identifying potential roadblocks to success, proposing solutions, implementing the means to those solutions, and analyzing the success or failure of any changes made.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Know your customer: by understanding the customer’s needs and wants, you can implement improvements that matter to them.
Let it flow: removing barriers to efficiency and reducing waste creates a smooth workflow.
Go to where the work happens: don’t manage from an office, see the problem firsthand.
Empower people: improvements and the resulting success require input from the “bottom up.”
Transparency: share plans, goals, and results with the entire team.

These principles can be applied to any problem in your operation, but continuous improvement is often used initially in smaller, incremental stages. These small changes are easier to implement, as they do not require a complete overhaul of company culture or the involvement of the entire staff. These can be “experimental” changes on a small scale, to test their effectiveness in specific situations or with a particular department. Breakthrough continuous improvements are larger in scale, and are most effective when a process or operation is in need of a complete overhaul. In either situation, proposed improvements should align with these five principles.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: In order to transform the vague idea of a potential improvement into a clear plan of action with defined results, continuous improvement plans often rely on setting “SMART” goals. SMART is an acronym for “Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Timely.” SMART goals are a litmus test for determining if what you want to achieve is realistic and worthwhile to spend the time, energy, and money pursuing. Have you set a specific goal that accurately reflects the improvement(s) which you are hoping to implement? Can you measure the progress in a clear and meaningful way, so you know where you are in the process and know when you have achieved the goal? Is the improvement achievable with your current staff and resources? Are the changes relevant to your operation’s mission, values, and culture? And finally, is the goal time-sensitive? A goal without a deadline is more of a dream.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Once your organization has committed to continuous improvement and SMART goals have been set, the next step is to create and standardize the processes you want to use in working toward those goals. Staff must be given the tools (and the training) to implement any intended changes, and also an opportunity to express constructive opinions concerning the “real-world” effectiveness of the improvements. Project leaders should monitor the progress of each improvement project throughout the process and measure the results using key performance indicators (KPIs) tied to the results you hope to achieve through the planned changes.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: If the process yields positive results, you are (as an organization) one step closer to achieving your goal of serving your customers more effectively. Share your successes with those who helped create them, with others in the organization who may benefit from the discovery, and, most importantly, with the customers whom you are doing this for in the first place!

articles.title: Best wildlife cameras 2026: The ultimate buying guide to every major camera brand
articles.author: Kimberley Lane

paras.en: Wildlife photographers need a camera that is reliable and built to capture fast-moving action at a moment's notice. A fast burst rate, accurate autofocus and robust handling are vital when it comes to wildlife cameras, or you'll end up with sad, blurry photos of an empty tree stump.
We've curated a list of the best models from each of the top camera brands, so no matter which system you want to invest in, there will be something for you here.

Kimberley Lane, senior e-commerce writer for Live Science, has tested a wide range of optical equipment, including a huge variety of cameras and lenses. With over 7 years of photography experience, her skills span across many different genres, including landscape and seascape photography, wildlife, astrophotography and portrait work. Her photos have been featured in numerous national magazines, including Digital Camera World and Cosmopolitan.
Best Canon cameras for wildlife photography

Canon's highest-resolution mirrorless camera with a 45MP stacked sensor, the R5 II is for wildlife photographers who want a professional workflow and need to crop aggressively. It's flexible across multiple wildlife types and delivers pro-level output without going all the way up to the R1.
- 45.5MP resolution produces beautiful images and allows a lot of cropping room
- Stacked sensor enables faster readout speed, better noise handling and no rolling shutter
- 30FPS blackout-free burst rate is ideal for wildlife photography
- Excellent autofocus on moving subjects
- Chunky grip easily handles larger lenses
- Excellent hybrid shooter, boasting up to 8K 60p RAW video
- Quite a bit more expensive than the new R6 III, which could be the more sensible option

The new Canon EOS R6 III is an absolute triumph for wildlife photography, and it has solved all the niggles we had with the R6 II when we reviewed it. It has blackout-free 40FPS shooting and an improved 32.5MP sensor, with pre-continuous shooting and up to 7K video. This camera is hard to beat for enthusiasts and intermediate-level shooters.
- Blisteringly fast blackout-free 40FPS bursts
- Improved 32.5MP resolution compared to the Mark II's 24MP sensor.
- Pre-continuous shooting ensures you never miss a shot
- Sticky and accurate subject tracking (most of the time)
- Compatible with faster CFexpress cards
- Excellent battery life — we easily took over 6,000 images before our SD card gave out
- CFexpress card slot comes at the expense of a second SD card slot
- New LP-E6P battery means you'll have to invest in new spares

A monster camera for professional wildlife and sport photographers who need unrivaled power and reliability and can afford to invest in their photography career. Even though it doesn't have the best resolution, the stacked sensor produces less noise and better image quality, and allows for a faster readout speed.
Read the full Canon EOS R1 review at our sister site, Digital Camera World
- Pre-continuous shooting to ensure you never miss a shot
- Built like a tank, with a large integrated vertical grip for professional sports and wildlife photography
- 9.44 million dot viewfinder is bright and detailed
- Not a small or lightweight camera — over 2.42 pounds (1.1kg) before you even add a lens
Best Sony cameras for wildlife photography

A big and welcome upgrade from the previous generation, with a new partially stacked sensor, improved AI autofocus and finally, a higher burst rate than the rather feeble 10FPS of the previous generation. The Sony A7 V is a very attractive option for wildlife, as well as general photography and hybrid shooting, but its Achilles heel is the shallow buffer, which fills up fast and will very quickly get annoying if you regularly shoot in bursts.
We will be reviewing the A7 V soon, but until then, you can read the full review at our sister site, Digital Camera World
- Blackout-free 30FPS burst rate with AF/AE tracking is much improved over the 10FPS in the previous model
- Features new partially stacked 33MP sensor to produce stunning and detailed images
- New AI subject detection can detect birds, animals and insects — including Eye AF
- This model now offers pre-capture, which captures images just before the shutter is pressed
- Handles noise well, which is an advantage if you're shooting at dawn or dusk, or are pairing it with a more affordable lens with an f/5.6 max aperture.
- Autofocus can struggle when shooting small birds or through foliage
- Buffer depth (~95 compressed RAW files) is shallow and will fill quickly

With Sony's highest resolution yet, the monstrous A7R VI is the newest and most expensive model in the R lineup. Sony has finally answered our prayers by boosting the burst rate from 10FPS in the previous model up to a massive 30FPS in this new one. For this price, that's more like it. Plus, with a massive 67MP, you'll get some serious cropping power, which comes in handy if you're shooting distant wildlife or birds.
We will be reviewing the A7R VI soon, but for now, you can read the full review at our sister site, Digital Camera World
- Massive 67MP offers exceptional detail and leaves tons of room for cropping
- 30FPS blackout-free bursts seriously levels up the R range like never before

- Offers Continuous Shooting Speed Boost, which allows you to assign a custom button to temporarily jump from a lower, more sustained burst rate to the maximum 30FPS instantly, which avoids filling up the card too quickly
- AI subject detection has animal, bird and insect modes and is generally very accurate
- Pre-capture records images before you fully press the shutter
- High resolution means noisy images — we definitely found this to be the case with the previous generation
- Autofocus can be tripped up if your animal is partially covered by reeds or branches
- The most expensive release in the R range

Experienced users looking for a balance of resolution and speed need look no further than the Sony A1 II. It has a 50.1MP stacked sensor, 30FPS bursts and Sony's class-leading AI autofocus, so what's not to love? That said, it's overkill for beginners and amateurs — plus we'd only recommend it if you can also invest in some of Sony's more expensive glass.
Read the full Sony A1 II review at our sister site, Digital Camera World
- A perfect blend of speed (30FPS blackout-free bursts) and resolution (50.1MP)
- Sticky, accurate AI autofocus with Eye AF for animals, birds and insects
- Both card slots accept CFexpress Type A or SD UHS-II/UHS-I
- RAW files offer incredible dynamic range
- Pre-capture starts taking images when the shutter is half-pressed
- Expensive, and will be wasted money unless you can also afford to invest in expensive lenses
- New Sony A7R VI is cheaper and has more resolution
- Overkill unless you're an experienced shooter
Best Nikon cameras for wildlife photography

For wildlife photography (and most other styles, too, while we're at it), the obvious choice for most Nikon shooters is the Nikon Z8. Often dubbed a "baby Z9", it has all the brains and brawn of the flagship Z9 in a smaller and more affordable package.

- Up to 120FPS bursts (11MP), or 20FPS sustained — all blackout-free
- It can record more than 1,000 RAW images before any buffering kicks in — insanely useful for wildlife
- Pre-release burst captures up to 1 second of images before the shutter is fully pressed
- 120FPS is only 11MP, which you likely won't need when you're buying a 45.7MP camera

If you saw the Z8 and thought, "Hey, I need something big and heavy", then the flagship R9 could be better for you. The integrated grip offers improved balance and weight distribution for longer lenses, although it's only compatible with CFexpress cards, making this model best suited for professionals.

- Advanced 3D tracking and dedicated animal/bird eye AF
- Stunning 45.7MP resolution from a stacked sensor
- 20FPS blackout-free burst shooting for RAW images, with an option for 120FPS bursts at 11MP
- Pre-release burst can capture images up to 1 second before the shutter is fully pressed
- Robust, and built like a tank for heavy shooting over long periods
- Only compatible with expensive CFexpress cards
- Not as travel-friendly as the Z8 due to the bigger and heavier body
- Not many people will use 120FPS for 11MP images
- 3.69 million-dot EVF resolution is a little low compared to other flagship models like the Sony A1 II and Canon EOS R1 (9.44 million)

For anyone on a moderate budget looking for a capable wildlife camera, the Nikon Z6 III has a partially stacked sensor, 20FPS RAW shooting and dedicated animal and bird detection modes, all wrapped up in a compact and lightweight body — the only downside being the rather limited 24.5MP resolution.
Read the full Nikon Z6 III review at our sister site, Digital Camera World

- 24.5MP resolution won't allow for heavy cropping
- Some users report that the autofocus struggles with birds in flight at a distance

Best OM System cameras for wildlife photography

Wildlife photographers who want a powerful system in a small package should look at the OM-1 Mark II — it can shoot a blisteringly fast 50FPS with full AF/AE tracking (or 120FPS with locked focus), and even though the 20.4MP resolution sounds a little on the low side, we were pleasantly surprised by the image quality.

- Accurate autofocus with bird and human modes
- Compact and lightweight, even when paired with long lenses
- Pro Capture captures images before shutter is fully pressed
- Buffer can hold around 213 RAW frames at 120FPS
- 20.4MP may be underwhelming for some users, and doesn't allow for heavy cropping
- Not enough of an upgrade if you already own the OM-1

If you're just getting into wildlife photography and don't need the best of the best, the OM-5 Mark II is a great camera for people who want to photograph wildlife among other styles. It lacks dedicated bird/animal subject detection, but on the whole, OM System's autofocus is still pretty good.

- Bird and animal subject detection modes

Best Fujifilm cameras for wildlife photography
With its speedy burst shooting, accurate autofocus and stacked sensor, the X-H2S is ideal for fast action shooting, birds in flight and hybrid photo/video shooters.

- Up to 40FPS blackout-free burst rate while maintaining full autofocus
- Animal and bird autofocus subject detection
- Compatible with both SD and CFexpress cards
- Sturdy build and large grip to balance long lenses
- Middle of the road 26.1MP resolution produces nice images, but doesn't leave room for heavy cropping
- Expensive compared to other APS-C models
- It's not a particularly small camera for an APS-C
- Users report the autofocus is not as good as Sony, Canon and Nikon.

The Fuji X-T5 is a compact APS-C camera to suit traveling photographers perfectly, but the small buffer and hit-and-miss autofocus are better suited to photographing slow-moving, larger mammals as opposed to fast action and birds. Still, it's a versatile option that can shoot multiple styles and produces beautiful 40.2MP images.
Read the full Fuji X-T5 review at our sister site, Digital Camera World
- High resolution 40.2MP produces beautiful images and allows for cropping on distant subjects
- Features an in-built 1.4x and 2x teleconverter in the shooting settings, extending your reach
- Animal, bird and insect tracking modes
- Compact and lightweight system compared to full-frame models
- Electronic shutter shoots up to 20FPS with a 1.29x crop, which is advantageous if you need extra reach for wildlife
- Autofocus occasionally misses — generally not as reliable as Sony, Canon or Nikon.
- Doesn't have the biggest grip for larger lenses
- Buffer fills up quite quickly, and users report that it takes a while to clear

The Fuji X-T50 is an attractive, compact option for beginner wildlife photographers who don't yet need an expensive model with all the bells and whistles. Still, the 40.2MP resolution is beautiful, and it can shoot 20FPS bursts, which is great for wildlife action.

- Beautiful 40.2MP resolution that allows for cropping
- 20FPS burst rate comes with a 1.29x crop, which will give you extra reach on your wildlife lens
- Like the X-T5, it features a built-in teleconverter (1.4x and 2x) to extend your wildlife reach
- Very compact and portable — would suit travel photographers well
- Buffer fills up quickly and takes a while to clear, limiting your bursts
- Autofocus isn't as good as Sony, Canon or Nikon
Best Panasonic cameras for wildlife photography

The Lumix G9 II is particularly well suited to birds and fast-moving subjects thanks to its high-speed bursts, improved animal tracking and the extra reach advantage of Micro Four Thirds lenses. It sacrifices some low-light performance compared to full-frame models, but for wildlife, where reach and speed matter, it's the standout choice from Panasonic.
Read the full Panasonic Lumix G9 II review at our sister site, Digital Camera World
- Up to 60FPS bursts with continuous autofocus
- Micro Four Thirds sensor gives extra reach with 2x crop factor — and allows for more compact lenses
- Pre-capture records up to 1.5 seconds before the shutter is fully released
- Animal and bird eye detection locks onto subjects accurately and quickly
- Smaller sensor produces more visible noise than a full-frame sensor
- 25MP resolution doesn't provide much room for cropping
- Electronic shutter can show rolling shutter
- While the autofocus is good compared to previous Panasonic bodies, it's still not as good as Sony/Canon/Nikon
The Lumix S5 II is for wildlife photographers who want full-frame image quality and strong modern autofocus, but don't want to pay Canon/Sony/Nikon flagship prices for their camera bodies and lenses.
Read the full Panasonic Lumix S5 II review at our sister site, Digital Camera World
- Full-frame sensor delivers better high ISO performance for low-light wildlife at dawn or dusk
- 30FPS electronic burst is great for fast action with continuous autofocus
- Works well with Sigma L-mount lenses for cost-effective setups
- Animal eye tracking to lock focus on stationary and moving animals.
- 24.2MP gives less room to crop when shooting distant subjects
- Less effective reach compared to Micro Four Thirds

This premium wildlife workhorse has a partially-stacked 24.1MP sensor and 70FPS blackout-free burst rate. It features animal and bird detection, but although the autofocus is generally very good, it still trails behind the best-in-class autofocus from the likes of Sony, Canon and Nikon.
Read the full Panasonic Lumix S1 II review at our sister site, Digital Camera World
- Partially stacked sensor eliminates rolling shutter and allows for faster readout speeds
- Blazing fast 70FPS blackout-free bursts with continuous autofocus
- Pre-burst captures images up to 1.5 seconds before you fully release the shutter
- Full frame sensor is better in low light than Micro Four Thirds
- 24.1MP resolution limits heavy cropping
- Users report occasional autofocus accuracy issues
What camera do most wildlife photographers use?

Dedicated wildlife photographers typically choose full-frame mirrorless cameras due to their larger sensor, better noise handling, accurate autofocus and rugged build. Many of these cameras also have fast burst rates, which is essential for capturing fast-moving wildlife or birds in flight.
Beginners and hobbyists can certainly get great shots with more portable models, but some compromises will have to be made in terms of speed and power.
What burst rate do I need for wildlife photography?

This depends on what kind of wildlife you're photographing, and how fast they move. Generally speaking, the best wildlife cameras have a burst rate of at least 20FPS (frames per second) — but the faster the better. If you photograph large, slow-moving mammals or stationary subjects, your burst rate doesn't need to be rattling off 40FPS at a time. If, however, you photograph birds in flight or fast moving animals, you will need a faster burst rate in order to capture that killer shot.
How many megapixels does a wildlife camera need?

There's no right or wrong answer here, but generally speaking, a higher resolution is preferred because it produces more detailed images, and you have more room to crop without losing image quality. However, more megapixels equals bigger file sizes, and you therefore need faster cards in order to keep up, especially when you're taking bursts.
That said, you can absolutely get some great shots with lower resolution cameras. We've been impressed by the quality of OM System cameras, and they typically only have around 20MP.
What is the best wildlife camera for beginners?

The most important aspect of a wildlife camera for beginners to prioritize is good autofocus. Provided your subject is in focus, you don't necessarily need the fastest burst rate, top of the line weather sealing or highest resolution.
For our money, Sony, Canon and Nikon offer the best autofocus on the market. We'd recommend the Sony A7C II, Canon EOS R7 or Nikon Zf for beginners.
How much should I spend on a wildlife camera?

You don't need to go overboard unless you're a professional wildlife photographer looking for the top of the range flagship models. You can get a really impressive wildlife camera for "most people" for anywhere between $2,000 and $3,000, but as many photographers will tell you, it's more beneficial to invest money in a better lens as opposed to splashing out on the very best camera.

articles.title: Ancient Indigenous people in New Mexico lived through extreme climate change 23,000 years ago, study suggests
articles.author: Patrick Pester

paras.en: Some of the first people in North America lived through extreme climate change at the peak of the last ice age, a new study suggests.

Researchers studied ancient pollen locked in rocks at White Sands National Park in New Mexico, which houses an archaeological site thought to contain the oldest human footprints in the Americas. The researchers previously dated those footprints to around 21,000 to 23,000 years ago, though their age is the subject of some scientific debate because they are significantly older than other Indigenous sites in the Americas.

The new findings, published Wednesday (Oct. 14) in the journal Science Advances, suggest that humans kept using White Sands after temperatures warmed and thus saw the landscape undergo rapid changes during the coldest era of the last ice age, known as the Last Glacial Maximum (26,500 to 19,000 years ago).

"It's remarkable that early humans in the region were real-time witnesses to a rapidly changing environment discernible within a human lifetime — that is really food for thought," study co-author Kathleen Springer, a research geologist at the U.S. Geological Survey, said in a statement.

The White Sands footprints suggest that people from Asia reached the Americas via the region around the Bering Strait much earlier than scientists initially thought, challenging a long-held assumption that humans arrived on the continent around 13,000 years ago. While some scientists have disputed the methods used to date the footprints, evidence is building that they are around 23,000 years old.

White Sands contains footprints from various time periods, including footprints of a caregiver and a toddler who were there 10,000 years ago. Over thousands of years, people trudged across the New Mexico landscape alongside iconic ice age animals, including mammoths and giant ground sloths. The researchers have also discovered sled-like drag marks alongside ancient footprints at White Sands, providing evidence for a kind of travois — a wooden frame made from two poles bound together — that people likely would have used for transporting goods.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: By looking at ancient pollen for the new study, researchers could deduce which plants grew across the millennia when humans lived in the area. The site's rock samples also contained waxes from plant leaves, membrane lipids from bacteria, and other organic molecules that helped the researchers better understand the environmental conditions of the time.
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The analysis revealed that around 24,200 years ago, White Sands had a large lake and its surrounding mountains were coated in conifer trees (Pinus, Abies, and Picea). Then, over the next two millennia, temperatures rose, the lake began to shrink, and the conifer trees were replaced by oak trees (Quercus) and sagebrush, according to the statement.
- Inuit figurine: A 700-year-old Indigenous carving of a European made a century before Columbus
- 'It gives us a glimpse of a different kind of Viking life': Archaeologist Neil Price on the sea-kings, sorcerers and Sámi who lived during the Viking Age
- Ancient Egyptians sacrificed pharaohs' servants so they could continue to serve their king in the afterlife, new study finds

"Throughout these periods of change, the people continued to visit and live in this area," study co-author Sally Reynolds, a paleoanthropologist at Bournemouth University in the U.K., said in the statement. "The sediments containing their footprints show us their environment changed significantly within individual human lifetimes."

The researchers speculated that people might have returned to White Sands at different times to benefit from the changing climate, with a shrinking lake potentially providing higher concentrations of animals and plants. However, while the footprints document that humans were present, they reveal little about their behavior.

"The footprints give us a snapshot of the people who lived there over 20,000 years ago," Reynolds said. "But they are not a continuous movie of their lives. They are individual frames — showing moments when humans, mud, water and chance came together."

L., Reynolds, S. C., & Bennett, M. R. (2026). Humans experienced abrupt environmental changes at White Sands during the Last Glacial Maximum. Patrick Pester is the trending news writer at Live Science. His work has appeared on other science websites, such as BBC Science Focus and Scientific American. Patrick retrained as a journalist after spending his early career working in zoos and wildlife conservation. He was awarded the Master's Excellence Scholarship to study at Cardiff University where he completed a master's degree in international journalism. He also has a second master's degree in biodiversity, evolution and conservation in action from Middlesex University London. When he isn't writing news, Patrick investigates the sale of human remains.

articles.title: 2 giant Ramesses II statues, one wearing a double crown, discovered by man in Egypt
articles.author: Owen Jarus

paras.en: While working on his land in a village in northern Egypt, a man made an astonishing discovery: the remains of two massive statues of Ramesses II.

The man, Khaled el-Shahat, immediately notified the Egyptian Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities, which sent a team to the village of Behbeit El Hagar to excavate and study the statues, the ministry said in a translated statement.

Ramesses II had one of the longest reigns in Egypt's history, ruling from around 1279 to 1213 B.C. During his 66 years in power, Egypt controlled an empire that stretched as far northeast as modern-day Syria. He initiated many building projects throughout the empire, and numerous Ramesses II statues have been found throughout Egypt.

Archaeologists had previously found architectural fragments bearing the name of Ramesses II at Behbeit El Hagar, which is known for its temple dedicated to Isis, a goddess associated with healing and magic, said Mahmoud Emam, an Egyptologist at Cairo University who has worked on remains from the site but was not involved with the recent excavation. He noted that the newly found statues were unearthed on the western side of the temple complex.

Both of the newfound statues were once larger than life, with the bigger one likely standing nearly 28 feet (8.5 meters) tall when it was originally built. However, most of what remains is its head, which is 5.2 feet (1.6 m) tall and depicts the pharaoh wearing the double crown of Upper and Lower Egypt.

Part of this large statue's back pillar has a hieroglyphic inscription that gives the pharaoh's "Horus" name: Hor-Ka-Nakht-Mery-Maat. This name means "Strong Bull, Beloved of Right, Truth," Joyce Tyldesley, a professor emeritus of Egyptology at the University of Manchester in the U.K., wrote in her book "Ramesses: Egypt's Greatest Pharaoh" (Penguin Books, 2001). In Egypt, it was common for pharaohs to have several alternate names with a Horus name, given in honor of the sky god Horus.

The second statue, which stands about 7.9 feet (2.4 m), also likely depicts Ramesses II, the statement said. The king is shown wearing the "Nemes" headdress, a type of striped headcloth that pharaohs wore, the Egypt Exploration Society notes on its website.
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Near this statue is a block of pink granite with two hieroglyphic inscriptions that name Ramesses II and describe him as "King of Upper and Lower Egypt" and the "Son of Ra," an ancient Egyptian sun god, the statement said.
The new finds add more evidence that Ramesses II was heavily invested in the site.

Previous discoveries include two architectural fragments bearing the name of Ramesses II near the Isis temple at Behbeit El Hagar, Emam and his colleagues reported in a 2017 paper. One is believed to be from the upper part of a statue, and another seems to originate from the upper part of a wall.

"We concluded that Ramesses II had undertaken major building works at the temple and recommended further archaeological investigations to shed more light on the early history of the site," Emam said. He noted that the site is threatened by urban growth and that excavation work should be carried out at the temple.
Live Science reached out to the team but did not hear back by the time of publication.
Are you a fan of mummies and hieroglyphs? Find out with our ancient Egypt quiz!

Owen Jarus is a regular contributor to Live Science who writes about archaeology and humans' past. He has also written for The Independent (UK), The Canadian Press (CP) and The Associated Press (AP), among others. Owen has a bachelor of arts degree from the University of Toronto and a journalism degree from Ryerson University.

articles.title: This Soldier Kept a Diary in the Trenches of World War I. A Child Found It at the Dump Decades Later, Pierced by a Bullet and Stained With Blood

paras.en: The day the boy found the diary, he’d been scrounging for treasures at the local dump in Stourbridge, England. He and his friends had entered through a small opening at the bottom of a wire fence. Then they spotted something among the bottles and cans: a nearly four-inch-long volume with a green cover, its pages turning in the wind.

The year was 1965, but the diary entries dated to 1918. Their author was a man named Corporal Claude Nuttall, who had served as an infantryman (or “Digger”) in the Australian Army during World War I. He met his wife, Violet Palfreyman, while recovering from an injury in an English hospital. Weeks after the wedding, he returned to the front.

Did Nuttall ever make it home? The boy wondered about the soldier’s fate, and the diary offered several ominous clues. The corner appeared to have been pierced by a bullet, and its pages were stained with blood. Nuttall’s last entry was dated August 10, 1918. The pages that followed were blank.
“Heavy bombardment by our guns. Push still in progress,” he wrote. “Packed up ready to move forward again. Prisoners still coming back. Wrote to Violet.”

The diary eventually made its way to Colin Reid, a former curator at the Dudley Museum and Art Gallery in England’s West Midlands, who spent decades researching the soldier’s story. The culmination of his efforts is the book The Digger’s Diary, which comes out this fall.

“At the start, I wanted to solve the mystery of Claude’s fate,” Reid tells Smithsonian magazine. “An emotional compulsion, I suppose. The fact that his diary was unfinished, bloodstained and had been punctured by a bullet compelled me to find out if he had survived and returned back to Violet.”

The story of the diary’s discovery begins with the Stourbridge dump. The boy who found the volume was 12-year-old Alan Southall, who held onto it for three decades. In 1996, he showed up at the Dudley Museum asking for Reid, who was then working on a World War I exhibition. Southall pulled out the diary, which he’d carefully tucked inside a plastic bag, and asked whether the curator wanted to put it on display.

But Southall had other questions, too. In The Digger’s Diary, the curator recalls what his visitor told him: “For 30 years, I’ve wanted to know Corporal Nuttall’s fate. But I have never done anything about it, because I don’t think things ended well for him.”

The diary went on view in the museum’s exhibition, titled “The Great War.” But when the show closed, Reid kept thinking about the little book with the green cover. About a decade later, he decided to write a book of his own. The curator tracked down Southall, who let him borrow the diary.

Reid got to work, searching for any information he could find about the Australian soldier. “The more I learned, the more I wanted to learn,” he tells BBC News’ Aida Fofana and Sarah Julian. “Right from the very first moment that I held the diary, I had that real sense of connection with it. I was really hooked.”
- On August 4, 1914, Australia entered World War I—the deadliest conflict in the country’s history.
- According to the Australian War Memorial, the country’s population was fewer than five million at the time, and the death toll was more than 60,000.

Born in 1895, Nuttall enlisted in the Australian Army’s 23rd Battalion in 1915, just after his 20th birthday. He traveled to the Western Front, where he fought the Germans. In his diary, he’d written that he’d been awarded a medal from George V; Reid had always wanted to know more about the courageous act that merited this reward. He found the answer in Nuttall’s military records: On his 21st birthday, in July 1916, the soldier had helped rescue injured soldiers from no man’s land, the perilous stretch of earth between opposing trenches.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Later that year, Nuttall was wounded in northern France. He was sent to a hospital in Stourbridge, where he met Palfreyman. The couple tied the knot in March 1918. “All excited,” the corporal wrote in his journal. “Married 12:30 p.m. All went well.” Five weeks later, he shipped out again. His service records show that he died on August 13, 1918, just three days after his final diary entry.

Thanks to Palfreyman’s relatives, Reid tracked down photos from the couple’s wedding. He also traveled to Cheltenham, the Australian suburb where the soldier grew up, to meet Nuttall’s family, as well as the French battlefields where Nuttall had fought and died.

In 2018, Reid and Southall met up with Arthur Thomas, the corporal’s nephew, to visit Nuttall’s grave in Harbonnieres, France. Together, they commemorated the 100th anniversary of his death. A few months later, the diary was returned to Nuttall’s family at a ceremony in Cheltenham.

“I keep saying that the saddest part is that my mother, her two sisters and even Claude’s own mother know nothing of this. I can’t tell them what’s happened,” Thomas told the Dudley News’ Kelly Harris in 2018. “I have seen pictures of Claude’s wedding and Violet’s family that they would never have seen.”

But what about the bloodstains? Was the bullet that struck the diary fatal? “I’m afraid that I can’t reveal that to you,” Reid tells Smithsonian. “It’s a huge spoiler, and the emotional climax of the book—definitely embargoed.”

He can, however, reveal Palfreyman’s fate, which was equally tragic. After Nuttall’s death, she married the owner of a carpet shop. The couple had a son named Eric and a baby girl who died soon after she was born. Palfreyman herself died from childbirth complications a few months later. “She and the child are buried together at Holy Trinity Church in Stourbridge,” Reid says, “barely 100 yards from the altar where she and Claude were married.”

The Digger’s Diary, as the author writes in the preface, is a “tribute to the man I discovered: a forgotten hero, a soldier of quiet fortitude and extraordinary courage.” But it’s also a tribute to the woman Nuttall fell in love with—and to Reid’s own wife, who shares her name. The book begins with a dedication page, which reads simply “For Violet.”

articles.title: On an Island Outside Paris, a Sprawling Contemporary Arts Center Aptly Called 'Large' Prepares to Open Its Doors

paras.en: Just outside of Paris, perched on an island in the Seine River, a massive, much-anticipated institution is preparing to open its doors. Spanning some 54,000 square feet, the capital region’s newest contemporary art center, which officially debuts this weekend, appears poised to live up to its name: Large.

The scale of the new development on Île Seguin is, in fact, large. Shining with a copper and aluminum exterior, Large is the centerpiece of a roughly 570,000-square-foot, $500-million development called Pointe des Arts, which includes a performing arts center, movie theater, sculpture garden, hotel, shopping district and more.
Though Large’s name is also meant to evoke the French phrase “prendre le large,” which means “to set sail,” the island it sits on is better known among Parisians for its rich automotive history.

Throughout much of the 20th century, the island belonging to the inner suburb of Boulogne-Billancourt was home to the original Renault car factory, an industrial and economic powerhouse for France. In the 1930s, more than 30,000 workers made their living at the plant. But after its closure in 1992, the island began to stall. The abandoned plant was not torn down until 2005, and the effort to turn the post-industrial site into a public space moved slowly.
- Renault company founder Louis Renault continued to produce vehicles under the German occupation of France in World War II, leading to his postwar arrest for collaboration.
- The Renault company was subsequently nationalized in 1945.

“In the face of trials and tribulations, the project called for a great deal of perseverance,” Pierre-Christophe Baguet, the mayor of Boulogne-Billancourt, says in a statement. “Over the course of almost 20 years, many succumbed to fatalism and discouragement and gave up on the site. Others sought to derail the project rather than to see it succeed. … It is a great victory over ignorance and prevailing selfishness.”

As an homage to the location’s history, Large’s inaugural exhibition, titled “Imaginary Engine,” will focus on the relationship between humans and machines, with a particular emphasis on cars. The show features more than 100 artworks created by 55 artists from 23 countries. The oldest pieces on display were made in the 1930s, while 17 pieces were commissioned for the museum’s opening.

“Opening a new institution is always rare, and doing it on an island so charged with memory is a real privilege,” Cecilia Alemani, who curated “Imaginary Engine,” tells ARTnews’ Sarah Belmont. “The Renault factory was dismantled long ago, and today a brand-new building rises in its place, open to everyone.”

The exhibition is separated into five thematic chapters, each exploring industrial constraints and mechanical language with a variety of media. Accompanying the exhibition, which runs through March 7, is a series of film screenings that center iconic cars and car chases, including The Blues Brothers, Thelma and Louise and Taxi Tehran.

Starting with “Imaginary Engines,” Large is meant to serve a similar function to the Museum of Modern Art in New York City. “Paris needed a place where it could showcase art by artists who live and work here, whether they are established or emerging,” Paula Aisemberg, Large’s director, tells the New York Times’ Tina Isaac-Goizé.
Large plans to operate by rotating temporary exhibitions throughout its vast public-facing space, 40 percent of which will cost nothing to visit. Visitors who are 26 or younger will be admitted free.

“‘Large’ is its name. It is an invitation to set sail, to shift our perspectives, and to broaden our horizons,” Laurent Dumas, president of Large, says in the statement. “Because art transforms our ways of seeing and understanding the world, it is essential that we share and transmit it.”
“Imaginary Engine” will be on view at Large in Boulogne-Billancourt, France, from October 17, 2026, to March 7, 2027.

articles.title: It's Official: Timekeepers Have Gotten Rid of the Leap Second—and Introduced the Leap Hour Instead

paras.en: Every four years, February gets an extra day. You’ve heard of these “leap” years, especially if an acquaintance was born on the unusual date of February 29. What you might not have heard of, however, is the leap year’s sporadic sibling: the leap second.

This lesser-known timekeeping fix was center stage at this week’s General Conference on Weights and Measures in France, where timekeepers decided today to return it to obscurity by getting rid of it altogether.

Traditionally, one Earth orbit around the sun determines the length of a year, and one Earth rotation on its axis determines the length of a day. Because it takes Earth around 365.25 days to go around the sun, timekeepers add that extra leap day once every four years to make sure our seasonal calendar stays aligned with the orbit.

Earth’s daily rotation, however, isn’t as regular, because the speed of the planet’s spin can change. In general, Earth’s rotational speed has been slowing down throughout history. But starting around 2020, it has increased. A number of factors can play a role in Earth’s spin, including the atmosphere, ocean currents, wind, volcanoes and melting polar ice.
This makes Earth’s rotation a “lousy” clock, Jeff Sherman, a physicist at the United States’ National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), tells CNN’s Katie Hunt.
Earth’s rotation does not exactly match the length of a day on our clocks. Right now, the average day on Earth is slightly longer than 24 hours. October 14, 2026, was 24 hours and 0.0006471 seconds.

Even as Earth’s spin wavers, our atomic clocks—crucial to keeping ultra-precise time in this age of computers, phones, GPS and satellites—tick at a stable rate. That’s because in 1967, the General Conference on Weights and Measures chose a reliable way to define a second with the help of the isotope cesium-133. When a cesium-133 atom undergoes a change between specific energy states, it emits radiation that oscillates in an exceptionally regular manner, Vahe Peroomian, a physicist at the University of Southern California, writes for the Conversation. As such, scientists reclassified a second as equivalent to 9,192,631,770 cesium-133 atom oscillations.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Today, Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) follows this principal. But astronomical time, or Universal Time 1 (UT1), follows Earth’s fickle rotation, sometimes leading to discrepancies between the two time scales. To keep these systems as aligned as possible, timekeepers have added 27 leap seconds to UTC since 1972. “We effectively stop our clocks for that second to give Earth the opportunity to catch up,” as Konstantin Bikos and Anne Buckle write for Time and Date.

The goal has been for UTC and UT1 to differ by less than 0.9 seconds, and a leap second has been added when the misalignment approaches that limit. Today, however, experts at the General Conference on Weights and Measures voted to increase this margin to one hour. This negates the need for a leap second and creates the much rarer leap hour, which will be added when UTC deviates from UT1 by 3,600 seconds. Such a change likely won’t be needed for hundreds or thousands of years.

“It’s kind of a philosophical discussion, because if a leap hour happens, it won’t be for a very, very long time,” Christian Bizouard, director of the IERS Earth Orientation Center in France, tells the Guardian’s Ian Sample. “What we are doing is pushing back the decision.”

The move caps off 30 years of debate, as the leap second has been highly controversial in the world of timekeeping. Leap seconds aren’t nearly as smooth of a fix as leap years are, and they can cause computer and website issues. Reddit famously crashed when a leap second was added on June 30, 2012. It’s “always been a problem,” Judah Levine, a former researcher at the NIST’s Time and Frequency Division, tells Scientific American’s Emma Gometz.

Instead of adding the entire second all at once, companies such as Google and Meta add the extra time in smaller segments in a tactic called “smearing,” according to the Conversation. It’s not a simple task, however, and companies that employ smearing have long lobbied to get rid of the leap second.

What’s more, with Earth’s recent spin acceleration, timekeepers around the world were facing the possibility of the world’s first negative leap second, in which a second would be subtracted from UTC. This sparked fears, akin to those surrounding Y2K, that our modern technologies wouldn’t be able to handle such a change.

“It’s never happened before, and therefore the software for that has never been tested,” Darryl Veitch, a researcher who leads the Timing Lab at the University of Technology Sydney, tells the Australian Broadcasting Corporation’s Ellen Phiddian. But others argued that it wouldn’t be much of a problem.
The vote means that in the future, UTC will be allowed to diverge from astronomical time more than ever before.

“Astronomers, Earth scientists and other users of Earth-orientation data will need to account for the growing offset when relating their observations and measurements to civil time,” Peroomian writes in the Conversation. As for everyone else, hopefully whatever technology rules everyday life when a leap hour does eventually come around will be better equipped for the time fix.

articles.title: Five dead, including suspect, in Oregon school shooting

paras.en: Oct. 15 (UPI) -- Three children, a teacher and a suspected gunman are dead following a shooting Thursday afternoon at an Oregon elementary school, authorities said.
Police identified the suspected shooter as a 16-year-old resident of Bend, a city of nearly 100,000 people in central Oregon, located about 130 miles east of Eugene.
Authorities said the shooting occurred at about 1 p.m. PDT at Silver Rail Elementary School.

The deceased victims have been identified only as children ages 5, 8, and 11, and a teacher. A 7-year-old student and a 54-year-old teacher were injured in the shooting and were transported to St. Charles Bend Medical Center with critical injuries, Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz told reporters during a press conference.
"This is a terrible tragedy and we are working hard to investigate this incident and get as much information as possible out to the public," Krantz said.
Dispatch received its first call about the incident at 12:59 p.m. from a person in a vehicle who said they had been shot at multiple times by a suspect with a long gun.

Dozens of calls followed, reporting that a shooter had entered the school, with the first responding officers arriving at the scene at 1:02 p.m., a minute after the school was directed to enter lockdown.
Moments after police arrived, an officer reported that the suspect had been shot by a community member who had witnessed the suspect enter the school and pursued the gunman.
Officers then entered the building and confirmed the suspect was dead, evacuated the facility and rendered emergency aid to those injured, Krantz said.
Including the shooter, five people were found dead at the scene, he said, adding that the families of the victims have been notified.
All students and staff evacuated from the school were transported to a local church used as a reunification site, authorities said.

"In August, every Bend police officer went through a full day of threat training at a local high school. And unfortunately, this is something we train for on a regular basis and we must," Krantz said.
The ensuing investigation will be lengthy, he said, adding that there will be a large police presence at the school for the next couple of days.
The website for Bend-La Pine Schools, the district that operates Silver Rail Elementary, states all schools will be closed Friday.

"This is something we never want to happen anywhere, but especially and particularly in our beautiful community here in Bend. There are not really any words that I can say to any of you that will make this better, but please know we are working hard to ensure we conduct a thorough investigation," Krantz said.

A preliminary investigation indicates the shooter gained access to the school by firing the long gun at locked doors, Krantz said, though he would not identify what specific weapon the suspect used nor how many shots were fired in the shooting.
It was also unknown at the time of the press conference what weapon was used by the member of the public who shot the suspected shooter or how many shots they had fired.

Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek, a progressive Democrat, thanked Silver Rail Elementary staff, parents and first responders who rushed to the scene. She also expressed gratitude toward the unidentified community member who engaged the suspected shooter, saying they "heroically intervened to save further loss of life."
"Your actions carry a heavy emotional burden and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you as well," she said.
She said all Oregonians mourn the shooting.

"This is a horrible day. No parent should have to have this kind of day and no community should have to live through this kind of day. And as we learn more about the children and the adults who have been killed or injured and their families and their loved ones we are going to do a lot of crying and we are going to cry together and we're probably going to cry privately," she said.
"We must come together and support each other, neighbor to neighbor, Oregonian to Oregonian."

articles.title: Movie review: 'Street Fighter' captures silly fun of video game

paras.en: LOS ANGELES, Oct. 15 (UPI) -- Street Fighter, in theaters Friday, is a fun live-action video game. The film celebrates the cartoonish absurdity of the game, though it exposes the limits of modern filmmaking while at it.
In 1987, Ryu (Andrew Koji) won the World Warrior Tournament. Then his master was murdered, so Ryu disappeared.
Even his best friend, Ken Masters (Noah Centineo), doesn't know where Ryu is. Ken became a popular fighter with endorsements and MTV promos.

When M. Bison (David Dastmalchian) puts on the second ever World Warrior Tournament in 1993, he invites Ken to lure Ryu. BIson has been trying to siphon off the psycho power of world class fighters but only Ryu has enough Hadouken for Bison.

If it weren't clear before, the mention of psycho power clarifies that Street Fighter knows what it is. Director Kitao Sakurai, with a script he wrote with T.J. Fixman and Dalan Musson, is not trying to explore the serious dramatic heft of the Street Fighter mythology.
These are beloved characters, and the film celebrates them. But, it celebrates them by having fun with them, not slavishly depicting the canon of the Capcom fighting game series.

All of the fight scenes are choreographed to accommodate the characters' special moves from the games. There may be some bona fide martial arts in between, but the point of the game was to use fighting moves that could not exist in real life. That's why it was fun to play.

There are plenty of real martial arts movies. There are far fewer live-action video game movies and even fewer of them are any good. So depicting Honda's (Hirooki Goto) Hundred Hand Slap and Dhalsim's (Vidyut Jammwal) Yoga Lance is unique.

This is also the first live-action Street Fighter movie that is actually about a fighting tournament. The previous two incorporated fights in their plots, but this one weaves a plot around the tournament.
Some of the characters get eliminated off-screen, but the film finds room for each character to have their moment.

Unfortunately, the main combat arena looks like a typically artificial screen environment. Whether green screen or LED, it's clear none of the fights were filmed in front of an actual live audience of extras.
Too many other scenes take place in dark chambers. Street Fighter is a colorful game. The film's costumes are good, at least.
At times, it tries too hard to be campy, from Ken's diva celebrity behavior to Bison's pseudo-wisdom. The 1994 Street Fighter was campy because of its sincere commitment to its own absurdity.
Dastmalchian even repeats the best line from Raul Julia's Bison in the 1994 Street Fighter, because it has become an internet meme more famous than the film from which it was derived.

Setting the film in 1993 comes with fun pop culture references and needle drops of the era. "Black Hole Sun," "Too Legit to Quit" and "Come Out and Play" are choice tracks. Although Meredith Brooks came later, her inclusion is fun too.

The film's introduction, and every character's flashback, are animated in anime style. The nod to animated Street Fighter animated movies and shows may overstay itself for viewers here for the live-action.

Street Fighter sets up a sequel that may or may not happen. It's bold, considering neither of the previous movies had sequels, but also it's not a dealbreaker. These kinds of movies always tease the next adventure, so it's part of the fun.

articles.title: 3 dead, 16 injured in fiery bus crash in Calgary, Canada

paras.en: Oct. 16 (UPI) -- Three people were killed and more than a dozen others were injured Thursday when a bus involved in a multivehicle crash erupted into flames in western Canada, authorities said.
A total of 16 people were injured, including a police officer who responded to the scene, authorities said during a press conference.
Of those injured, 10 were transported to local hospitals, one in critical condition and nine with non-life-threatening injuries.
Five others were classified as "walking wounded," meaning they were cleared at the scene but taken to the hospital for further assessment, authorities said.
Calgary Police Service Staff Sgt. Andy Woodward told reporters that the incident occurred at about 1 p.m. MDT in northeastern Calgary.

He said a city bus collided with a white car that then crashed into other vehicles. The bus continued through an intersection and hit a city bus parked at a bus stop, causing the second bus to erupt into flames.
That second bus then crashed into additional vehicles.
At least eight vehicles were involved in the crash, according to authorities, who said the cause of the incident remains under investigation.
The second bus was powered by natural gas, which authorities said was believed to be the cause of the explosion and the subsequent fire.
"I've worked as a police officer for 36 years and I think this is probably the biggest scene that I've worked on," he said.
Calgary Fire Department Chief Steve Dongworth told reporters that the incident occurred close to a fire house and that the blaze was "a relatively quick knockdown."
Because of the threat posed by the natural gas, the hazardous materials unit was called to the scene, he added.
"It was fairly involved. It wasn't a catastrophic fire, but it was a serious fire inside, particularly the liquid natural gas bus," he said, stating there was also a small fire in the initial bus.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney offered his sympathies to those affected by the crash online.
"To the families enduring this heartbreaking loss, to those recovering and to everyone grieving in the community, know that Canadians are holding you close in our hearts," he said in a statement.

articles.title: Zach Bryan’s ‘Young Manhood And Other Donatable Organs’: Stream It Now
articles.author: Jessica Nicholson

paras.en: Zach Bryan is back with new music, as his EP Young Manhood And Other Donatable Organs is out Friday (Oct. 16) via Warner Records.
The eight-song collection includes collabs with Lana Del Rey (“Lies”) and Turnpike Troubadours (“Plainsman”). Other tracks on the new EP include “Robot Killed The Working Man” and “Backwards.”

The fresh set marks Bryan’s first new music since his sixth studio album, With Heaven On Top, which released in January and debuted atop the all-genre Billboard 200 chart (soon after, he also released an acoustic version of With Heaven On Top). The 25-song album included “Plastic Cigarette,” which rose to No. 13 on the Billboard Hot 100 and No. 2 on the Hot Country Songs chart.

Bryan also just announced his upcoming stadium tour, the 2027 Young Manhood And Other Donatable Organs Tour, which will play 19 stadiums across North America and Australia next year. The tour will also feature support from John Fogerty, Ryan Bingham and The Texas Gentlemen, Vance Joy, Fey Fili, Gabriella Rose and Emma Ogier.

Tickets for his tour go on sale to the public Friday, Oct. 23 at 10 a.m. local time at zachbryan.com. The trek launches in North America on April 28 at U.S. Bank Stadium in Minneapolis, and will include stops at Chicago’s Soldier Field, Atlanta’s Mercedes-Benz Stadium and Philadelphia’s Lincoln Financial Field, before heading to Australia with performances at Melbourne’s Marvel Stadium, Sydney’s Accor Stadium and Brisbane’s Suncorp Stadium.
Bryan is a touring titan. On Billboard’s 2025 year-end Boxscore Top Tours chart, he ranked No. 13 globally with $159.6 million in gross revenue from 941,000 tickets sold.

Bryan earned a Hot 100 chart-topper in 2023, with the Kacey Musgraves collab “I Remember Everything.” In addition to With Heaven On Top, Bryan’s 2023 self-titled project also topped the Billboard 200.
Stream Young Manhood And Other Donatable Organs below.

articles.title: A$AP Rocky Brings Trippy ‘Shroom Clouds’ to Streaming Services for the First Time: Listen
articles.author: Michael Saponara

paras.en: A$AP Rocky’s Don’t Be Dumb – Disc 2 is finally on the way. The Harlem rapper set the deluxe project’s rollout in motion with the release of its lead single “Shroom Clouds,” which hit streaming services for the first time on Friday (Oct. 16).

Fans of the Mob frontman might be familiar with “Shroom Clouds,” which was previously titled “Mushroom Clouds” and saw Rocky perform it live at a 420 Weedmaps event and Governors Ball in 2021, as well as during his Amazon Music Live set in 2022.

A$AP Mob’s Hector Delgado helms the trippy production, while Rocky delivers a catchy chorus. “Super stoned, super high/ March, April, May, shroom, July/ Super stoned, super high/ See mushroom clouds in the sky,” he raps.
Speaking to Billboard earlier this week, Rocky confirmed that Disc 2 is on the horizon and detailed what songs will be making the cut while teasing the “next chapter” of his career.

“This music video — I don’t know if you remember that — was a fan favorite. I performed it a few times, but now we gonna re-release it,” he said. ”Disc 2 is all of the songs that I dropped that those alter egos didn’t get an album to live on, because the next chapter is right after that.”

Rocky’s Don’t Be Dumb arrived in January and served as his first LP since 2018’s TESTING. The experimental album debuted atop the Billboard 200 with 123,000 total album-equivalent units earned, which marked his first No. 1 in over a decade.

After wrapping up his European trek, the 38-year-old will be bringing the Don’t Be Dumb World Tour to five arenas across Australia and New Zealand this December. General tickets will be on sale on Friday at 1 p.m. local time.

articles.title: The Avalanches Press Play on ‘No Bad Memories’: Stream It Now
articles.author: Lars Brandle

paras.en: The release of a new Avalanches album is never a trifling matter.

With their debut 2000 album Since I Left You, the Australian electronic act let loose into the world a masterpiece. A peerless, timeless work, its creators meticulously sewed thousands of vinyl samples from the likes of Françoise Hardy, Sérgio Mendes, Raekwon, Wayne and Shuster, and even Madonna.
Fast-forward a quarter century, Since I Left You sits in a class of all-time classics. Fresh as a field of daisies.
Then, the “difficult second album.” The Avalanches recorded and rejected the followup. Years went by without a peep, save for the score to the King Kong stage musical and a batch of remixes.
When their full-length sophomore collecting Wildflower finally bloomed, 16 long years had passed. Wildflower went straight to No. 1 on the ARIA Albums Chart.
A third album travelled at comparative light-speed in 2020, We Will Always Love You, and later scooped the coveted Australian Music Prize, for the best album of the year.

Now led by Robbie Chater, Tony Di Blasi and Andy Szekere, The Avalanches rumble on with their fourth studio effort No Bad Memories. It’s an album stacked with tracks (31 of them) and guests, including Karen O, John Glacier, Jamie xx, Barry Can’t Swim, Rivers Cuomo and Mike Patton.

No Bad Memories (via Modular Recordings/Universal) explores “the magical intersection of advertising, memory and nostalgia,” reads a statement accompanying the project, “examining how jingles, sonic logos, commercials and the sounds of technology quietly embed themselves in our lives, becoming inseparable from the memories they soundtrack.”
Sonically, it’s a joy. With bounce and soul. The Avalanches manage to harness the energy of a litter of Pomeranians.

“Our album No Bad Memories is out in the world today,” reads a statement from the act. “We’re beyond grateful for the endless enthusiasm and love our music receives after all this time. Thank you for taking the time to listen, we hope you enjoy it.”

Timing out at 52 minutes, No Bad Memories is accompanied by a music video for “I Give Everything I Have 2 U” featuring Loaded Honey. Haley Joel Osment stars in the visual, shot by cinematographer Andrés Arochi (Long Legs) on location in Tokyo.

“Working with our friend Haley on the visual for this song was such a thrill,” The Avalanches say of the Sixth Sense actor. “A one-take scenario with Haley trying to navigate the Shibuya traffic, a huge camera strapped to the outside of his windshield is not a bad memory indeed!”
Avalanches dates are coming up in the United States, Continental Europe, the United Kingdom and Asia, followed by a tour of Australia in early 2027.
Stream No Bad Memories and watch the music video for “I Give Everything I Have 2 U” below.

articles.title: Daisy Edgar-Jones Reveals She Might Be “Slightly Deaf” in One Ear After Filming ‘Twisters’
articles.author: Carly Thomas

paras.en: Twisters has had a lasting impact on Daisy Edgar-Jones, but not necessarily in the way that she wanted.

During a recent episode of Jake Shane‘s Therapuss podcast, the actress revealed that she might be “slightly deaf” in one ear after shooting the 2024 action-adventure thriller, directed by Lee Isaac Chung.

“I think I still am slightly deaf in my left ear because there was so much debris and wind that was entering from a sharp left,” she said. “It was a windy shoot. It was quite ironic because we were shooting in Oklahoma and often would have to shut down filming because of an actual wind storm, to then recreate a wind storm once it’s passed. It was a wild experience.”

Twisters, which served as a standalone sequel, came nearly two decades after 1996’s Twister. The film followed Kate Carter (Edgar-Jones), a retired tornado-chaser and meteorologist who is persuaded to return to Oklahoma to work with a new team and new technologies. There, she meets Tyler Owens (played by Glen Powell), a content creator who posts his storm-chasing adventures.
The Sense and Sensibility star definitely wasn’t afraid to get in on the action, previously telling The Hollywood Reporter that she got “a bit addicted” to doing stunts after filming Twisters.

“It was so stunt heavy and I’d never done really proper stunts, so I was so curious to see how they were going to achieve a lot of the action sequences, but I’m a bit addicted now, I’ve got the bug,” Edgar-Jones said in 2024. “It was so much fun. I mean we had a phenomenal stunt department who really just helped to immerse us in it, also keep us safe. Most of the stunts were sort of being battered by wind, rain and debris so it was definitely an interesting filming experience.”

articles.title: ‘Grey’s Anatomy’ Boss Meg Marinis on Texas Spinoff, Ellen Pompeo and Season 23 Premiere Cliffhangers
articles.author: Jackie Strause

paras.en: [This story contains some spoilers from the Grey’s Anatomy season 23 premiere, “Collide.”]
Twenty-three seasons in and Grey’s Anatomy is not going anywhere.

“No one has said anything to me about when the last season of Grey’s is going to be,” showrunner Meg Marinis tells The Hollywood Reporter when chatting about the new season, which returned Thursday night.

That doesn’t mean she doesn’t ask. As the person charged with running ABC‘s long-running, hit medical drama, Marinis wants to be prepared for whenever that day comes. “But it really seems like they want it to be a collaborative decision with Shonda,” she says of show creator Rhimes. “The series has done so much for the studio and network, they [would] want to do it right. And they’re not ready.”

They are in expansion mode, instead. Grey’s, whose previous spinoffs were Private Practice and Station 19, is getting a new spinoff this 2026-2027 season that will be set at a rural West Texas medical center. Marinis co-created and is writing the untitled series with Rhimes, and Grey’s star/executive producer Ellen Pompeo is also exec producing the new show.

“It’s related to Grey’s, but its stories are going to be different,” teases Marinis, who counts Texas as her home state. She’s always wanted to explore “what’s happening in medical deserts,” as well as “the disparity between people who can afford excellent healthcare and the people who can’t.” The latter comes up in the season 23 premiere of Grey’s, “Collide,” which welcomed Pompeo’s Meredith back to the hospital after the season 22 ending that sparked wedding bells for her and Nick (Scott Speedman).
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: When Grey’s returned, one month had passed since the exits of beloved doctors Teddy (Kim Raver) and Owen (Kevin McKidd), and the episode’s ending sets up more than enough threads to follow in coming weeks. Below, Marinis talks about all of it, including more on the spinoff, how she really feels about medical show competition (we’re looking at you, The Pitt) and how much Pompeo will be on screen this season.

Congrats on the news about the Grey’s spinoff! We know that the series (which doesn’t yet have a name) will premiere sometime in the 2026-2027 season and that it’s set at a rural West Texas medical center — “the last chance for care before miles of nowhere.” You and Grey’s creator Shonda Rhimes are co-creating and writing the show, and Ellen Pompeo is executive producing. How has it been working on this second show amid the Grey’s schedule?
(Laughs.) I have a great team here at Grey’s that I lean on, and Shonda’s doing the new one with me so it’s easier when there’s two of us!
Where are you in your work on the spinoff? Is there a timeline?

We are working away. I can’t say much, but we’re far enough along where I’m really, really excited. We’re digging into the actual communities and true stories of what happens out in rural West Texas. There’s so much going on there that I haven’t seen on TV. I’m thrilled to be able to dive into that world. It’s so different from Grey’s. It’s related to Grey’s, but its stories are going to be different.
Previous Grey’s spinoffs were Private Practice and Station 19, but this feels a world away from Grey’s‘ Seattle hospital. Were there lessons learned from those two shows that you are applying now?

The only lessons are good lessons from those two. They were very successful spinoffs with hardcore fan followings. I loved both of them. This one is something dear to my heart [Marinis is from Houston, Texas] and being on a medical show like Grey’s, and hearing a lot about what’s happening in medical deserts, it’s hard to show that in Seattle. I’ve always been really interested in showing it, and in doing a small town show in Texas.
Will Grey’s launch the Texas show in-show this season?

We have thoughts based on airing schedule and things like that, but we’re still working it out, also because there are so many things going on on Grey’s, I want to make sure to do it where it’s servicing both shows equally.
How do you view this within the larger Grey’s franchise? Does it signal anything about the flagship?

It’s just expanding the flagship. No one has said anything to me about when the last season of Grey’s is going to be. I think it’s never! I always ask and they’re like, “Not now!” You always want to be prepared, as a showrunner of a season 23 show, that you’re aware of when that decision is going to happen. But it really seems like they want it to be a collaborative decision with Shonda. Because the series has done so much for the studio network, they want to do it right. And they’re not ready.

We last spoke after last season’s finale and the exits of Kim Raver and Kevin McKidd’s Teddy and Owen, respectively, which you said was a difficult decision and related to the budget, which is something shows are experiencing across the industry. How did you approach season 23 with your very large ensemble? Will there be characters we see more or less of? Are you still feeling those constraints?

Not yet. I mean, you always feel the general constraints of a large ensemble and what’s going on in the industry, so I’m mindful of how many times we go out on location and things like that. So the general constraints, yes. But no, those conversations usually are when they approach me later in the season — to drop that news on me!

We’re in a positive place right now. On the show, the hospital is having some budget issues as well, but that’s mainly continuing on what we started last year about what’s happening to research funding and funding for healthcare in general. Now Grey Sloan is just feeling more of it.
How much time has passed since the finale to start this premiere, and how is the hospital rebounding from losing veteran doctors, Teddy and Owen?

It’s been about a month. We did that for a couple of reasons. I’ve done direct pickups for the past couple of seasons and I wanted to do something different, to start stories in different places. Also, I didn’t have Nick [Scott Speedman] available to me at the beginning of this season — he was left in the hospital in the finale, and he was busy on [his ABC show] R.J. Decker. That played into the decision. And I really wanted time for this VIP floor to come into play. We didn’t see that floor when we left the season last year.
