paras.en: [An edited transcript of the interview follows.]
Hey Erika, thanks so much for taking the time to talk. I know you’ve been busy!

Hey! And, yeah, you could say that. On September 22 we announced the first microbe we made for Mars, which was a really cool milestone. It’s a useful and safe thing for us to send to Mars and to use to prepare for the first human mission. It’s the very first step toward this bigger picture—this really inspiring vision of terraforming Mars and making it a habitable, beautiful place.
So this microbe—what’s so special about it, and what exactly is it supposed to do?

What’s cool about it is that we’ve engineered it so that it can directly use the nutrients in Martian regolith, water and processed atmosphere—which is really useful! The idea is that you can go to Mars, and you can feed it dirt, water and air, and use it to build bioplastic houses for astronauts.

Yeah. This is a derivative of a terrestrial bacterium called Cupriavidus necator, which naturally produces bioplastic kind of for the same reason that when you eat too many doughnuts, you put on weight in your hips. When this organism has too much carbon around, it creates these big vacuoles of bioplastics, which is a class of materials we’re all familiar with in everyday life. We use them to make everything from compostable cups to 3D printing filament—and that’s essentially how we’d like to make houses on Mars.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: So the astronaut houses would have these 3D-printed panels that hold up the structure, and then it would have this plastic lining that holds in the pressure so that you can breathe and that also shields you from radiation.
We’re calling this engineered microbe sPL.001—a special strain made by Pioneer Labs, and the very first of several, in fact. We’ve got plans for four more.

Something to help you build houses seems like a pretty good first step. You mentioned there are more microbes in the works. Presumably they’d do other things—because if we’re trying to build some kind of self-sustaining habitat on Mars, we need obviously more than just big domes made of bioplastic, right?

Absolutely. So let me give you some context first: we’re called Pioneer Labs, and that name is referring to this ecological idea of a pioneer species. On Earth, nature is really good at taking hostile environments—like after a volcanic eruption or a forest fire—and rebuilding a complex ecosystem one step at a time, and the very first steps are executed by really hardy organisms called pioneer species.

They’re often lichens. My favorite, though, is dandelions. They can grow in these really harsh environments, and their presence makes that environment more hospitable for a wider diversity of organisms.

I need to be clear, though: this very first microbe, sPL.001, can’t grow outside on its own on Mars, and that’s important because we don’t want to contaminate Mars accidentally. Yet it’s useful for making these habitats that more stuff can grow in. We think there are four other microorganisms that could complement this first one; altogether we think this could scale up to let us make arable land that’s suitable for agriculture—growing beautiful green plants and making food.
So we’ve talked about this first one for helping to build shelters on Mars. What about the others?

We have candidates for the others now, so nothing is finalized yet, but the idea is each additional microbe type can be another step in this ecological succession for Mars. So consider this a sneak peek.

About half the team is now working on windows. Because if you want to make greenhouses, for instance, you need transparent materials to let the sunlight in. And ideally you’d be able to manufacture those at scale with biology. Imagine growing microbes in a pond that secrete something that floats to the surface, and then you can peel what will become a nice big greenhouse panel right off the top.

And the other half of our team is working on getting rid of the perchlorate in Martian regolith. Perchlorate is a compound that’s poisonous to humans, and there’s so much of it there that Mars dirt can be poisonous to humans, too, as it is now. But there are microbes we’ve found that are able to eat that toxin and degrade it. We’ve found some actually that can eat it directly out of simulated Mars dirt—just add water! So now we just have to push the concentrations up, because Mars has more perchlorate than any organism on Earth has ever experienced naturally. And just like with all our other work, we’re using evolution to try to make an organism that can tolerate it.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Okay. And so the whole idea is that by growing these things locally—by living off the land, so to speak—you’re able to be more efficient and cost-effective, and ultimately self-sustaining, because you don’t have to bring everything from Earth?

Yeah. The reason we haven’t already done a human mission is that humans, with all our radiation shielding and food and so on, are just so heavy. And it’s just so hard to get that much mass to Mars to allow people live for a period of time, and then it’s even harder to bring them back. So it’s incredibly helpful to use resources that are on-site. And indeed, that’s what frontier civilizations have always done.

I want to be upfront about my own biases here: I think this is such a cool idea. But as with pretty much every other aspirational project related to human spaceflight, let alone otherworldly settlement, this one has its critics, too. And I think if I could summarize the sorts of criticisms I’ve seen, it would be three interlinked questions: Why terraforming? Why Mars? And why now?
That is, assuming these bioengineered bugs could also be really useful on Earth, why not just focus your efforts here?

You and I and everyone who’s ever lived is really lucky to live on the one planet we know of that has a functional biosphere. That’s why we’re here breathing, right, because we have a whole planet worth of photosynthesis that’s cranking out oxygen for us all the time. We just call it “nature” and tend to take it for granted.

When we go to space, nature is the one thing that we’re missing. It’s the thing we leave behind when we go away from Earth. Well, I love the biosphere, and I think we should bring it with us. I would love for any future humanity that ventures off into the stars to have more interaction with all sorts of delightful types of life rather than less.

This runs counter to typical visions for the future, I think, where there’s this tendency to think that progress means less nature and fewer trees and we all live in cities with big skyscrapers. That makes me sad, and I don’t think it has to be that way, and so I’m trying to fix it.

Mars specifically is this fascinating world in part because it’s almost like a long-lost twin of Earth. Four billion years ago, both planets had liquid water. And Mars, to this day, even after its climate has been substantially altered, still has all the raw materials for life in abundance in a way that the moon doesn’t and that even Venus doesn’t. Venus doesn’t have a lot of water left, and Mars does—it’s got a whole northern hemisphere that’s permafrost, with huge amounts of buried ice. If only we could warm it up, Mars might become a pretty nice place to live.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: And I think that the instinct to go searching outward is just a thing people have. Not everyone wants to be an explorer, but for people who do, Mars is this incredibly intriguing target. And whoever goes first, I’d love for them to have flowers when they live somewhere that’s not Earth.
Flowers on Mars! Maybe it’ll be a dandelion, even.
That would be Pioneer species number six, ha.

Your announcement of sPL.001 made quite a splash, of course. I’m wondering, though, outside of the millions of people who saw your social media post or watched the slick promotional video introducing Pioneer Labs, what the reactions have been from some of your peers in bioengineering, planetary science, astrobiology, and so on. Has it been mixed?

So far, the reaction has been overwhelmingly positive. And I think that’s partially because we took our time preparing for this. We didn’t just announce that we’d engineered the first organism for Mars. We also released a paper showing how we did it, a second paper about a proposed planetary protection framework for thinking about the risks of actually sending such things to Mars and a third paper offering a complete techno-economic analysis for the use cases.

We’ve shown sPL.001 would be extremely dead if it gets outside on Mars, so, in many ways, this is less risky than sending a human complete with a diverse and complex microbiome on her skin and in her gut. And we’ve shown how this could actually be useful, right—not just how to grow the organism but all of the equipment that has to surround it in order to feed it, heat it, purify products from it and actually build houses. We’ve quantified how much all that mass is, how many launches you’d need to get it to Mars and the total footprint it would have.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: So we really put our best work into trying to introduce this idea to people in a way that shows why it’s so cool and valuable but also is thoughtful about the ethics. This work has value even if we never terraform Mars. Practically speaking, this is just a good thing to do for the first human mission.

And so—especially on X, where this really went viral—I think there were more people who applauded the fact that we had also released a paper about the ethics than there were people who were like, “Er, we should never go to Mars.”
You’d have to go over on Bluesky to see more of those reactions, I think.

Let me try to “both sides” this a bit. I want to double down on the very valid point you’re making: if we’re trying to weigh risk and potential impact, landing a single human—or even a single piece of human excrement, let’s say—on Mars, that’s an orders-of-magnitude bigger deal than landing an enclosed bioreactor.

But I also inquired about the reactions of your peers because peer review is important in science, and it’s not clearly something that’s happened for any of those three papers you mentioned. There’s a disclaimer near the end of each one that basically says this has not and will not be submitted for peer-reviewed publication because that goes against the “open science” policy of the Astera Institute, a billionaire-backed nonprofit for incubating transformative science and technology that partly funded the work.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: So with that in mind, I have to ask: Who is independently evaluating this stuff? You’re saying that it’s safe to send sPL.001 to Mars, and in the second paper that you mentioned, yes, you’re proposing a protocol for ensuring that nothing bad can happen in terms of biocontamination. But who’s validating these assertions? That seems like a pretty important step in the process, so I’m wondering why you’re skipping it.

My hope is for us to get to share the science we’re doing openly and very quickly. And I should say that we at Pioneer Labs don’t make NASA policy—and that NASA, in fact, isn’t the only organization that makes policy for the whole world, either. There are a lot of discussions that have already been happening about how to update things like planetary protection frameworks for the upcoming new era of human interplanetary spaceflight.

We clearly need new frameworks. Historically, NASA policy has been to stringently sterilize everything that goes to Mars, and you obviously can’t do that for a living human! So we’ve decided to throw our hat in the ring and make suggestions about what that new framework could look like. The goal of the Planetary Protection paper we released is for it to be discussed by COSPAR [the Committee on Space Research], which is the main body that makes policy suggestions to the world. My co-founder Una Nattermann will also be on NASA’s newly convened M-FORCE tiger team, which will make recommendations to COSPAR. Our goal here is to participate in the discussion.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: And similarly, we’ve made suggestions about what it could look like to do the first biomanufacturing on Mars. We call this a “reference architecture,” which is a type of paper or engineering document that the space science community often uses. These aren’t usually published in a traditional science journal. I think space science is a discipline that certainly sometimes uses peer review to great effect, but not all of the science happens specifically through journals.

We do currently have funding from the Astera Institute, which believes very strongly that the current peer review journal system is incredibly toxic for science and for innovation. I don’t think anyone really disagrees with that. But as you say, there is this downside to being forced not to participate in traditional journals, which is getting this question about who certifies it. We have, ahead of time, already shared these papers with various colleagues, some of whom are acknowledged in them for the feedback they provided.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Also, there’s no stamp of approval, including from a journal, that means something is definitely right, which means even if we did send it to a journal, that doesn’t mean it’s better. We’re just trying to do the best science we can, and part of the challenge is we have to chart new territory about what it looks like to do this without this kind of crutch of journals dictating what is correct—which we all know to not be true anyway.

I should say the question doesn’t necessarily come from an adversarial place. You’ve stated elsewhere that Pioneer Labs is hopeful to hit the 2031 launch window for Mars. And that’s practically tomorrow, as far as developing a payload and securing a rocket ride is concerned, right? So it would seem in your best interest to try to bring everybody on board, so to speak, as quickly and fully as possible by addressing any significant concerns that exist.
Relatedly, maybe, I wonder if there’s anything you could tell me about what that 2031 mission would notionally look like?

Yeah, I agree. Flight testing is incredibly difficult in terms of the amount of prep that needs to go into it and the magnitude of engineering that needs to go right. That’s even more true for a Mars mission because Mars is so far away. So we’ve released that third paper, the reference architecture, in part because we’re interested to see how the space science community reacts, especially to different possibilities for what the first flight test could look like.

Here’s one example of what the first flight test could be. Wouldn’t it be so cool to go to Mars and do a search-for-life experiment there, where you take a scoop of Mars dirt, you add water, and you incubate it and see if anything grows? Because Mars had nice liquid water back when there was very nascent life on Earth, and there seem to have been giant impacts ping-ponging around the solar system—so maybe one of those impacts sent something to Mars, and maybe today it’s not growing because Mars is too harsh. Maybe it’s dormant in the soil or the ice. One way to find it would be an “enrichment”-type search-for-life experiment. You could sample some dirt or ice, see if it grows anything under more hospitable conditions and do the same after adding fertilizers to see if it’s nutrient-limited.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Now in order to do that experiment correctly, you do need a positive control, so you need to know that your device worked and that stuff can grow in it, and here is where the first microbe we engineered comes in. You could bring sPL.001 as your positive control and confirm that, yes, this organism that’s been carefully selected to die if it gets outside on Mars can in fact grow in a sealed container using the nutrients in Mars dirt.

I think this would be great for everyone. Like, the best-case scenario is you find life on Mars—but even if you don’t, by testing this organism’s growth on Mars you’ve now derisked this big thing that would allow you in the next test to actually use it for engineering and biomanufacturing.

So this is one possible example of a pretty small first step toward deliberately sending terrestrial life to Mars. It’s safer than sending a human. It has some basic science benefit. And it can be scaled up to do things like testing a larger bioreactor—depending on how big a step the space science community feels comfortable taking and which scientific risks we want to address and eliminate.

Speaking of scientific risks, the loudest critics I’ve seen of this work are astrobiologists interested in finding life on Mars who worry that something like sPL.001, if sent there, still poses unacceptable chances for contaminating the planet and irreparably sabotaging the search. Then there’s the more extreme ethical criticism of possible terraforming, perhaps best summarized by the late, great Carl Sagan: “If there is life on Mars..., Mars then belongs to the Martians, even if the Martians are only microbes.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Yeah, I don’t agree with that second one.

In general, human astronauts on Mars would massively expand our ability and flexibility to search for life. The search for life doesn’t end because you’ve sent humans. Here on Earth, we still go out and look for dinosaur bones even though we already know they’re there. On Mars, the search could and would continue, which reflects something good about humans. We’re curious about our surroundings and we want to know more, and I think that’s something we should encourage.

It’s really complicated, of course, but here are some simple facts to think about. Here on Earth, we have a word for being vegetarian. But we don’t even have a word for trying not to eat microbes, because it’s totally infeasible! There are many different types of life deserving of our respect, but that doesn’t mean a very simple life-form on Mars should unduly eliminate any possible benefit humans could gain by going there.

I think we’re overdue for a big-picture shift in our approach to Mars, which we’ve been treating solely as this object of scientific study, with incredibly strict protocols for what you can send there and how sterile it needs to be—because this isn’t the only relationship that we could have with Mars, right? Like, humanity could live on Mars, and in that scenario, you then have to weigh the potential value of the scientific knowledge of the planet’s history and its former or extant life against the value of humanity having another home.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: And just practically speaking, I do think humans are gonna go to Mars someday, so we have to figure out how to do it in a thoughtful way that sets us up for success in living there, as well as in understanding the planet and its history. I don’t think the answer is to get totally tied in knots and paralyzed by the ethics.

That brings me to my final question. You’ve stated in various places that you hope within your lifetime to look up at the little red dot of Mars in Earth’s sky and see that it’s slightly tinged with green—presumably from imported terrestrial life. What do you think is the biggest hurdle to overcome for that? Would it be scientific, technical, political, ethical?

If you had asked me this question two years ago when we began, I would say the biggest hurdle is a technical one. That’s why I was excited to work on sPL.001—because I perceived myself as someone who knows how to solve science problems, and I was looking for a big juicy target to sink my teeth into.

And now when you ask me, I actually do think maybe the hurdle is more social and political in a similar way to how on Earth we struggle to figure out the collective action puzzle of who pays for addressing climate change. Part of why I like working on the Mars case is that I think in some ways it’s much simpler. There’s no NIMBYism on Mars. And I’m hopeful that together, both the technical and the social things that need doing to make humans on Mars happen could be useful right here on Earth, too.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

articles.title: Google’s quantum Willow chip may be able to grow ‘magic states’

paras.en: Quantum computers promise exponential computational power by processing many possibilities simultaneously. But the machines we have today are still far from this ideal. For one, their bits, called qubits, are prone to frequent errors, and as a result, quantum computers are limited for now. To overcome errors, the machines need to tap into so-called magic states—and scientists at Google Research think their quantum chip could help get them there. In a new study published today in Science, the researchers show how to supply magic states more cheaply using a gardening-inspired technique called cultivation.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Traditional computers build every calculation from a few simple logic gates, such as AND, OR and NOT. By contrast, “quantum computers have their own analogy of these operations called the Clifford gates,” explains Emma Rosenfeld, a researcher at Google Quantum AI and the study’s lead author. Clifford gates, however, can be imitated by a normal computer. “But there is one particular gate that unlocks the quantum computer’s power,” Rosenfeld says. “Physicists call it a non-Clifford gate, most often a T gate.” This extra gate is produced using a magic state.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: A quibit in a magic state is prepared in a very specific blend of the states 0 and 1 (occupying a mixture of states is a specialty of quantum computers). Fed into a calculation, it is used up to perform the extra gate, and any flaw in the state becomes a flaw in the gate. “It has to be made very, very precisely,” Rosenfeld says.

If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.

The standard recipe to make magic states is called distillation, and it creates fewer, more accurate quantum states from many imperfect ones. “You can have up to 95 percent of your quantum computer being spent just generating these high-fidelity magic states,” Rosenfeld says. To bypass this bottleneck, in 2024 her colleagues at Google Research proposed an alternative technique called cultivation, which works on a single state.

Using Google’s Willow chip, Rosenfeld’s team encoded a rough magic state in a few qubits and then measured it. Measuring a quantum state typically collapses it, forcing it into one of two possible answers. So instead of asking the question, “Are you 0 or 1?” which collapses the quantum state to either of those two options, the team asked, “Are you the right magic state: yes or no?”

States that pass this test are then spread across more qubits for stronger protection, hence the gardening name: the state starts small, gets checked and then grows. Without cultivation, about four attempts in 1,000 produced a faulty state. With it, errors fell by roughly 40-fold. The experiment used 54 physical qubits out of Willow’s 105.

“The Google experiment shows that cultivation works in practice,” says Kenneth Brown, director of the Duke Quantum Center at Duke University, who was not involved in the study. He notes, however, that the technique relies on a quality assurance step that rejects low-quality states, discarding 92 percent of attempts.

The result is still far from what practical applications demand. For example, using a quantum computer to break the current RSA-2048 encryption employed in website security, banking and electronic ID cards would require magic states that would fail only once in 10 billion tries. To simulate molecules, a use Rosenfeld says is more attainable, we would need such states with only one error in a million to one in 100 million. Right now the team stands at roughly one error in 10,000 attempts. Still, the new work represents a step in the right direction, she says.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: “We’re more galvanized than ever to get to these near-term scientific applications,” Rosenfeld says.

articles.title: What happens when you lose your voice?
articles.author: Laura Sanders

paras.en: A voice matters not just to the person who is speaking, but to the people listening, too. A study on moms and their daughters demonstrates the power of a voice by showing that moms’ voices reduced a measure of stress in the daughters. The same wasn’t true for texting.

In the second episode of The Deep End: Talk to Me, you’ll hear more about the ripple effects created by a lost voice. Jules Rodriguez says that as his voice slipped away, it felt like he was fading. But could a new, more realistic digital voice step in and change his story?
Hear about a tough medical decision Jules and his family were facing, and whether a sophisticated voice clone could influence his choice.

[reporter audio] Hi, this is Laura calling. This is Laura Sanders from Science News. Is now an OK time to talk about your paper coming out? I would love to start with just the very big picture question of why you did this study. Why did you do this study? What were you hoping to find?

Laura Sanders: I’m a neuroscience reporter with Science News, which means I spend a lot of time reading research papers about the brain. One of my very favorite scientific papers, and there are a lot of them, so this is really saying something, is a study published way back in 2012.
[voice] Researchers at the University of Wisconsin have found the sound of a mother’s voice triggers a physical response.

Sanders: Sixty-eight girls, all between the ages of 7 and 12, came into a lab in Madison, Wisconsin. For the experiment, these girls were asked to tell a story out loud and then perform a tricky subtraction problem in their heads. The whole time, they were being watched and evaluated by the researchers. I get sweaty just thinking about it. OK, so after that ordeal, the girls were separated into groups. Some girls got to see their moms in person and talk with them after their stressful performance. Some got to talk to their moms on the phone. Some got to text with their moms. And some just had to sit alone wondering what had just happened to them.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Later on, when researchers measured stress hormones in the girls, they found something startling. The girls who had talked to their moms, either in person or on the phone, had lower levels of the stress hormone cortisol than the girls who had just texted or had no contact.
The authors conclude that there’s something especially soothing about hearing a mom’s voice, some alchemy of familiar and calming sounds that a daughter’s brain wants to hear.
[voices] So call your mother. Good advice at any time.
Sanders: In a full circle sort of way, I tell my own mom about the study after calling her to complain about a bunch of stuff.

[phone call] The talking mattered. The texting did nothing. The phone call and the in-person lowered their cortisol levels. Well good. So, the voice. That’s what you just did for me. That’s the deal. Well I’m glad. That’s just excellent. Thanks, Mom. All right. Yeah, talk to you later. Bye. Bye.

Kate Nilson: And, you know, it’s so funny. Every time I’m with my parents, I think I need to record their voices. How can I be in this world and not have their voices recorded? So I need to get on that.
Sanders: That’s speech-language pathologist Kate Nilson, a person very familiar with the specialness of voices.
Nilson: Just for all the reasons we just talked about, right? So when I get stressed out, I can just listen to my own mom’s voice. I mean, I’m in my 40s and I still need my mom, so.
Sanders: I mean, yes, listen to the nice comforting sounds my mom makes on the phone when I go through my laundry list of problems.
[phone call] Yeah. I hear it in your voice. Oh, that’s sad. Get me some phone numbers and I’ll make calls. That’s pretty intensive stuff.
[intro] Hey mom, can I tell you something? The voice is absolutely an integral part of your identity. Do you want to talk? That added layer of it being you. Hello? Your voice. Hi! Your voice is you.

Sanders: This desire to capture voices that have special meaning to us, to hold them close, is a perspective I heard over and over. That’s because voices don’t just mean something to the people who make them. Voices mean just as much to the people hearing them.
Welcome to this second episode of The Deep End, Talk to Me, from Science News. I’m Laura Sanders, and today we’re going to explore what it means to lose the ability to talk.
Sanders: Jules Rodriguez has a unique perspective on the human voice.
Jules: Your voice is different because it’s a big part of your identity. I knew early on, my voice may disappear, so we made sure to record it while I still had it.

Sanders: Jules is a podcaster, former science teacher, comedian, husband, and dad who lives in Miami. He was diagnosed with ALS in 2020. The progressive nature of the disease means that people start losing strength and the ability to move, all while their brains and cognition are unaffected. That loss includes the muscles that are required to talk.
MA: I still remember the first time. This was in 2022, the summer of ‘22, that I heard the first little crack in his voice that let me know something’s changing.
Sanders: That’s Jules’ wife, MA. When I was first connected to Jules and MA, I learned they had a podcast called The Couple Shift.
[podcast]: Well, hello there, everyone. Welcome to episode zero of our brand new podcast.
Sanders: About their marriage and themselves as they dealt with life, careers and family. I started listening at the beginning.
[podcast] My name is Maria Aleandra. I am a life and business coach, and this is my amazing hubby. Julian Tomas. And I’m a former teacher and amazing husband. He sure is.
Sanders: They were so sweet with each other. Playful, teasing, funny, yet sincere and loving. Listen to them being cute.

[podcast] So I got frustrated. And by lash shout, it’s like an outburst. It’s a [beep] what the hell? You know, that kind of deal. Do we have to bleep out? We do. Yes. Sorry. Gosh darn it. I should know better. Is that what you’re going to tell me? Yeah, that’s what my look is saying right now.

Sanders: They started recording their podcast in 2019, before Jules’ ALS diagnosis. As I listened, moving from early episodes to later ones, I got this feeling of time zooming past, just so fast I couldn’t catch it.
[podcast] We went to go see the doctor again to get his final assessment, I guess.
Sanders: Unlike the Jules and MA from early episodes, I already knew the twist, the gut punch of what was coming.
[podcast] Unfortunately, the news is that he believes it’s ALS or SMA, which is spinal muscular atrophy. It was a really hard hit in the balls. And it’s been a very difficult couple weeks.
Sanders: As I moved through the episodes, I started hearing a difference in Jules’ voice. His voice got slower, weaker, fuzzier. I asked him recently what that was like.
Jules: It’s strange with the podcast because you can hear my real voice slowly decay till we stop.

MA: Yeah. It’s really this archive of what he sounded like, little by little as it changed. And it was, yeah, like very disarming to get to that moment. And then you begin to get used to it and you sort of work around it and appreciate that it’s still there. Yeah, that was really, really difficult for me.
Sanders: Jules and MA even talk about this very process on their podcast, of having a record of their voices through time. Here’s a clip from 2024 when Jules could still talk, but with difficulty.

[podcast] To me, it’s so weird. Yes. We’re such different people and different mindsets and just different, well, lack of experience and dealing with all this. It’s so freaking beautiful, though, because you can see the whole evolution of us. It’s a living legacy of a life lived. A living legacy. A living legacy of a life lived. You and your words. Me and my words.

Sanders: In those last episodes, I was hearing the change in Jules’s voice. I was also hearing his emotions. I was hearing his weariness. Jules compares the process of losing his voice to a Back to the Future moment that any person raised in the 80s will remember. It’s when Marty sees a photograph of his family in a timeline that no longer exists.
[movie audio] Just as I thought. This proves my theory. Look at your brother. His head’s gone. It’s like he’s been erased.
Jules: For me, it felt like I was fading away. Like when Marty McFly was seeing his family fade away in the picture he had in Back to the Future.
Sanders: A piece of Jules was fading away. A really important piece that tells other people something about his internal state, his emotions, where he’s been, and what’s happening now.

Voices are packed with all sorts of signals. Sometimes they’re a little bit unexpected, like when a guy you don’t know all that well says “about” and you realize he is Canadian. Sometimes they’re absolutely obvious, like a strong Southern drawl. Voices can signal energy levels, whether your allergies are acting up, where you were born, and how old you are. Here’s Greg Bryant of UCLA.

Bryant: Cues are any kind of property that might predict something about the sender. You can tell, for example, how big a person is by hearing their voice. You can tell if they’re male or female generally by hearing their voice. You can tell if they’re old or young, right? So there’s all these kind of basic properties of a person that are indexed in a voice.
Sanders: Voices can carry emotions too. A smile, for example, has subtle sound cues.

Bryant: There’s a slight increase in pitch when you smile and then you change what are called formants. The formants are structures in the speech signal underlying what your perception of vowels is. They’re energy bands that are associated with resonating chambers in your throat and in your mouth. And so when you are moving your tongue around and changing your lips and doing other things going, ahowowowow, you’re changing the formants. That’s the resonating bands of energy in the voice. So when you smile, then the formants change a little bit. And it’s detectable. It’s subtle, but you can hear it for sure.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Sanders: See if you can detect it here. It’s Jules introducing an episode of their podcast in 2020.
[podcast] So my wife comes to me today, and she says, babe, I have diarrhea.
Sanders: So setting aside the content he chose to share, which was a bold choice, you can hear the grin in his voice.
[podcast] Before we get into that, though, I also want to say one quick thing. Happy birthday, my love.

Sanders: That’s because his smile pulled his lips slightly upward and changed the shape of the air coming out, thereby changing the sound of his voice. All of these signals in the voice exist because voices are made by bodies. Bodies that move, smile, change, grow older, get sick. Our voices are actually a stunningly sophisticated bit of biology.

Jessica Pietrowski: You think about how, you know, we’re just talking, we’re just voicing, we’re barely even thinking about what we’re doing, but actually upwards close to a hundred muscles are being used.
Sanders: That’s speech-language pathologist and scientist Jessica Pietrowski of UC Davis.

Pietrowski: When we go to voice, we have to take a breath. Breath comes up, the diaphragm is contracting to get that breath. Breath comes up below the vocal folds, these tissues here, vibrates the vocal folds, creates a tone. That tone comes up through the oral cavity and other spaces, and resonates. And then you have to articulate it, and, and make the sounds clear and sharp. And then you have speech. And so really, you know, we’re not thinking about this as we’re doing it, but it’s incredibly complex and intricate and really an incredible human feat.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Sanders: Right now, as I say these words to you, I’m pushing air out of my body and using my muscles to move my diaphragm, face, throat, and mouth to make tiny ripples of sound shaped with a precision far below the level of my conscious perception. This mechanical, biological, physical feat is what allows me to shape air into sounds that then move to your ears.
Sergey Stavisky: So this is a very engineering-y perspective, but one thing about voices, it is our fastest means to communicate what we’re thinking.
Sanders: Sergey Stavisky co-directs the UC Davis Neuroprosthetics Lab, focused on using technology to replace or repair parts of the damaged nervous system.

Stavisky: So it’s actually, if you step back, kind of magical. So you have some idea in your mind, and your brain is able to take that idea, form it into language. So that’s already a complicated step. And then it’s able to move almost a hundred muscles in your tongue, in your jaw, and in your larynx to vibrate air in this exquisitely precise way.
Sanders: But then, even more magic happens when those vibrations move into someone else’s ear.

Stavisky: Those vibrations are going to fly through the air and they’re going to hit someone else’s eardrum and it’s going to vibrate that, and it’s going to vibrate the hair cells. And it’s going to send a bunch of nerve signals to their brain and they’re going to first make sense of the sounds you’re making amidst all of the other sounds, whether there’s background conversation or a train rumbling by or a dog barking. But then beyond that, they’re going to not just hear the words you just said, but remember all the previous words, put them together and like get the same idea in their brain. I mean, it’s telepathy through mechanical means.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Sanders: Telepathy through mechanical means. When you step back and think about it, it’s an absolute marvel. So here I am floating these ripples out toward my microphone. And then through more technology, they are reaching you, where your own amazing machinery senses those ripples and turns them into meaning. So with these ripples, I’m putting something into your mind.

Stavisky: We have this like shared scaffolding of understanding where I can pretty much visualize anything I want and with enough words, make someone else put that into their mind. And I think that’s a really remarkable ability. And that’s like the basis of civilization and learning and science and connection.

Sanders: But there’s something happening before all of this muscle moving and air rippling, and it’s something that Stavisky just mentioned. My words first started taking shape somewhere else. They started in my brain. Certain clusters of my synapses fired as I thought about what to say. This intricate path from brain to muscles to sculpted air is behind every word we say.
Casey Harrell: Hello there and thanks for being patient with me as I was running a bit late.
Sanders: When I met Casey Harrell on Zoom, I asked him to tell me a little bit about himself.

Casey: That is both the easiest and the hardest question to answer, right? So my name is Casey Harrell, and I am 47 years old. I grew up in the Atlanta area and have lived in the Bay Area for the past 23 years, most of them with my wife, Levana, and our seven-year-old daughter, who is going on 17. I spent most of my professional career as a climate campaigner and have went all over the globe, fighting companies who are destroying the earth and trying to bring some justice to our planet and the people who inhabit it.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Sanders: Like Jules, Casey has ALS. The disease has taken a lot from him. He can no longer move most of his body. That includes speech muscles.
Casey: I began to lose my ability to talk shortly after my diagnosis in 2020.
Sanders: With time, he could no longer talk clearly enough to be understood.

Casey: Then it became a slow-motion car crash of multiple years before almost no one would be able to understand me. A few other friends who were around often would be able to understand some of what I was saying. I relied upon my assistant and my wife to basically serve as my translators to other people. I did not go anywhere, even a video call without them, either one or both.

Sanders: Casey’s life in the Bay Area was changing in difficult, almost impossible ways. Like Jules, Casey had received an ALS diagnosis in 2020. Like Jules, he had a kid, a partner, a career, a big, full life. And then wham, life threw them one of the biggest curveballs you can imagine. These two men, separated by 3,000 miles, Jules in Miami, Casey in Oakland, were both facing big losses. And one of the biggest of all was their ability to talk.
Speech-language pathologist Kate Nilson walks me through some of the standard approaches that she uses when she’s working with people who face similar futures. There’s a process called voice banking.

Nilson: So voice banking is the idea of recording specific sentences that you might not actually say in real life, but predetermined sentences that you record that give the software the combinations of sounds that it needs to make a computer voice that sounds like you.
Sanders: That process has actually improved quite a bit in recent years.

Nilson: When I started doing this, it was 1600 sentences. Now it can be an app on your phone that you do at home. It can be a website that you go to. The software that I use most of the time is 50 sentences. It can be done in like 15 minutes. It’s really come a long way and the voices are pretty darn amazing in how how true to the person they are. But they are still a computerized voice, right? They’re they’re they’re taking combinations of sounds and splicing them together. So it sounds computerized.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Sanders: Voice banking has the benefit of being flexible. This voice can say anything a person wants, but it sounds off. There’s another approach. This one’s called message banking.

Nilson: So the idea of message banking is we just record an entire message. So instead of using that computer voice to say, “Good night, honey, I love you,” we can just record someone saying, “Good night, honey, I love you,” with their voice, like, with their true inflection and meaning.
Sanders: The beauty of these messages is that they capture the quirks of a person’s voice.
Nilson: You know, I live in Minnesota, and so there’s a lot of ooftas and doncha knows, and those kinds of things that do not come out right when you type them into a computer.
Sanders: Nilson encounters these sorts of sounds when she’s helping people save recordings of their voice for the future.
Nilson: You gotta get all those right sayings with the right, you know, “o’s” in them.
Sanders: These recorded messages are often things like an inside joke with the exact right timing or a favorite little nickname for someone special.

Nilson: It can be really emotional. And that’s, when you’re recording the sentences that are predetermined and they’re not sentences that you would normally say, that can be easy. But when your family has written down a list of meaningful words that they want to hear in your voice and you know that you’re recording it because you might lose your voice, that can be really emotional. And it can be hard. And I fully understand that, but we can also have fun with it.
Sanders: Pre-recorded jokes come up pretty often when people are choosing what messages to preserve for later use. And swear words come up surprisingly often too, Nilson tells me.

Nilson: I had someone come in just the other day, and they had an entire category of recorded cuss words. So that’s important. Well, right? I mean, you don’t want them to be monotone when you’re frustrated. You want the right emphasis to come out on that.
Sanders: It takes the sails out of it for sure if it’s monotone.
Nilson: Yeah, exactly. I mean, that’s communication, right? That’s important communication. So I guess it doesn’t really surprise me anymore, but it’s fun nonetheless.
Sanders: She says some people come to her with entire folders of swears, folders that she refused to share with me for the story, by the way.

Nilson: The best part is it was a swear folder with all these different swear words and like different sayings and whatever. And then just one of them had a call-out to a specific person. And I was like, what did that person do to you that he’s the only one that has a specific? And then he laughed and he typed out, “If you knew him, you’d understand.”
Sanders: All of these quirks, the swears, the smiles in the voice, the familiar jokes, all of these things make a particular voice special. Jules created a banked voice. He didn’t love the result.
Jules: What I learned from banking my voice was that it really wasn’t my voice. It was more like a robot trying to emulate my voice. It had no emotion or tone behind it.

Sanders: This was a problem because it got in the way of something Jules wanted to do. The turmoil of ALS forced some clarity for him about what he wanted out of life, what he wanted to spend his time doing. And one of those answers, it turns out, was comedy. After his diagnosis, while he still had his voice, he performed stand-up a few times.
Sanders: But as his voice got harder to use, things changed. Jules could still talk, but it took a lot of work, especially since he was often using a mask for extra oxygen.
MA: He was wearing the mask pretty much the entire time. So his voice was very labored, because you have to take the breath in to utter anything. So it was very choppy. But he did have a voice.
Sanders: With time, a live performance with his original voice became impossible. The next option was to use a banked voice, but that wasn’t good enough for a comedy performance.
MA: So then he started to lose his voice and he was like, I don’t, you know, I can’t pull this off with a banked voice because it’s so robotic. It’s monotone. You can’t really do it.
Sanders: Jules couldn’t pull off a comedy show. But could there be a different way, a different voice?

I’m going to step back here and give you more context about Jules and about ALS. ALS is progressive and relentless, which means over time, more and more of the motor neurons in the brain and spinal cord are affected, and symptoms get worse.

And though this progression varies quite a bit from person to person, the median survival time after an ALS diagnosis is about 30 months. Time is short here. This diagnosis forces big choices about how to live and what a person wants their remaining time to include, for them and for their family. In the middle of everything else going on, Jules was facing a choice that many people in his situation must confront, whether or not he would get a tracheostomy.
That’s a procedure in which doctors place a tube in the throat. This tube is then connected to a ventilator that breathes for a person.

The procedure can leave a person unable to speak again, with whatever residual voice they might have left. Now, we have spent this episode on what it feels like to lose your voice. Jules was losing his. So it might seem like this part of the decision wouldn’t matter all that much. But to a person who’s losing their voice, and to their family, this moment marks an end point. It’s a hard stop.
MA: He was someone who didn’t want to do a tracheostomy. He was opting for, once I’m done, that’s it. And that was our plan.
Sanders: As Jules and MA confront this decision, could a different sort of voice change the story?
Jules: So when I first heard my cloned voice, it felt like I reappeared. When my wife first heard it, she cried because of how close it sounded like me before I lost my voice.
Sanders: This is The Deep End. Talk to me. I’m Laura Sanders. If you like this podcast, tell your friends and leave us a review. It helps the show a lot.

Send us your questions and your comments at podcasts@sciencenews.org. The Deep End is a production of Science News. It’s based on original reporting by me, Laura Sanders. articles.title: A duo goes against the tide to explain an origin of human endurance
articles.author: Elizabeth Pennisi

paras.en: Two researchers may have opened floodgates on the debate over why humans can run marathons, swim the English Channel or dive a hundred meters and back on a single breath and their ape cousins can’t.

Humans evolved endurance for feats like these not just by running down prey on the African savanna, but also by diving for food in lakes or coastal waters, the duo propose September 17 in PaleoAnthropology. The hypothesis adds complexity to a decades-old theory that puts the drivers for evolution exclusively on land. But it coexists with a history of pushback for any water-related ideas.

The work is causing ripples among anthropologists. “I could not work out [at first] if this was groundbreaking or dumb,” says Christian Tryon, a paleoanthropologist at the University of Connecticut in Storrs.

In 1960, researchers came up with what’s been called the aquatic ape or waterside hypothesis, which suggested that our ancestors evolved longer legs and other adaptations from swimming for their suppers in watery habitats. Popularized in media accounts but not adequately vetted in peer-reviewed journals, the idea was shunned by the scientific community as additional fossils pointed away from a life in water. More recently, the dominant theory has been that it was landlocked human ancestors who gradually developed our remarkable endurance. “There’s been this reluctance to really think about anything sort of water-related as important in human evolution,” Tryon says.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Yet evolutionary anthropologist Josephine Joordens, a self-professed “water person” who trained as a marine biologist, had long wondered whether coastal life was vital to the evolutionary process, because it provides easy access to both water and land resources. Joordens combined forces with Erika Schagatay, a physiologist at Mid-Sweden University in Östersund, to formulate what they call the “dive first, run later” hypothesis.

Schagatay — herself a freediver — has spent decades observing and monitoring modern sea foraging people such as the Ama in Japan and the Sama-Bajau in Southeast Asia. Joordens studied fossil evidence and combed the literature about aquatic activities. Our evolution “was likely a very complex and very dynamic process,” says Joordens, of the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology in Leipzig, Germany.

They propose some Homo species wound up shallow-water diving repeatedly about 2 million to 3 million years ago, much the way the Sama-Bajau do today. These people spend four to six hours per day repeatedly diving several meters deep to catch fish and collect shellfish and other food. They evolved bigger spleens than their non-diving counterparts and, it seems, enhanced respiratory and cardiovascular capacity. They have the ability to “pace” breathing periods and breath-holding to avoid fatigue. In our ancestors, that could have paved the way for the cardiorespiratory stamina needed in modern endurance running, Schagatay says.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: These Homo divers evolved heavy bones to help stay underwater and downward facing noses to keep water out, the two suggest. They eventually passed those endurance-boosting traits on to other populations with lighter bones and a more terrestrial lifestyle.

The study “shows there is a lot of evidence” for forage diving as an early evolutionary driver, says Leslea Hlusko, a paleobiologist at the Centro Nacional de Investigación sobre la Evolución Humana in Burgos, Spain.

This idea is not a retread of the aquatic ape theory, says Christopher Ruff, a biological anthropologist at Johns Hopkins School of Medicine. “Occasional aquatic foraging is quite a different proposal“ from the discredited theory’s primarily aquatic existence and should be taken seriously, Ruff says.
Not everyone thinks the dive first idea holds water.

Multiple factors work against the idea that diving could have helped humans become better endurance runners, says Daniel Lieberman, a paleoanthropologist at Harvard University. He argues that endurance diving does not require an enhanced aerobic capacity: It slows the heart rate, whereas running speeds it up. He disputes how and why heavy bones arose; they could have developed in people who used their bodies for heavy work and not because such bones helped divers with buoyancy issues. Nor is the downward pointed nose meaningful given that many diving mammals have forward facing noses. Other reasons, such as keeping the air in nostrils moist, were probably more important in selecting for this feature, he says.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: What’s more, many people around the world have long relied on running down game for food, says archaeologist Eugène Morin of Trent University in Peterborough, Canada. “Diving is costly and the [caloric] returns are low,” so early humans would not choose to dive if other foraging opportunities existed, he argues.

Critiques aside, “the simple ‘ape walked out from forest to savanna’ story clearly does not cut it anymore,” says Pascal Gagneux, a biological anthropologist at the University of California, San Diego. Coastal routes around Africa, along Africa’s lakeshores and out of Africa “must have played a huge role” in human evolution, Gagneux says.

The pair knows they risk the ire of their peers in presenting this “dive first” hypothesis, but Joordens says, “we are both in our early 60s and we both have beautiful careers, so we thought ‘whatever happens, happens.’”
And Tryon ultimately found the paper worth the read. “If nothing else, it gets people thinking and it gets people looking.”

articles.title: To turn invisible, we need to tweak the path light travels
articles.author: Sofia Caetano Avritzer

paras.en: It’s pretty hard to fight an opponent you can’t see. That’s what makes Invisible Woman an invaluable member of the Fantastic Four. She can disappear in the blink of an eye and take out entire factions of enemies, all while her adversaries kick and punch empty air.

Characters with invisibility powers — Marvel Comics’ Invisible Woman (aka Sue Storm), H.G. Wells’ Invisible Man and The Incredibles’ Violet Parr — can do all sorts of cool things. Escape embarrassing situations. Snoop on other people. Go places where they’re not allowed.
Short of a theoretical invisibility cloak, that kind of lurking is impossible for us. But some animals can hide in plain sight by turning nearly transparent.

Invisibility is useful for animals that spend a lot of time in places with no good hiding spots, such as the air or open ocean, says Kate Feller, a visual ecologist at Union College in Schenectady, N.Y.

The secret to invisibility is all about light. “The way we see things is when light is reflected back off of an object onto our eyes,” Feller says. The more light that can pass through something undisturbed, the harder it is to see that thing.
Light can’t easily pass through most animals, but those with nearly invisible body parts have tricks to get around this hurdle.

Animals get their colors from pigments, compounds that appear as different colors depending on which wavelengths of light they absorb and which they reflect. Green pigments, for instance, reflect green light and absorb all other colors. Invisibility requires getting rid of these colorful compounds.

Most baby fish lack pigments at first, helping them hide from predators. Some species stay see-through their whole lives. One is the ghost catfish (Kryptopterus vitreolus). With a body that’s fully transparent from gills to tail, it looks like a floating head from afar.

It’s hard to hide every body part, though. Eyes need light-absorbing pigments to see. And even clear stomachs will show up if animals eat colorful food. A ghost catfish eats only small bits of food and its long, thin, tubelike stomach stretches out a meal, helping the organ stay hidden, says Qibin Zhao, a physicist and materials scientist at Shanghai Jiao Tong University in China. Blood can’t be transparent either due to the iron-rich hemoglobin molecules that carry oxygen. So up close, the ghost catfish’s blood vessels are still visible.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: But even pigment-free objects are not entirely invisible. Light travels at different speeds through different materials so will bend or bounce when it goes from one material to another. That can create a shine, like sun reflecting off a puddle.

That’s not a big problem for a glasswing butterfly (Greta oto): Its wings have fewer reflective scales than other butterflies’ wings. The wings are also covered in tiny wax bumps that make light’s transition from air to tissue more gradual, so light passes through the wings mostly undisturbed.

Invisible Woman uses a completely different vanishing trick than real-life transparent animals. Instead of letting light pass through her, she bends lights rays to completely avoid her body. The rays never even touch her, so they are not reflected or absorbed, making her invisible to any onlookers.

In 2006, scientists proposed that this same logic could be used to create an invisibility cloak. But in practice, a material that perfectly bends light rays is expensive, hard to make and can divert only a narrow band of light at a time. That’s just enough to make a single-colored object disappear but not an entire human.

And there’s another problem: With no light getting into the cloak, a person inside can’t see out. Luckily, Sue Storm has the ability to use cosmic rays to see while she’s invisible, allowing her to protect the world from supervillains like Doctor Doom.

articles.title: One Common Eating Habit Is Linked to Higher Risk of 2 Liver Diseases
articles.author: David Nield

paras.en: Published in Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology, the comprehensive study analyzes data from 199,155 individuals, with a median age of 59. Participants are enrolled in ongoing health research and complete food and lifestyle questionnaires every 2–4 years.

The authors of the new study, from Oregon Health and Science University (OHSU) and Massachusetts General Hospital, found a 28 percent higher risk of cirrhosis and a 36 percent higher risk of MASLD among late-night eaters compared to those with more standard eating times.
Late-night eating was defined as eating "after bedtime" or "between dinner and bedtime."
To put that increased risk into perspective, cirrhosis remained uncommon, with 315 cases among nearly 200,000 participants over the follow-up period.
The researchers think that our circadian rhythms, the built-in cycles that sync our bodies with daytime and nighttime, may explain the link.
"A few studies have hinted at this idea, but this is among the first long-term analyses to explicitly draw the connection to fatty liver disease," says hepatologist Robert Wilechansky, from OHSU.

"We know the liver is very much in tune with the body's circadian rhythms. So we're interested in changing the timing of eating in a way that could make a difference in health, without changing the composition of what people eat."

The median follow-up time for the study was 16 years, with adjustments made to factor in variables including age, body mass index (BMI), and physical activity. The late-night eating association remained significant after the adjustments.

While the study can't prove direct cause and effect, and other factors might be at play here – sleep timing and quality weren't accounted for in this analysis, for example – the researchers suggest that the different way the body processes food at night could be having an influence.
We all have multiple circadian clocks running in our bodies, and the liver does its own timekeeping as well as connecting to the main circadian rhythms.

It's possible that the liver isn't prepared to efficiently deal with food late into the evening, resulting in more fat building up and blood sugar levels rising – though these ideas will need further testing.
"Our findings add to the growing body of literature linking late-evening eating patterns to adverse metabolic and liver outcomes," write the researchers in their published paper.
"This relationship is biologically plausible; higher evening caloric intake may lead to obesity and metabolic derangement via decreased insulin sensitivity and lower energy utilization at night."

Further research could look at exactly what late-night eating consisted of – in this analysis the snacking time was logged, but not the snack – as well as measuring indicators like blood sugar and liver fat more directly.
An OHSU team that includes Wilechansky is already recruiting for a more thorough clinical trial.
"The effects of late-evening food intake on liver disease should be further studied in diverse populations, incorporating liver imaging and markers of liver disease severity," write the researchers.
"Confirmation of these results would have the potential to impact best practices in nutrition for chronic liver disease."

MASLD, also known as fatty liver disease, is when metabolic issues (such as obesity) lead to fat building up in the liver. In some people, it can cause scarring, which can then lead to cirrhosis, where the liver is permanently damaged and can eventually start to fail.

Knowing more about how these two conditions are triggered or exacerbated will help with prevention and treatments going forward. It could be that one way of reducing your risk of liver disease is as simple as being disciplined about eating times – an easier ask than a diet or exercise regime.
"We are seeing over and over again that the timing of behaviors, whether it's sleep, eating or exercise, really matters," says sleep and circadian physiologist Andrew McHill, from OHSU.
The research has been published in Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology.

articles.title: Millions of Americans Use Cannabis to Help Them Sleep. It Could Be Doing The Opposite.
articles.author: Peter Dockrill

paras.en: An estimated 22 million Americans currently use cannabis as a form of sleep aid, and almost one in four says they're likely to try the drug to help them sleep.
But despite the widespread view that cannabis can help you get a good night's rest, the evidence is starting to suggest otherwise.

In recent years, scientists have linked cannabis to sleep disruption, and reviews have suggested that the drug may in fact have an overall detrimental effect on sleep quality, despite what many users might think it's doing for them.
A new study in JAMA Network Open highlights this paradox, suggesting a possible disconnect between the sleep quality of cannabis users and their own perception of how well they're sleeping.

In an analysis of 35 years of observational data from participants in the Coronary Artery Risk Development in Young Adults (CARDIA) study, researchers found that cannabis use was associated with multiple objective measures of poorer sleep.
Subjectively speaking, however, based on questionnaires in which participants rated their sleep quality, there was no sign that people using the drug felt their sleep was negatively affected.
"This study challenges the common belief that cannabis helps people sleep better," says epidemiologist Thanh-Huyen T. Vu from Northwestern University.
"Our findings suggest cannabis may actually be associated with poorer sleep quality, even if people don't perceive those changes."

The CARDIA study began recruiting participants in 1985 from four sites across the US, ultimately involving over 5,000 people. Participants completed several follow-up examinations as the study progressed, with the ninth follow-up assessment taking place in 2022 (year 35 of the study).

In the new analysis by Vu's team, the researchers looked at data from 1,266 participants in the CARDIA cohort, including 1,128 people who self-reported sleep assessments at the end of the study period.

They also analyzed objective sleep data from 891 participants who used a wrist-worn tracker to monitor their sleep for seven days, with 753 people contributing to both the subjective and objective analyses.

After adjusting for age, race, sex, education level, smoking and alcohol use, and other factors, the researchers found that greater lifetime cannabis use was associated with a lower sleep percentage (the amount of time asleep during sleep periods), higher sleep fragmentation, and waking up for longer periods during sleep.

Each additional year of cannabis use was linked with poorer sleep, equating to 10 percent higher odds of a low sleep percentage (spending less than 85 percent of the sleep period asleep), 4 percent higher odds of high sleep fragmentation, and 21 percent higher odds of prolonged waking up (spending at least 30 minutes awake in total during sleep periods).

Among recent cannabis users (participants who had consumed the drug within the last 30 days), cannabis use was linked with longer sleep duration (20 minutes extra per night), but also with lower sleep percentage, higher sleep fragmentation, and longer periods of waking up, compared to people who had never used the drug.

Yet despite all these objective measurements indicating poorer sleep, neither lifetime nor recent cannabis use was associated with the participants reporting lower subjective sleep quality, the researchers note.
"This was one of the most interesting findings," says Vu.
"The wearable device detected more nighttime disruption among participants with long-term cannabis exposure, but the participants themselves generally did not report worse sleep."

While we can't be entirely sure why this is happening, the researchers say the discrepancy could have important public health implications, especially given cannabis's popularity and reputation for being a supposed sleep aid.
"Individuals may not perceive declines in sleep quality or may interpret longer sleep duration as improved sleep despite objectively poorer sleep," the researchers write in their paper.
"Thus, cannabis-related sleep disturbances may go unrecognized."

The researchers note that previous studies examining cannabis's effects on sleep quality have shown mixed results, but they observe that many studies have been limited by small samples, short follow-up periods, or cross-sectional designs that didn't examine how long-term cannabis use is associated with sleep quality, and few studies have incorporated objective sleep data.
Further, some studies examining the effects of medical cannabis may have only looked at sleep as a secondary outcome, or may have assessed it alongside other factors that may affect sleep.

"One possible explanation for the small improvement in subjective sleep quality observed in these medical cannabis studies is that most participants were from clinical populations with pain, cancer, or sleep disorders," the researchers write.
"Cannabis may improve perceived sleep quality by reducing symptoms that interfere with sleep, even when objective sleep measures show little or no change."
Given this was an observational study, the research can't establish whether cannabis use directly caused the sleep disturbances people experienced.

The researchers also acknowledge a number of limitations, including that they didn't track cannabis potency or timing relative to sleep, and while their study did incorporate objective sleep measurements, they were only able to access a week's worth of sleep tracking data (over a study period lasting decades).
They suggest future long-term studies with objective sleep assessments will be able to better clarify how cannabis use influences sleep.
In the meantime, if you really want to aid your sleep, the research team says following the conventional advice is probably a smarter choice than consuming cannabis.

"Keep a regular bedtime, make your bedroom cool, dark and quiet, and avoid looking at phones and other screens right before bed," says neurologist and study co-author Kristen L. Knutson from Northwestern University.
"It can also help to establish a calming routine before sleep, such as reading, meditating or taking a shower."
The findings are reported in JAMA Network Open.

articles.title: New Electrical Test Can Help Identify Signs of Extraterrestrial Life in Space
articles.author: David Nield

paras.en: If there is extraterrestrial life out there, it's certainly done a great job of staying hidden so far (at least as far as the official scientific consensus goes).

International researchers led by a team from the University of Osaka in Japan have now developed a new electrical technique for spotting signs of life outside of Earth's atmosphere – and it promises to be simpler than current approaches to alien detection.
The method focuses on amino acids, the building blocks of proteins, and details have been published in Nature Communications.
Amino acids come in two mirror-image forms, the L-form and the D-form, and the balance between them in a sample can indicate if the amino acids were produced by something living or non-living.

In scientific terms, the form (or 'handedness') of an amino acid is called its chirality, and the technique developed by the researchers can spot this chirality using a tiny gap between two gold nanowires.
"The single-molecule detection and discrimination of molecular chirality demonstrated here highlight a fundamental advance in chemical sensing," write the researchers in their published paper.

Amino acid chirality can already be analyzed using an approach called liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry (LC–MS), but the instruments needed for it are bulky and require large samples and multiple chemical processes. It's not ideal for packing onto the back of a lunar buggy.
What the researchers have developed here is much, much smaller.
The two gold nanowires are barely separated from each other and create an electrical tunneling current between them – a quantum effect where electrons 'leak' across the gap.

As a solution containing amino acid molecules is dropped onto a microchip holding the gap, the current changes in a way that can be measured, revealing which forms the amino acids are in. Machine learning was used to identify the L-form and D-form molecules from the electrical spikes.

"By combining our nanogap tunneling technique with artificial intelligence, we were able to distinguish between the L and D-forms of amino acids with over 80 percent accuracy," says bioengineer Takahito Ohshiro, from the University of Osaka.
"This is the first discrimination of amino-acid chirality at the single-molecule level."

It's going to take more testing and development to get this into a fully working amino acid scanner that can be added to an astronaut's toolkit, but the researchers have already tested the approach against current methods.
"We analyzed natural samples from the Murchison meteorite in Australia and soil samples from the Atacama Desert in Chile," says nanotechnologist Masateru Taniguchi, from the University of Osaka.
"Our method was comparable to traditional methods, as both were capable of capturing the major features of amino acid composition."

Of course, this isn't a long-range alien life detector – we're still going to have to get hold of samples to test – but the nanogap device promises a relatively straightforward, compact testing mechanism that needs less preparation and requires fewer molecules.

Potentially, it could be fitted on probes and rovers without a human crew, perhaps beaming back news about signs of life discovered on distant moons and planets. That's still some way off for now, though.

One of the challenges researchers need to overcome next is preparing the sensor for molecules that it may not have come across before or been trained on. The machine learning component here was crucial to the study's success.

The technology is now ready to be taken further – for chemical analysis on Earth as well as beyond – and if we do one day detect life on an alien landscape, this might be the approach that makes the discovery.

"These results establish a targeted single-molecule electrical approach for chiral amino acid analysis and provide a foundation for future applications to study chemically complex samples, including those relevant to astrobiological research," write the researchers.
The research has been published in Nature Communications.

articles.title: Rare study reveals a striking divide inside an Alzheimer’s patient’s brain

paras.en: Rare study reveals a striking divide inside an Alzheimerâs patientâs brain

- A rare examination of an Alzheimerâs patientâs brain revealed that regions cleared of amyloid plaques had remarkably little of the harmful tau buildup associated with memory loss, while neighboring areas showed extensive damage. The discovery suggests that removing amyloid may have lasting protective effects and could help slow Alzheimerâs progression, especially when treatment begins early.

An unusually detailed examination of an Alzheimer's patient's brain has revealed striking differences between regions where treatment successfully removed harmful amyloid plaques and areas where those plaques remained. The regions cleared of amyloid showed little or no buildup of tau tangles, another protein abnormality strongly associated with brain cell damage and declining memory. Nearby areas that still contained amyloid, however, showed much higher levels of tau and evidence of continued neurodegeneration.

paras.en: The discovery offers rare evidence from a human brain that removing amyloid plaques may provide protection against other damaging processes involved in Alzheimer's disease (AD). The results also suggest that clearing amyloid thoroughly, particularly early in the disease, could help limit tau accumulation and slow the progression of brain damage.

Researchers from the Perelman School of Medicine at the University of Pennsylvania presented the findings at the 2026 Alzheimer's Association International Conference. The study was also published in JAMA.

"Seeing both disease patterns side-by-side in the same brain gave us a rare opportunity to understand how amyloid removal affects other proteins that contribute to Alzheimer's disease," said co-senior author David Wolk, MD, co-director of the Penn Memory Center and director of the Penn Alzheimer's Disease Research Center. "The findings provide some of the clearest human evidence to date that anti-amyloid therapies may limit the accumulation of tau and slow the brain changes that lead to memory loss and cognitive decline."
